overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Standard APR removes the rectum, anus and sphincter complex and creates a permanent end colostomy; there is no restorative colorectal anastomosis.
Plan for abdominal and perineal surgical phases, potentially prolonged lithotomy or a turn to prone jackknife.
Presacral bleeding, long exposure and perineal reconstruction can increase access, warming and analgesic requirements.
Recovery planning must address perineal pain/wound risk, bladder function, stoma assessment and positioning-related injury.

sources.label: StatPearls: abdominoperineal resection (2024)
Multidisciplinary guidance: well-leg compartment syndrome after pelvic surgery (2019)

sections.title: Extent, permanent stoma & reconstruction
bullets: Confirm abdominal approach, perineal approach and whether a flap will reconstruct the pelvic/perineal defect. A flap reconstruction can substantially change case duration, positioning, incision distribution and postoperative pressure restrictions.

Standard APR differs from LAR: the anal sphincter complex is removed and intestinal continuity to the anus is not restored. Additional bowel work may still be performed in a complex case, so obtain the actual operative plan rather than assuming there can be no other anastomosis.

sources.label: StatPearls: abdominoperineal resection (2024)

sections.title: Preoperative reserve, bowel preparation & aspiration
bullets: Review functional reserve, cardiopulmonary disease, anemia, renal function, nutritional status and recent intake/losses. Bowel preparation, poor intake, vomiting and an existing ileostomy can produce clinically important depletion before an apparently elective operation.

For elective colorectal resection, the ASCRS/SAGES guideline typically recommends mechanical bowel preparation combined with oral antibiotics, not mechanical preparation alone. The surgical protocol and contraindications determine the actual regimen; do not extrapolate this to acute obstruction.

Clear liquids up to 2 hours before anesthesia belong to an appropriate elective fasting pathway, not to patients with obstruction, impaired emptying or other elevated aspiration risk. Carbohydrate-loading evidence in this guideline primarily concerns patients without diabetes; individualize rather than applying it automatically.

Confirm recent antithrombotic exposure and the postoperative thromboprophylaxis plan before choosing neuraxial analgesia. An elective enhanced-recovery pathway must be modified for sepsis, significant coagulopathy or hemodynamic instability.

sections.title: Lithotomy, Trendelenburg & well-leg compartment syndrome
bullets: Document positioning with the surgical team. Pad vulnerable areas, avoid compression at the fibular head and calf/popliteal region, keep joints within a tolerable range and reassess access and pressure points after final positioning.

Prolonged lithotomy and head-down positioning can impair lower-leg perfusion, particularly when the legs are elevated above the heart. Minimize unnecessary duration and pressure; discuss safe opportunities to reduce leg elevation or head-down tilt during lengthy pelvic operations.

Postoperative severe leg pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, weakness or paresthesia requires urgent assessment for well-leg compartment syndrome. Preserved pulses do not exclude it. Do not dismiss the symptoms as routine positioning discomfort or attribute them automatically to neuraxial analgesia.

sections.title: Prone perineal phase & team turn
bullets: Some surgeons perform the perineal portion prone in jackknife after the abdominal phase; others remain in lithotomy. Agree on the sequence before induction and account for drapes, stoma, lines and any epidural during the turn.

After repositioning, verify airway security, ventilation, IV/monitor function and pressure protection. Keep the abdomen and chest appropriately supported and protect the face and other vulnerable contact areas.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum, ventilation & robotic access
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce respiratory compliance and functional residual capacity and can increase airway pressure, atelectasis and CO₂ absorption. Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted/ideal body weight, not actual weight in obesity, and individualize PEEP and respiratory rate.

Reassess tube depth and bilateral ventilation after positioning and insufflation. Cephalad diaphragmatic movement can promote endobronchial migration; rising pressure is not automatically bronchospasm.

Secure the airway, IV connections and monitoring before docking because access may become restricted. Agree on how the team will obtain emergency patient access and coordinate all subsequent table or patient movement with the surgical/robotic team.

Sudden bradycardia during insufflation can reflect vagal peritoneal stretch. Notify the surgeon, interrupt the provoking insufflation and support circulation while evaluating other causes; persistent instability requires more than treating the monitor number.

sections.title: Perfusion, fluids & blood loss
bullets: Aim for adequate perfusion without either fluid overload or undue restriction. Balanced chloride-restricted crystalloid is generally preferred for elective maintenance and boluses; routine colloid use does not have a demonstrated benefit in the colorectal recovery guideline.

Differentiate volume depletion, anesthetic vasodilation, positional effects and bleeding before repeatedly giving fluid. Treat vasodilation appropriately when volume is adequate; avoid prolonged hypotension and tailor pressure goals to baseline and organ risk.

Use trends in pressure, clinical perfusion, losses and laboratory data rather than a single CVP or urine-output value as a direct volume measurement. High-risk patients or substantial losses may justify invasive monitoring and goal-directed assessment.
Plan access and blood availability for the surgical extent and patient reserve. Reoperative or deep pelvic dissection can bleed substantially despite a minimally invasive skin incision.

sections.title: Presacral bleeding & operative escalation
bullets: Dissection near the presacral venous plexus can cause significant bleeding. Anticipate access and blood availability according to tumor extent, reoperation, prior treatment and reserve rather than assuming an end colostomy makes the operation low risk.

Communicate rapidly about blood loss and hemodynamic changes and use laboratory-guided replacement and resuscitation appropriate to the evolving situation. Maintain warming and reassess postoperative support requirements.

sections.title: Multimodal analgesia & regional options
bullets: Establish opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia before induction when possible. Acetaminophen and an appropriate regional or local technique can reduce opioid exposure; tailor the plan to incision, renal/hepatic function, bleeding risk and chronic opioid use.

Thoracic epidural is an option for open colorectal surgery with an acute-pain service, but is not routinely recommended for laparoscopic resection. Hypotension, motor effects, urinary catheter needs and anticoagulation timing influence the choice.

Abdominal-wall blocks address somatic incision pain but do not reliably replace treatment of deep visceral or perineal pain. Match coverage to the actual incisions rather than offering the same block for every colorectal operation.

NSAID-associated anastomotic-leak signals are molecule/class dependent; diclofenac has the strongest signal in the guideline discussion. Do not label all NSAIDs either universally safe or universally prohibited: reconcile anastomotic, renal, bleeding and cardiovascular risks with the surgical pathway.

sources.label: ASCRS/SAGES: enhanced recovery after colon and rectal surgery (2023)

sections.title: Antibiotics, temperature & nausea prevention
bullets: Confirm that surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis has been given at the appropriate preincision time and that redosing follows the selected drug, elapsed time and blood-loss protocol. Oral bowel-preparation antibiotics do not replace perioperative IV prophylaxis.

Use active temperature monitoring and warming for long operations and significant exposure or fluid administration. Normothermia and sensible glucose management belong to the infection-prevention pathway, not just the final emergence check.
Use multimodal PONV prophylaxis tailored to patient and anesthetic risk, and minimize avoidable opioids. Retching, delayed oral intake and rescue sedation can undermine early recovery.

sources.label: ASCRS/SAGES: enhanced recovery after colon and rectal surgery (2023)
ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Perineal pain, flap protection & wound risk
bullets: Abdominal-wall analgesia alone may leave substantial perineal pain. Plan analgesia for both operative fields and consider neuraxial or other regional strategies only when appropriate to coagulation, hemodynamics and postoperative care.

Prior radiation, malnutrition, obesity, diabetes and steroid exposure can increase perineal wound problems. Coordinate positioning and pressure avoidance with the reconstructive team rather than applying generic sitting or lying instructions.

sources.label: StatPearls: abdominoperineal resection (2024)
ASCRS/SAGES: enhanced recovery after colon and rectal surgery (2023)

sections.title: Emergence & enhanced recovery
bullets: Assess ventilation, hemodynamics, temperature, pain and airway swelling before extubation, particularly after long Trendelenburg positioning. When a neuromuscular blocker was used, verify quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

Routine nasogastric tubes are discouraged after uncomplicated elective colorectal surgery. This does not prohibit therapeutic decompression for obstruction, persistent gastric stasis or a specific surgical indication.

For suitable elective patients, offer early oral intake and progressive mobilization according to the recovery pathway; the guideline supports a regular diet within 24 hours. Hemodynamic instability, obstruction, ileus or a complication requires individualized reassessment rather than forcing the pathway.

Plan urinary catheter removal around the operation and retention risk. The guideline generally favors removal within 24 hours after colonic/upper rectal resection and 24–48 hours after mid/lower rectal resection; these are not automatic deadlines after complex pelvic dissection.

sections.title: Colostomy, bladder function & disposition
bullets: Observe stoma perfusion and communicate a dusky or progressively ischemic appearance promptly. A colostomy usually does not have the same high-output fluid-loss profile as an ileostomy; identify the actual stoma type.
Pelvic autonomic nerve injury can affect bladder function. Individualize catheter management and assess persistent retention instead of treating it as a minor inconvenience.
Handoff should include perineal reconstruction/pressure restrictions, blood loss, analgesia, leg-position duration or concerns and the required level of postoperative observation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Clarify fistulotomy, LIFT, draining seton or another repair: sphincter involvement, infection and operative extent vary substantially.
A selected low/simple fistula is different from complex or Crohn-associated disease; abscess or systemic illness may change urgency and disposition.
Choose anesthesia for position, airway access and procedure extent; coordinate local-anesthetic exposure and postoperative analgesia.
Recovery priorities include pain control, safe voiding and recognition of worsening infection or bleeding, with clear seton/wound instructions from the surgeon.

sources.label: ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)
Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)

sections.title: Fistulotomy, LIFT & seton: not interchangeable
bullets: Fistulotomy may be appropriate for selected simple low fistulas with normal baseline sphincter function. It is not a generic treatment for every transsphincteric tract or a patient with continence risk.

LIFT means ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract and is a sphincter-preserving option for appropriate transsphincteric disease. A draining seton can control local infection as part of staged treatment.
A cutting seton is not sphincter-sparing and is used selectively. Confirm which type is planned rather than documenting only “seton” and assuming a uniform postoperative course.

sources.label: ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & ambulatory suitability
bullets: Review cardiopulmonary reserve, OSA/obesity, prior anesthetic problems, anticoagulants, baseline pain/opioid use and history of urinary retention. Small surgical extent does not eliminate sedation, airway or discharge risk.
Confirm whether active infection, systemic illness or a more extensive operation changes the ambulatory plan. Coordinate expected positioning, duration and local-anesthetic use before induction.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)
ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)

sections.title: Abscess, systemic infection & antibiotics
bullets: An acute anorectal abscess generally requires prompt drainage. Antibiotics are usually reserved for cellulitis, systemic infection or immunosuppression rather than automatically prescribed after uncomplicated drainage in an otherwise healthy patient.

Systemic toxicity, hemodynamic instability or rapidly progressive perineal infection is not a routine ambulatory-fistula scenario. Escalate urgently and use an emergency source-control/resuscitation plan as indicated.

sources.label: ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)
ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Crohn disease & complex fistulas
bullets: Crohn-associated fistulas often require combined medical and surgical management, and the presence of active proctitis or complex anatomy changes the surgical strategy. Do not extrapolate simple fistulotomy recommendations to all Crohn disease.

Review current disease activity, immunosuppression, nutritional status and systemic infection concerns with the treating team. Draining setons may be part of disease control rather than a one-stage definitive cure.

sources.label: ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)

sections.title: Local anesthesia, sedation, neuraxial or general anesthesia
bullets: Local anesthesia with appropriately monitored sedation, neuraxial anesthesia and general anesthesia are all used in selected anorectal operations. Choose according to procedure, patient tolerance, airway/aspiration risk, position and local expertise.

Sedation can progress to airway obstruction or hypoventilation, particularly in obesity/OSA or prone positioning. Titrate carefully and retain the ability to rescue the airway; increasing sedation is not a substitute for an inadequate surgical block.

Spinal anesthesia can provide effective conditions but may increase urinary retention or delay mobility/recovery. Weigh dose/technique, expected duration, contraindications and discharge requirements rather than calling it universally preferable.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)

sections.title: Prone jackknife versus lithotomy
bullets: Prone jackknife offers surgical exposure but makes airway access and ventilation rescue less straightforward. Secure and verify the airway plan before positioning and avoid compression of the chest and abdomen.

Protect the eyes/face, arms, breasts/genitalia and pressure points as appropriate to position. Lithotomy generally permits easier airway access but still requires careful leg support and avoidance of peripheral nerve compression.

If operative duration or complexity increases, reassess positioning, anesthetic depth and airway security instead of allowing a short-case sedation plan to drift into prolonged inaccessible deep sedation.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)
Multidisciplinary guidance: well-leg compartment syndrome after pelvic surgery (2019)

sections.title: Local-anesthetic coordination & toxicity prevention
bullets: Confirm the planned block/infiltration drug and total dose with the surgeon; account for all injections and other local-anesthetic exposure. Patient size, formulation, comorbidity and additional injections affect the safe plan.

Use careful injection technique and monitoring appropriate to the block and setting, and retain immediate access to the institution’s LAST response resources. Do not assume that a small operative field implies a small local-anesthetic dose.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)

sections.title: Procedure-matched analgesia
bullets: Coordinate local anesthesia with systemic multimodal analgesia and titrated rescue opioids as appropriate. The extent of dissection, active infection and previous procedures determine pain needs more than the title “fistula repair.”

Do not automatically transfer hemorrhoidectomy-specific PROSPECT recommendations for pudendal block or topical treatments into fistula surgery as though they had identical evidence. Use procedure-specific judgment and the actual surgical pain plan.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)
PROSPECT: haemorrhoid surgery pain guideline (2023)

sections.title: Fluids & urinary-retention prevention
bullets: Avoid routine excessive IV fluid administration in a short, stable anorectal case, because bladder distension and postoperative retention can complicate recovery. Replace actual deficits and losses; do not apply a rigid fluid cap to a depleted or unstable patient.

Pain, opioids, neuraxial anesthesia, baseline urinary disease and surgical extent contribute to retention. Review risk and a bladder assessment plan before discharge rather than assuming every patient has the same voiding requirement.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)

sections.title: Bleeding risk & antithrombotic reconciliation
bullets: Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet treatment and any neuraxial plan before the procedure. Bleeding risk and medication management must be individualized with the procedural and prescribing teams.

At handoff, communicate the procedure, hemostasis concerns and analgesia already given. Unusual bleeding or progressive systemic symptoms requires assessment rather than assuming an uncomplicated seton placement.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)
ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)

sections.title: Wound, seton & postoperative expectations
bullets: Ensure the patient receives surgeon-specific instructions for the wound/seton, bowel regimen and follow-up. A draining seton deliberately maintains drainage and should not be confused with a failed closed wound.

Worsening pain, fever/systemic illness or retention with escalating symptoms warrants evaluation for infection or another complication. Avoid masking progressive symptoms with repeated sedation or escalating opioids alone.

sources.label: ASCRS: anorectal abscess and fistula guideline (2022)
Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)

sections.title: PACU, discharge readiness & return precautions
bullets: Assess alertness, stable ventilation/oxygenation, hemodynamics, pain, PONV and safe mobility before discharge, with suitable supervision and written instructions. Residual sedation and OSA may require longer observation.

Have an explicit pathway for inability to void, painful bladder distension or recurrent retention. Severe or worsening pain, fever/systemic illness or significant bleeding warrants clinical review rather than escalation of home opioids alone.
If neuromuscular blockade was used for general anesthesia, confirm quantitative recovery before extubation; a brief procedure does not eliminate residual-block risk.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Treat obstruction as an elevated aspiration-risk condition regardless of the reported fasting interval. Distension, vomiting and fluid sequestration may coexist with major intravascular depletion.
Assess for strangulation, ischemia, perforation or sepsis; resuscitation and urgent source-control planning proceed together.
Anticipate induction hypotension and plan airway protection, decompression, vasoactive support and monitoring for the actual physiologic state.
The postoperative plan may require continued ventilation or critical care; do not impose the elective colorectal ERAS pathway on an unstable emergency patient.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)
Anesthetic management of intestinal obstruction: review (2016)

sections.title: Cause, severity & source control
bullets: Clarify obstruction level and cause, duration, vomiting/distension, imaging findings and concern for ischemic bowel or perforation. The planned operation may progress from adhesiolysis to bowel resection, stoma or more extensive source control.

Review perfusion, mental status, renal function, gas/lactate trends and infection/sepsis indicators. A reassuring single blood-pressure reading does not exclude clinically important depletion or evolving shock.
Coordinate timely surgery and resuscitation. Do not delay urgent source control to satisfy an arbitrary fixed fluid volume or a set number of hours of “normal” urine output.

sources.label: Anesthetic management of intestinal obstruction: review (2016)
ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Gastric decompression & residual aspiration risk
bullets: Use nasogastric decompression selectively for significant gastric stasis/distension and aspiration risk in collaboration with the surgical team. Confirm function and communicate the amount and nature of ongoing losses.
An NG tube does not guarantee an empty stomach or eliminate aspiration risk. Maintain a full-stomach airway plan even after substantial drainage.
Therapeutic decompression for obstruction is different from routine postoperative NG use after uncomplicated elective resection; reassess the ongoing indication daily.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)
Anesthetic management of intestinal obstruction: review (2016)

sections.title: Airway protection & induction planning
bullets: A rapid-sequence approach with a cuffed tracheal tube is commonly appropriate for emergency obstruction, but integrate anticipated airway difficulty and physiologic instability into the airway strategy rather than using a one-size-fits-all induction.
Prepare suction, oxygenation/rescue equipment and assistance. Titrate induction choice and dose to shock and reserve; a standard elective bolus can precipitate profound hypotension.
Use cricoid pressure according to the applicable airway protocol and release it if it impedes laryngoscopy or airway management. Airway protection must not prevent effective oxygenation or rescue.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Resuscitation & hemodynamic support
bullets: Replace losses and restore perfusion using repeated assessment rather than fixed liters based solely on obstruction level. Balanced crystalloid is generally favored in emergency laparotomy, but fluid selection must also account for measured deficits and acid–base status.

Vomiting and sequestration can coexist with vasodilation from sepsis or anesthesia. When hypotension persists despite appropriate volume assessment, use cause-directed vasoactive support rather than repeated uncritical fluid loading.
Avoid both unresolved hypoperfusion and excessive edema-producing resuscitation. Individualize arterial pressure goals and use clinical/laboratory trends to assess response.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)
Anesthetic management of intestinal obstruction: review (2016)

sections.title: Electrolytes, renal function & acid–base patterns
bullets: Prolonged proximal vomiting can produce hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; ischemia, sepsis or poor perfusion may instead produce metabolic acidosis. Mixed disorders are possible, so do not infer the gas from the diagnosis alone.

Follow potassium, renal function and acid–base status and replace deficits with monitoring appropriate to severity. Ongoing NG losses, renal impairment and rapid resuscitation can change the picture during surgery.
Interpret lactate as part of the perfusion/ischemia assessment rather than a standalone rule-out test or a mandatory normalization target before time-sensitive source control.

sources.label: Anesthetic management of intestinal obstruction: review (2016)
ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Access, laboratory surveillance & blood readiness
bullets: Obtain reliable access and consider an arterial line early when instability, repeated gases or major surgery warrants it. Central access is selected for support and access needs, not automatically required for every obstruction.
Plan blood availability for potential resection, ischemic bowel or significant bleeding, and reassess laboratory/coagulation needs as the operative extent becomes clear.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Antibiotics & temperature
bullets: Coordinate therapeutic antibiotics for suspected infection/sepsis and surgical prophylaxis as appropriate. Confirm adequate preincision coverage and redosing; a prophylaxis timing checklist is not a reason to defer treatment of suspected sepsis.
Monitor temperature and use active warming with warmed fluids/blood as indicated. Prolonged exposure and resuscitation can contribute to hypothermia and impaired recovery.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Ventilation, distension & intraoperative changes
bullets: Use lung-protective ventilation, typically 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, with individualized PEEP and adjustment for gas exchange and hemodynamics. Abdominal distension and any pneumoperitoneum can impair compliance.
Avoid nitrous oxide when expansion of closed gas-filled bowel would worsen distension. Reassess ventilatory mechanics and perfusion after decompression, insufflation or major operative changes.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)
OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024)
Anesthetic management of intestinal obstruction: review (2016)

sections.title: Analgesia in the unstable or septic patient
bullets: Use a multimodal plan tailored to perfusion, renal function and surgical extent, with titrated opioids when needed. The analgesic choice should not compromise hemodynamic resuscitation or postoperative respiratory safety.

Neuraxial techniques require specific assessment of sepsis, coagulation, anticoagulants and hemodynamic reserve. Do not automatically transfer an elective thoracic epidural pathway to a shocked emergency patient.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)

sections.title: Extubation versus continued support
bullets: Consider consciousness, oxygenation/ventilation, perfusion, temperature, metabolic abnormalities and expected postoperative course. Ongoing shock, major resuscitation or respiratory failure may make continued ventilation and ICU care appropriate.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, verify quantitative recovery with an adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. Clinical strength tests alone do not establish recovery.
Postoperative NIV/CPAP is not a substitute for airway protection in active vomiting or substantial aspiration risk; select respiratory support and monitoring for the patient’s actual condition.

sources.label: ERAS Society: emergency laparotomy, intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)
APSF: ASA/ESAIC neuromuscular blockade guideline summary (2023)

sections.title: Handoff, decompression & recovery trajectory
bullets: Communicate the cause and extent of disease, resection/anastomosis/stoma, residual concerns, antibiotics, losses, resuscitation, support and laboratory trends. Set explicit triggers for reassessment of perfusion and organ function.
Reassess ongoing NG need and nutrition with the surgical team. Early recovery elements may be useful, but feeding, mobilization and device removal must be adapted to stability and bowel function.

Persistent or new deterioration warrants prompt investigation for inadequate source control, ischemia, infection, bleeding or other complications rather than being labeled an expected consequence of emergency surgery.

bullets: Elective minimally invasive colectomy and emergency colectomy for obstruction, perforation or sepsis have different aspiration, resuscitation and recovery requirements.
Anticipate insufflation/positioning effects, potentially restricted robotic access and the possibility of conversion to open surgery.
Protect perfusion while avoiding both excess fluid and unnecessary restriction; use an incision-appropriate opioid-sparing analgesic plan.

Uncomplicated elective recovery favors early intake/mobilization and no routine NG tube. Escalating pain, instability or failure to recover warrants evaluation rather than automatic continuation of ERAS milestones.

sections.title: Operation, indication & approach
bullets: Clarify the segment being removed, open versus minimally invasive approach, planned anastomosis or stoma, and whether the indication is malignancy, inflammatory disease or an emergency. The extent and physiologic burden matter more than the small external incisions.

Prior operations, adhesions, inflammatory disease and unexpectedly difficult dissection can prolong surgery or require conversion. Ensure the analgesia, access and postoperative plan can accommodate an open incision.

Plan access and blood availability for the surgical extent and patient reserve. Reoperative or deep pelvic dissection can bleed substantially despite a minimally invasive skin incision.

sections.title: Multimodal analgesia & regional options
bullets: Establish opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia before induction when possible. Acetaminophen and an appropriate regional or local technique can reduce opioid exposure; tailor the plan to incision, renal/hepatic function, bleeding risk and chronic opioid use.

Abdominal-wall blocks address somatic incision pain but do not reliably replace treatment of deep visceral or perineal pain. Match coverage to the actual incisions rather than offering the same block for every colorectal operation.

NSAID-associated anastomotic-leak signals are molecule/class dependent; diclofenac has the strongest signal in the guideline discussion. Do not label all NSAIDs either universally safe or universally prohibited: reconcile anastomotic, renal, bleeding and cardiovascular risks with the surgical pathway.

sections.title: Anastomosis, oxygen delivery & surgical communication
bullets: Support systemic perfusion, normothermia and oxygenation and promptly communicate sustained hypotension or major bleeding. An anastomosis is not protected by either deliberate dehydration or indiscriminate fluid loading.

sections.title: Emergence & enhanced recovery
bullets: Assess ventilation, hemodynamics, temperature, pain and airway swelling before extubation, particularly after long Trendelenburg positioning. When a neuromuscular blocker was used, verify quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

Routine nasogastric tubes are discouraged after uncomplicated elective colorectal surgery. This does not prohibit therapeutic decompression for obstruction, persistent gastric stasis or a specific surgical indication.

For suitable elective patients, offer early oral intake and progressive mobilization according to the recovery pathway; the guideline supports a regular diet within 24 hours. bullets: Choose routine recovery versus higher-acuity care according to reserve, intraoperative instability, respiratory support, sepsis and blood loss, not simply the laparoscopic label.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Expect significant postoperative and defecation-related pain despite a relatively short operation. Plan multimodal analgesia before the patient reaches PACU.
Match anesthesia to prone/lithotomy access, comorbidity and procedure extent; sedation is not automatically low risk in a prone patient.
The PROSPECT guideline supports bilateral pudendal block as part of the analgesic strategy, with appropriate expertise and nerve-injury precautions.
Urinary retention, nausea, constipation and bleeding can prevent an otherwise planned same-day discharge.

sections.title: Excision extent & expected pain
bullets: Confirm the operative technique and extent rather than treating all hemorrhoid procedures as identical. The PROSPECT recommendations address pain after hemorrhoid surgery, with evidence mainly from excisional procedures and variable baseline analgesic regimens.
Analgesia should cover the immediate postoperative period and painful bowel movements after discharge. Discuss rescue medication and a bowel regimen as part of the perioperative plan.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & ambulatory suitability
bullets: Review cardiopulmonary reserve, OSA/obesity, prior anesthetic problems, anticoagulants, baseline pain/opioid use and history of urinary retention. Small surgical extent does not eliminate sedation, airway or discharge risk.
Confirm whether active infection, systemic illness or a more extensive operation changes the ambulatory plan. Coordinate expected positioning, duration and local-anesthetic use before induction.

sections.title: Local anesthesia, sedation, neuraxial or general anesthesia
bullets: Local anesthesia with appropriately monitored sedation, neuraxial anesthesia and general anesthesia are all used in selected anorectal operations. Choose according to procedure, patient tolerance, airway/aspiration risk, position and local expertise.

Sedation can progress to airway obstruction or hypoventilation, particularly in obesity/OSA or prone positioning. Titrate carefully and retain the ability to rescue the airway; increasing sedation is not a substitute for an inadequate surgical block.

Spinal anesthesia can provide effective conditions but may increase urinary retention or delay mobility/recovery. Weigh dose/technique, expected duration, contraindications and discharge requirements rather than calling it universally preferable.

sections.title: Prone jackknife versus lithotomy
bullets: Prone jackknife offers surgical exposure but makes airway access and ventilation rescue less straightforward. Secure and verify the airway plan before positioning and avoid compression of the chest and abdomen.

Protect the eyes/face, arms, breasts/genitalia and pressure points as appropriate to position. Lithotomy generally permits easier airway access but still requires careful leg support and avoidance of peripheral nerve compression.

If operative duration or complexity increases, reassess positioning, anesthetic depth and airway security instead of allowing a short-case sedation plan to drift into prolonged inaccessible deep sedation.

sections.title: Local-anesthetic coordination & toxicity prevention
bullets: Confirm the planned block/infiltration drug and total dose with the surgeon; account for all injections and other local-anesthetic exposure. Patient size, formulation, comorbidity and additional injections affect the safe plan.

Use careful injection technique and monitoring appropriate to the block and setting, and retain immediate access to the institution’s LAST response resources. Do not assume that a small operative field implies a small local-anesthetic dose.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of the Ambulatory Anorectal Surgery Patient (2016)

sections.title: Baseline analgesia & opioid rescue
bullets: PROSPECT recommends acetaminophen plus an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor when not contraindicated, and a single IV dexamethasone dose as part of multimodal care. Select agents for renal, bleeding, gastrointestinal and metabolic risks rather than prescribing them universally.

Reserve opioids for rescue when feasible because nausea and constipation can worsen recovery and pain with defecation. Persistent severe pain still requires assessment and appropriate treatment, not withholding analgesia to meet an opioid-free target.

sections.title: Pudendal block: role & evidence boundary
bullets: Bilateral pudendal block is recommended in the updated PROSPECT strategy. Use an appropriately trained operator and consider the risk of pudendal nerve injury, particularly with blind techniques.

Perianal infiltration is not recommended by the updated guideline as a routine postoperative analgesic adjunct because supporting evidence was insufficient. This is distinct from using local anesthesia as the primary anesthetic technique for a selected operation.
Do not present a regional technique as a substitute for baseline systemic analgesia, postoperative assessment or treatment of surgical complications.

sections.title: Fluids & urinary-retention prevention
bullets: Avoid routine excessive IV fluid administration in a short, stable anorectal case, because bladder distension and postoperative retention can complicate recovery. Replace actual deficits and losses; do not apply a rigid fluid cap to a depleted or unstable patient.

Pain, opioids, neuraxial anesthesia, baseline urinary disease and surgical extent contribute to retention. Review risk and a bladder assessment plan before discharge rather than assuming every patient has the same voiding requirement.

sections.title: Bowel regimen & surgeon-directed topical therapy
bullets: A postoperative laxative/bowel regimen is supported to reduce painful defecation. Coordinate the actual regimen and hydration advice with the surgeon and the patient’s medical conditions.

The PROSPECT review supports selected topical treatments, including topical metronidazole, in the pain strategy. Oral metronidazole is not recommended solely for analgesia; distinguish pain treatment from antibiotics for a diagnosed infection.

sections.title: Nausea prevention & recovery comfort
bullets: Use patient-risk-based PONV prophylaxis and opioid-sparing strategies. Dexamethasone may contribute to both analgesia and nausea prevention; avoid duplicating doses across the anesthetic and surgical plans.
Treat vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake before discharge, especially when they interfere with analgesia, hydration or safe recovery.

sections.title: Bleeding, retention & disproportionate pain
bullets: Assess concerning bleeding, hemodynamic symptoms or pain that is escalating rather than following the expected trajectory. Do not assume that all postoperative perianal pain is routine hemorrhoidectomy pain.

Urinary retention is particularly relevant after hemorrhoid surgery. Evaluate painful inability to void with the local bladder pathway; persistent or recurrent retention together with worsening pain/systemic symptoms may signal more than an isolated bladder problem.

bullets: Confirm how low the planned resection/anastomosis is and whether a diverting ileostomy is anticipated. Diversion changes postoperative fluid/electrolyte planning and may require a later closure operation; it does not make recovery identical to a routine colectomy.

sections.title: Preoperative reserve, bowel preparation & aspiration
bullets: Review functional reserve, cardiopulmonary disease, anemia, renal function, nutritional status and recent intake/losses. Bowel preparation, poor intake, vomiting and an existing ileostomy can produce clinically important depletion before an apparently elective operation.

For elective colorectal resection, the ASCRS/SAGES guideline typically recommends mechanical bowel preparation combined with oral antibiotics, not mechanical preparation alone. The surgical protocol and contraindications determine the actual regimen; do not extrapolate this to acute obstruction.

Clear liquids up to 2 hours before anesthesia belong to an appropriate elective fasting pathway, not to patients with obstruction, impaired emptying or other elevated aspiration risk. Carbohydrate-loading evidence in this guideline primarily concerns patients without diabetes; individualize rather than applying it automatically.

Confirm recent antithrombotic exposure and the postoperative thromboprophylaxis plan before choosing neuraxial analgesia. An elective enhanced-recovery pathway must be modified for sepsis, significant coagulopathy or hemodynamic instability.

sections.title: Lithotomy, Trendelenburg & well-leg compartment syndrome
bullets: Document positioning with the surgical team. Pad vulnerable areas, avoid compression at the fibular head and calf/popliteal region, keep joints within a tolerable range and reassess access and pressure points after final positioning.

Prolonged lithotomy and head-down positioning can impair lower-leg perfusion, particularly when the legs are elevated above the heart. Minimize unnecessary duration and pressure; discuss safe opportunities to reduce leg elevation or head-down tilt during lengthy pelvic operations.

Postoperative severe leg pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, weakness or paresthesia requires urgent assessment for well-leg compartment syndrome. Preserved pulses do not exclude it. Do not dismiss the symptoms as routine positioning discomfort or attribute them automatically to neuraxial analgesia.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum, ventilation & robotic access
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce respiratory compliance and functional residual capacity and can increase airway pressure, atelectasis and CO₂ absorption. Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted/ideal body weight, not actual weight in obesity, and individualize PEEP and respiratory rate.

Reassess tube depth and bilateral ventilation after positioning and insufflation. Cephalad diaphragmatic movement can promote endobronchial migration; rising pressure is not automatically bronchospasm.

Secure the airway, IV connections and monitoring before docking because access may become restricted. Agree on how the team will obtain emergency patient access and coordinate all subsequent table or patient movement with the surgical/robotic team.

Sudden bradycardia during insufflation can reflect vagal peritoneal stretch. Notify the surgeon, interrupt the provoking insufflation and support circulation while evaluating other causes; persistent instability requires more than treating the monitor number.

bullets: If an ileostomy is created, track output together with intake, urine output, weight and renal/electrolyte trends. Dehydration can develop even when output does not meet a single textbook high-output cutoff.

High-output losses may deplete sodium and magnesium as well as water. Instructions to drink unlimited plain water can worsen sodium depletion in high-output states; use a clinician-directed oral rehydration and replacement plan.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Creation for acute obstruction/sepsis, elective diversion and reversal of an established stoma are different operations with different physiologic risks.
An ileostomy may cause water, sodium and magnesium depletion with renal dysfunction; assess the patient, not output volume alone.
Reversal may require adhesiolysis, bowel resection and an anastomosis. It should not automatically be treated as a short superficial procedure.
Plan postoperative monitoring for hydration, bowel function, anastomotic complications and stoma perfusion when a stoma remains.

sections.title: Creation versus closure: clarify the operation
bullets: Identify ileostomy versus colostomy, loop versus end stoma, reason for diversion and whether the operation is local closure or a more extensive intra-abdominal reconstruction. Existing adhesions and bowel disease may change the plan.
Reversal restores continuity and introduces an anastomotic healing risk; an operation described as “stoma closure” may still require significant abdominal dissection or conversion.

sections.title: High-output stoma & preoperative depletion
bullets: Review measured output and intake trends, thirst, weight change, postural symptoms, urine output and recent admissions for dehydration. Output around 1.5–2 L/day often prompts concern, but clinically significant depletion has no universally reliable volume threshold.

Check renal function and sodium, potassium and magnesium where losses or illness warrant it. Magnesium depletion may reflect both reduced absorption and renal loss; correction should follow laboratory values, symptoms and renal function.
A high-output state may reflect short bowel, infection, medication changes or intermittent obstruction. Do not assume all watery output is normal stoma behavior.

sections.title: Replacement strategy: more than plain water
bullets: Treat severe dehydration or oliguria with supervised IV replacement and reassessment. Choose fluid composition for the actual electrolyte/acid–base deficits and perfusion rather than using one fixed volume for every stoma patient.

For established high-output physiology, large volumes of hypotonic fluid can worsen sodium loss. Appropriate glucose-saline oral rehydration and a specialist-directed intake plan differ from simply instructing the patient to drink more plain water.

Antimotility or antisecretory therapy and magnesium supplementation may be needed, but confirm the diagnosis and coordinate with the surgical/intestinal-failure team. This reference is not a high-dose self-treatment protocol.

sections.title: Fasting, obstruction & aspiration risk
bullets: A functioning stoma does not rule out obstruction. Pain, distension, vomiting or a marked change/cessation in output requires reassessment before routine elective fasting assumptions are used.
If obstruction or emergency physiology is present, plan decompression and airway management under the emergency pathway. A completed fasting interval does not prove an empty stomach in this setting.

sections.title: After reversal: bowel function & anastomosis
bullets: Expect bowel function to change after restoration of continuity. Distinguish expected recovery from persistent vomiting/distension, worsening pain or systemic deterioration that may indicate obstruction, ileus, leak or infection.

Use the relevant colorectal recovery pathway when clinically appropriate, but do not force oral intake or discharge in a patient whose perfusion, bowel function or laboratory abnormalities remain concerning.

sections.title: Emergence & enhanced recovery
bullets: Assess ventilation, hemodynamics, temperature, pain and airway swelling before extubation, particularly after long Trendelenburg positioning. When a neuromuscular blocker was used, verify quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

Routine nasogastric tubes are discouraged after uncomplicated elective colorectal surgery. This does not prohibit therapeutic decompression for obstruction, persistent gastric stasis or a specific surgical indication.

For suitable elective patients, offer early oral intake and progressive mobilization according to the recovery pathway; the guideline supports a regular diet within 24 hours. Hemodynamic instability, obstruction, ileus or a complication requires individualized reassessment rather than forcing the pathway.

Plan urinary catheter removal around the operation and retention risk. The guideline generally favors removal within 24 hours after colonic/upper rectal resection and 24–48 hours after mid/lower rectal resection; these are not automatic deadlines after complex pelvic dissection.

bullets: Communicate preoperative depletion, replacement given, renal/electrolyte abnormalities, remaining stoma and planned output monitoring. A patient with high-output losses may need ongoing replacement and laboratory follow-up beyond PACU.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Plan for a shared airway with irrigation, blood and dental debris; choose airway protection for the actual treatment, not simply the label “dental.”
Adapt assessment, communication and induction to the adult’s needs, including disability, severe anxiety, OSA and relevant medical comorbidity.
A nasal tube may improve access, but assess its risks; throat packs are selective and require explicit insertion/removal accounting.
Recovery includes airway safety, pain, nausea, bleeding and a clear caregiver-supported discharge plan when needed.

sections.title: Treatment scope, setting & indication
bullets: Dental rehabilitation may combine examination, imaging, restorations and extractions. If a complete awake examination was not possible, agree on the authorized scope and how unexpected findings will be handled rather than assuming unlimited treatment consent.

General anesthesia may enable necessary care when less restrictive approaches are unsuitable or unsuccessful, including severe dental phobia or inability to tolerate treatment. The decision should weigh dental benefit, alternatives and anesthetic risk, not a disability diagnosis alone.

Match the setting to airway/medical complexity, procedural extent and recovery needs. The BSDH guideline is UK-based, largely expert consensus; its service and legal requirements are not automatically US rules.

sections.title: Medical assessment, medications & baseline function
bullets: Obtain a reliable history from the patient and, with appropriate permission, carers, records and treating clinicians. Review prior anesthesia/airway difficulty, OSA, cardiopulmonary disease, aspiration concerns, renal/hepatic disease and current medication exposure.

Establish baseline communication, mobility, swallowing/feeding needs and behavior so emergence and discharge can be assessed meaningfully. Distress or limited speech can make routine pain and nausea assessment less reliable.

Plan investigations and optimization according to actual risk, not automatic testing solely because GA is needed for dental care. If examination or investigations cannot be completed, explicitly assess the resulting uncertainty and whether the setting or plan must change.

sections.title: Capacity, consent & communication
bullets: Do not infer incapacity from intellectual disability, autism, anxiety or difficulty speaking. Assess the adult’s ability to make the particular decision and use communication support; obtain consent or authorization under the applicable local law and policy.

Discuss the dental procedure and anesthesia, realistic alternatives and possible changes in treatment, including extractions where relevant. Involve the legally authorized decision-maker when required while preserving the patient’s participation and preferences.

Plan sensory adjustments, a quieter waiting area, familiar carers and the minimum necessary personnel when these help. Document triggers, calming strategies and information the recovery team will need.

sources.label: BSDH 2022: general anesthesia in adult special care dentistry

sections.title: Preparation, premedication & induction
bullets: Agree on the journey from admission to induction before the day of treatment when possible. Familiarization, topical anesthetic for cannulation and a trusted support person may reduce distress without simply escalating sedative medication.

Any premedication requires an individualized prescribing and supervision plan that accounts for comorbidity, drug interactions, cooperation and airway risk. This reference does not endorse an unsupervised one-dose-fits-all sedative regimen.

When cooperation limits IV access or an awake technique, make an explicit risk-based plan with experienced assistance and rescue resources. Do not treat behavioral difficulty as proof that inhalational induction or preservation of spontaneous breathing guarantees airway safety.

sources.label: BSDH 2022: general anesthesia in adult special care dentistry

sections.title: Anticipated difficult airway & rescue strategy
bullets: Assess mouth opening, jaw relationship, tongue/soft tissue, neck mobility, OSA, prior airway records and feasibility of mask or supraglottic rescue. Dentofacial deformity or disability does not predict one identical airway problem in every patient.

When difficult intubation is anticipated, consider an awake strategy especially if ventilation may be difficult, aspiration risk is increased, brief apnea may not be tolerated or emergency invasive airway access may be difficult. Choose the approach with the necessary skills, cooperation and resources.

Prepare primary, backup and rescue plans before induction, with oxygenation maintained throughout airway management. Limit repeated unsuccessful attempts and reassess ventilation and elapsed time rather than persisting with a failing technique.

A nasal route describes where the tube enters, not how it is placed: awake flexible-scope, video-assisted and other techniques have different indications. Select a method for the patient rather than declaring one device best for all jaw surgery.

sections.title: Nasotracheal route: preparation & contraindications
bullets: A nasal tube often improves oral access, but surgical convenience does not override safety. Assess nasal patency, prior nasal surgery, recurrent epistaxis, obstructing lesions and clinically important bleeding risk before selecting the route.

Suspected skull-base fracture or unstable midface injury is a major reason to avoid routine nasal instrumentation. Elective orthognathic planning must not be transferred unchanged to a patient with facial trauma.

Use an appropriate topical vasoconstrictor and lubrication according to patient risk and local practice; include any topical lidocaine in the total local-anesthetic exposure. Advance gently along the nasal passage and stop/reassess significant resistance rather than forcing the tube.

Choose tube diameter, length and configuration together. A smaller preformed nasal RAE tube is also shorter and may place the cuff too proximally; verify cuff position, depth and ventilation rather than selecting diameter alone.

Confirm tracheal placement with waveform capnography and assess bilateral ventilation. Recheck after neck movement: flexion may advance the tube and extension may withdraw it, risking displacement or cuff contact with the cords.

sections.title: Shared-airway setup & maintenance
bullets: Discuss the required oral access and likely irrigation, bleeding and debris with the dentist. The BSDH guideline suggests a cuffed endotracheal tube as the default secure-airway approach for special care dentistry, while acknowledging weak evidence.

A supraglottic airway may impede access and does not provide the same protection against irrigation or contamination. The guideline limits its routine role to selected short, simple procedures with an otherwise straightforward airway; do not generalize that option to extensive treatment.

Secure the tube and circuit away from the working field, confirm that the surgeon’s access does not compromise ventilation and maintain ongoing airway monitoring. Airway repositioning or exchange remains an anesthesia task agreed with the procedural team.

If ventilation deteriorates, ask the dentist to stop and restore airway access immediately. Assess displacement, obstruction, contamination and anesthetic causes rather than assuming the problem is merely the dental instrument position.

sections.title: Throat packs, suction & foreign-body accounting
bullets: Do not treat a throat pack as mandatory or as a substitute for a secured airway and suction. DAS/BAOMS/ENT-UK no longer recommend routine anesthetist-inserted throat packs in adults; consider the particular operative debris risk and potential harm.

If a pack is used, agree who inserts and removes it, formally record insertion and removal and maintain an explicit reminder/count process. Communicate its presence at every relevant handoff; a change of team increases the risk of forgetting it.

Account for the pack and other dental materials before extubation; when fixation will restrict mouth access, confirm removal before final maxillomandibular fixation. Clear blood, clots and debris with appropriate suction and direct inspection where needed.

Retained packs can cause serious postoperative airway obstruction. An apparently completed operation or documented dental count does not replace positive confirmation that an anesthetic throat pack has been removed.

sections.title: Local anesthetic, vasoconstrictors & medication reconciliation
bullets: Agree on dental local anesthesia with the operator and record the agent, concentration, total dose, injection sites and timing. Reconcile topical airway anesthetic with injected local anesthetic rather than treating them as unrelated exposures.

Account for renal/hepatic disease, cardiovascular disease and interacting medications when selecting systemic and local treatment. Communicate all intraoperative analgesics so recovery or discharge prescriptions do not inadvertently duplicate therapy.
Explain the expected numbness and protective-care instructions to the patient or caregiver when relevant; include injection sites/type and expected duration in the dental recovery handoff.

sections.title: Bleeding, irrigation & perfusion
bullets: Multiple extractions and mucosal work require ongoing assessment of hemostasis and swallowed or suctioned blood. Incorporate the patient’s bleeding history, antithrombotic exposure and liver/renal disease into the plan rather than assuming all dental treatment has trivial bleeding risk.

Distinguish irrigation from blood in the operative field and maintain communication about unexpected bleeding. Fluid therapy should support the actual patient and losses; neither a fixed large fluid load nor routine deliberate hypotension is established for adult dental rehabilitation.
Active oral bleeding or inability to clear secretions can change the extubation and discharge plan. Obtain adequate hemostasis and reassess the airway before proceeding to routine recovery.

sections.title: Fire risk in the shared oral field
bullets: An oral field can bring ignition sources, gauze/drapes and oxygen or nitrous oxide together. Electrosurgery, lasers and even drill sparks can ignite combustible material; assess the planned equipment and gas delivery before it is used.

Avoid oxygen pooling beneath drapes, keep susceptible materials moist where appropriate and allow alcohol-containing preparations to dry. Coordinate oxidizer delivery and ignition-source use under the institution’s fire-prevention protocol without compromising necessary oxygenation.
Nitrous oxide supports combustion and is not a safe way to dilute oxygen near an ignition source. No single oxygen concentration or waiting interval makes every oral procedure fire-safe.

sections.title: Extraction pain: nonopioid-first treatment
bullets: For acute pain after dental extractions, the 2024 ADA-endorsed guideline favors nonopioid treatment, typically an NSAID alone or with acetaminophen when appropriate. Its scope is extraction pain and temporary toothache treatment, not every major maxillofacial operation.

Check NSAID contraindications and renal, bleeding, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks, and account for liver disease and cumulative acetaminophen exposure. Review combination products to avoid duplicate acetaminophen.

Reserve opioid prescribing for selected situations where appropriate first-line treatment is insufficient or unsuitable. Avoid routine “just-in-case” opioids and consider sedation, OSA, other CNS depressants and caregiver understanding.

sections.title: PONV & assessment in a patient with limited communication
bullets: Plan nausea prevention and treatment using the patient’s risk and the anesthetic/procedural course. Persistent vomiting increases difficulty maintaining hydration and safely recovering after oral surgery.

Use the patient’s usual communication methods and caregiver knowledge to distinguish pain, nausea, fear and other causes of distress. Agitation is not automatically an indication for more sedative medication.

Before discharge, ensure vomiting is controlled and pain is acceptable using an assessment approach appropriate to the individual. Provide a feasible medication plan rather than instructions the patient or caregiver cannot follow.

sections.title: Emergence: clean airway, recovery & rescue readiness
bullets: Verify pack/material accounting, oral hemostasis and clearance of blood, clots and debris. Assess the original airway risk together with any new trauma or swelling caused during the procedure.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9. A short dental anesthetic does not eliminate residual-block risk.

Choose extubation timing and technique according to airway contamination, reflex recovery and ease of rescue. Difficult-airway patients need a planned reintubation strategy and suitable personnel/equipment; deep extubation is not a default solution to prevent agitation.

sections.title: Recovery, caregivers & discharge instructions
bullets: Provide appropriately staffed and monitored recovery until airway protection, ventilation, circulation and consciousness are satisfactory. OSA, residual sedation, bleeding or a difficult airway may require additional observation or a higher-acuity setting.
Handoff should include the treatment performed, extractions/sutures, pack removal, local anesthetic, analgesia and next-dose timing, bleeding concerns, airway events and communication/handling needs.

Provide accessible written and verbal instructions, a responsible escort/support plan, expected oral numbness and bleeding guidance, medication directions and a contact route for urgent concerns. Follow the local anesthesia-discharge policy for supervision and activities after GA.

Breathing difficulty, inability to handle secretions, uncontrolled bleeding, persistent vomiting or unexpectedly prolonged impaired consciousness warrants urgent assessment rather than reassurance that these are normal after dental work.

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical review
bullets: Adult clinical review draft for anesthesia professionals, not a patient-specific order set. Local difficult-airway, medication, monitoring and recovery policies and specialist clinical review remain essential before release.

The UK special-care guideline is largely expert consensus; legal/service requirements are jurisdiction-specific. Orthognathic ERAS remains an evolving evidence base without a universally adopted protocol. Published local practice, low-pressure targets and drug regimens are not automatically standards of care.

The throat-pack recommendation concerns routine anesthetist-inserted packs in adults, not a ban on every surgically indicated pack. Older reviews and an editorial support selected physiology/safety principles, not fixed incidence estimates or comprehensive emergency algorithms.

bullets: Bimaxillary surgery combines maxillary and mandibular osteotomies; shared-airway access, bleeding and postoperative swelling are central concerns.
Plan nasal intubation or an appropriate alternative around airway anatomy, nasal safety and the need to assess dental occlusion.
Use individualized blood conservation and multimodal analgesia; deliberate hypotension and TXA are not universal fixed-dose or fixed-pressure protocols.

bullets: Clarify maxillary Le Fort I osteotomy, mandibular advancement/setback or bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, and whether both jaws or additional facial structures will be addressed. The extent and sequence determine access, bleeding and postoperative airway concerns.

Agree on occlusal checks, expected fixation and whether temporary intraoperative fixation will remain after surgery. A nasal tube may facilitate alignment, but final airway decisions must account for patient-specific risks.
Do not assume that every patient is a healthy young adult. Syndromic craniofacial anatomy, OSA and cardiopulmonary disease may materially change induction, blood-pressure tolerance and recovery.

Ask about OSA, baseline airway support, respiratory symptoms, cardiac/cerebrovascular disease and renal function. These influence anesthetic drug effects, deliberate-hypotension suitability and postoperative monitoring.

Review bleeding history, hemoglobin and relevant medication exposure based on operative extent and patient risk. Discuss expected blood loss and transfusion readiness before induction rather than relying on a historical transfusion percentage from a small series.

sections.title: Tube protection, access & surgical positioning
bullets: Secure the tube in a position that permits assessment of facial symmetry and occlusion without placing traction on the nose or circuit. After final positioning and draping, verify depth, ventilation and continued access to the airway circuit.

Protect eyes and pressure points and ensure access/monitoring remains usable throughout a potentially long procedure. Reassess after head movement or surgical manipulation because a nasal tube can be displaced even when it was initially well positioned.

Select IV access, laboratory surveillance and invasive pressure monitoring for the actual bleeding risk, reserve and hemodynamic strategy. If deliberate hypotension is planned, use monitoring capable of following rapid changes and reassess organ-perfusion risk continuously.

sections.title: Throat packs, suction & foreign-body accounting
bullets: Do not treat a throat pack as mandatory or as a substitute for a secured airway and suction. DAS/BAOMS/ENT-UK no longer recommend routine anesthetist-inserted throat packs in adults; consider the particular operative debris risk and potential harm.

If a pack is used, agree who inserts and removes it, formally record insertion and removal and maintain an explicit reminder/count process. Communicate its presence at every relevant handoff; a change of team increases the risk of forgetting it.

sections.title: Blood conservation & TXA: evidence with limits
bullets: The vascular maxillomandibular region can bleed substantially during osteotomy and dissection. Use surgical hemostasis, appropriate local measures, warming and a coordinated blood-management plan rather than relying only on lower arterial pressure.

The 2026 review summarizes evidence that TXA can reduce blood loss in orthognathic surgery, but does not establish a universal regimen. Confirm dosing, timing, renal adjustment and patient-specific contraindications with the local protocol and current drug reference.

Do not copy a concentration reported in a paper into a weight-based administered dose, or apply trauma-trial dosing/outcomes as if they were orthognathic-specific evidence. Reconcile units and the actual indication before administration.

Escalate unexpected hemorrhage with the surgeon, reassess airway contamination and perfusion, and obtain testing/blood support appropriate to the magnitude and trajectory of loss. A minimally invasive-looking oral incision does not establish low hemorrhage risk.

sections.title: Controlled hypotension: selective, not automatic
bullets: Deliberate hypotension may improve the operative field and reduce bleeding in selected patients, but risks inadequate cerebral, myocardial and renal perfusion. It is not a universal requirement for orthognathic surgery.

Individualize the pressure plan to baseline, comorbidities, head position and clinical perfusion. Published low MAP ranges in selected young healthy cohorts are not validated safe targets for every adult; this reference intentionally gives no universal minimum MAP.

Avoid or substantially modify the strategy when cardiovascular, cerebrovascular or renal disease or other perfusion vulnerability is present. Do not deepen hypotension to improve visibility while significant hypovolemia or hemorrhage remains uncorrected.

Choose titratable anesthetic/vasoactive measures and communicate changes with the surgeon. Bradycardia, new instability or evidence of poor perfusion requires cause-directed reassessment, not simply another hypotensive-agent dose.

sections.title: Trigeminocardiac reflex: sudden bradycardia during manipulation
bullets: Mechanical stimulation in the trigeminal distribution can trigger vagally mediated bradycardia, hypotension and occasionally severe bradyarrhythmia/asystole. Consider the surgical timing while also checking oxygenation, ventilation, drugs and other causes.

Immediately ask the surgeon to stop the provoking traction/manipulation and assess circulation, oxygenation, ventilation and anesthetic depth. Correct hypoxemia/hypercarbia and inadequate anesthesia as indicated.

Persistent clinically important bradycardia may require an IV anticholinergic and further resuscitation according to the rhythm and hemodynamics. Refractory instability or arrest requires prompt escalation, not waiting for the stimulus alone to resolve it.
Routine prophylactic anticholinergic treatment is not reliably protective and remains debated. Gentle manipulation, communication and readiness to recognize the event remain important.

sources.label: Trigeminocardiac reflex in maxillofacial surgery: review

sections.title: Fluid balance, edema & steroid coordination
bullets: Provide fluid and blood replacement for actual losses and perfusion while avoiding unnecessary overload that can aggravate tissue swelling. Do not interpret an edema concern as a prohibition on crystalloid or needed resuscitation.

Head-elevated recovery and swelling-reduction measures are commonly used when clinically appropriate. Steroids may reduce early edema and PONV, but dose and duration vary; avoid treating small-study high-dose regimens as a universal standard.
Reconcile steroid dosing between teams and consider glucose and patient-specific risks. Reduction in facial swelling does not prove that the airway is safe for extubation.

sections.title: Multimodal pain treatment & regional options
bullets: Combine appropriate nonopioid medication, local/regional techniques and titrated opioid rescue according to surgical extent and patient risk. Consider renal function, bleeding risk, liver disease, OSA and the cumulative sedative burden.

Maxillary and mandibular blocks may reduce opioid requirements, but trials are heterogeneous and analgesic benefit is not uniform. Use trained operators, appropriate monitoring and a documented total local-anesthetic dose across all teams.

A dental-extraction analgesic guideline is not a complete protocol for bimaxillary osteotomy. Preserve adequate analgesia while avoiding excessive sedation that can worsen airway obstruction after fixation or swelling.

sources.label: Orthognathic ERAS anesthesia: narrative review (2026)
ADA: adult acute dental pain guideline summary (2024)

sections.title: PONV prevention with restricted mouth opening
bullets: Orthognathic patients may have substantial PONV risk; vomiting is especially concerning when jaw fixation limits airway access. Plan prevention before emergence rather than relying on rescue treatment after repeated vomiting.

Use risk-based multimodal prophylaxis with different drug classes, appropriate opioid-sparing analgesia and consider propofol-based TIVA when suitable. Coordinate dexamethasone already given for edema with the antiemetic plan.
Persistent nausea/vomiting requires timely treatment and reassessment of blood/secretions, hydration and airway safety. Confirm that recovery staff understand the fixation and release plan.

sections.title: Maxillomandibular fixation & emergency release
bullets: Clarify whether wires, elastics or no postoperative MMF will remain and how mouth opening is restricted. Before fixation limits access, positively confirm throat-pack removal and clear the oropharynx.

Agree with the surgeon on the exact emergency-release method and have the appropriate equipment immediately available wherever the patient recovers. Wire cutters are relevant for wire fixation; elastics require a release plan suited to that system. A generic “cutters available” note is not enough if staff do not know what to release.

If obstruction, vomiting with threatened airway protection or need for urgent reintubation occurs, summon help, support oxygenation and coordinate prompt release as needed to establish a safe airway. Release alone does not necessarily resolve edema or airway contamination.

AO references describe fracture care, not an elective orthognathic protocol; the general release-readiness principle applies, but the treating surgeon must specify the actual fixation system and instructions. Do not import trauma fixation durations into elective jaw-surgery aftercare.

sections.title: Extubation strategy & delayed extubation
bullets: Assess new anatomy, edema, bleeding, airway contamination, residual anesthesia and ease of reintubation as well as baseline airway difficulty. Favor fully awake extubation with intact protective reflexes when obstruction/aspiration risk is significant.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, verify quantitative adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9. Clear blood/secretions, confirm hemostasis and pack removal, and have suitable assistance and reintubation equipment in position.

Significant swelling, ongoing bleeding, inadequate ventilation or difficult rescue may justify delayed extubation in an appropriately monitored setting. A cuff leak can add information but does not guarantee success; absence of a leak is also not a standalone decision rule.

For selected high-risk airways, an airway exchange catheter may preserve reintubation access when used by experienced clinicians. It carries displacement, perforation and barotrauma risks; it is not routine for every patient or a casually used oxygen insufflation device.

sections.title: Postoperative airway surveillance & handoff
bullets: Recover with appropriate oxygenation/ventilation monitoring and head elevation when suitable. Swelling, hematoma, reduced tone, residual blockade and opioids can cause obstruction after an initially reassuring extubation.

Escalate progressive swelling, respiratory effort/stridor, inability to manage secretions, worsening oxygenation or altered consciousness promptly. Do not wait for severe desaturation before calling for airway help.

Communicate airway difficulty and tube route, osteotomies, bleeding/transfusion, pack removal, fixation type/release method, drugs given and the required monitoring level. Staff should know who to call and how to obtain rapid surgical and anesthesia assistance.

Provide surgeon-specific instructions on fixation, diet, oral care, nausea, bleeding and emergency contact arrangements. Admission/discharge should follow airway risk and recovery, not a fixed fast-track deadline.

sections.title: Fire risk in the shared oral field
bullets: An oral field can bring ignition sources, gauze/drapes and oxygen or nitrous oxide together. Electrosurgery, lasers and even drill sparks can ignite combustible material; assess the planned equipment and gas delivery before it is used.

Avoid oxygen pooling beneath drapes, keep susceptible materials moist where appropriate and allow alcohol-containing preparations to dry. Coordinate oxidizer delivery and ignition-source use under the institution’s fire-prevention protocol without compromising necessary oxygenation.
Nitrous oxide supports combustion and is not a safe way to dilute oxygen near an ignition source. No single oxygen concentration or waiting interval makes every oral procedure fire-safe.

bullets: Adult clinical review draft for anesthesia professionals, not a patient-specific order set. Local difficult-airway, medication, monitoring and recovery policies and specialist clinical review remain essential before release.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: First identify catecholamine, cortisol and aldosterone secretion; “adrenal mass” does not mean nonfunctioning.
Plan for the actual approach, laterality, tumor size/invasion and possible open conversion.
Tumor manipulation, insufflation and adrenal-vein ligation can produce major changes; the endocrine phenotype determines the most likely mechanism.
Document the postoperative steroid, glucose, potassium and blood-pressure plan before surgery.

sections.title: Hormone phenotype before the operation
bullets: Review the biochemical workup and clinical findings. Evaluate relevant cortisol autonomy, primary aldosteronism and pheochromocytoma before intervention; do not infer hormonal silence from absent classic symptoms.
Adrenal biopsy or ablation also requires appropriate hormone assessment. Unrecognized catecholamine secretion can turn an apparently routine intervention into a cardiovascular emergency.

sections.title: Cardiovascular and metabolic optimization
bullets: Assess BP/rhythm, cardiomyopathy, glucose, potassium, kidney function, volume status and medications. Use phenotype-specific preparation rather than one generic adrenal anesthetic.
Suspected catecholamine secretion warrants the dedicated pheochromocytoma preparation pathway; cortisol excess and aldosterone excess need different metabolic and replacement plans.

sections.title: Airway and organ reserve
bullets: Cortisol excess may bring obesity, OSA, myopathy and cardiopulmonary disease. Preoxygenation, careful titration and a recovery plan should reflect those findings rather than assuming a small laparoscopic incision means low risk.
Catecholamine cardiomyopathy changes induction tolerance and fluid/vasoactive choices. Select drugs to the cardiac state and avoid excessive sympathetic stimulation when PPGL is present.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.
