sections.title: Approach, position & pneumoperitoneum
bullets: Confirm transperitoneal versus retroperitoneal access, side, unilateral versus bilateral resection and possible conversion to open surgery. Suspected invasive malignancy or adjacent-organ involvement changes exposure and bleeding preparation.

Secure airway, IVs and pressure points before lateral/prone positioning or robot docking. Pneumoperitoneum and positioning can reduce compliance and alter venous return; use lung-protective ventilation and individualized PEEP, CO₂ management and hemodynamic assessment.

Hemodynamic or ventilatory deterioration after insufflation warrants reassessment of pressure, positioning, bleeding and CO₂ absorption. Coordinate pauses or undocking if needed; do not keep treating a mechanical problem with escalating drug doses alone.

sections.title: Blood loss, fluids & hemodynamic differential
bullets: Prepare access and blood availability for the planned exposure and tumor complexity. An endocrine explanation for instability must not distract from hemorrhage, impaired venous return, anesthetic effects or cardiac dysfunction.

Use physiology-guided balanced crystalloid and blood replacement when needed, avoiding both depletion and overload. Urine output and blood pressure alone are imperfect volume indicators, especially during pneumoperitoneum or in catecholamine cardiomyopathy.

sections.title: Manipulation, vein ligation & tumor removal
bullets: Ask the surgeon to announce manipulation and ligation/removal. For a catecholamine-secreting tumor, be ready to transition from hypertension treatment to hypotension treatment promptly.

For a confirmed nonfunctioning mass, do not automatically use PPGL blockade or presume a hormone-withdrawal crisis. Unexpected instability still warrants a full mechanical, bleeding, drug and cardiac differential.

sections.title: Who needs glucocorticoid replacement?
bullets: Overt Cushing syndrome after unilateral adrenalectomy requires empirical postoperative glucocorticoid replacement under AAES guidance. In mild autonomous cortisol secretion, early cortisol or stimulation testing can guide the need; a universal “all unilateral cases need lifelong steroids” statement is incorrect.

Bilateral adrenal removal requires a planned endocrine-replacement pathway. Clarify prior steroid exposure, remaining adrenal tissue and discharge education rather than leaving replacement decisions until unexplained hypotension occurs.

sections.title: Potassium and antihypertensive changes
bullets: After removal of an aldosterone-producing lesion, previous potassium supplements and potassium-retaining drugs may become inappropriate. Arrange reassessment and serial potassium/renal-function checks rather than continuing the preoperative regimen by default.
Blood pressure may improve over time but is not guaranteed to normalize immediately. Titrate treatment to measured response and symptoms.

sections.title: Glucose and unexplained postoperative hypotension
bullets: In PPGL, monitor for hypoglycemia after resection and delayed BP instability. Cortisol-producing tumors introduce additional adrenal-insufficiency risk; assess both endocrine and nonendocrine causes of hypotension.
Persistent vasopressor need, arrhythmia, major blood loss or metabolic instability calls for monitored higher-acuity care. Communicate the tumor phenotype and replacement/monitoring plan explicitly.

bullets: Match analgesia to minimally invasive versus open exposure. Use multimodal non-opioid therapy/local or regional options when suitable, with opioids titrated to need; consider renal function, coagulation and respiratory risk.

Assess temperature, ventilation, pain, hemodynamic support and quantitative neuromuscular recovery before extubation. OSA, poor cardiac reserve or ongoing vasoactive support changes the recovery setting; mobilization and VTE prevention remain important.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Catecholamine excess can cause severe BP lability, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy; even a normotensive presentation does not prove a nonsecretory tumor.
Prepare functional PPGL with specialist-directed blockade and volume assessment; if beta blockade is needed, establish alpha blockade first.
Laryngoscopy, insufflation and tumor manipulation can trigger hypertension, followed by profound hypotension after vein ligation/removal.
Postoperative priorities are BP instability, hypoglycemia, arrhythmia and any adrenal-replacement requirement.

sections.title: Secretory status, location & associated disease
bullets: Review metanephrines, imaging, symptoms and prior episodes; clarify adrenal pheochromocytoma versus extra-adrenal paraganglioma and the exposure needed. A functional paraganglioma shares catecholamine hazards but is not necessarily an adrenal-replacement problem.
Consider hereditary syndromes, bilateral disease and catecholamine-related cardiac injury. Symptoms and resting BP do not fully predict the response to manipulation.

sources.label: AAES: adult adrenalectomy clinical practice guideline (2022)

sections.title: Preoperative blockade: alpha before beta
bullets: For functional PPGL, coordinate alpha blockade with endocrinology and surgery; AAES recommends preoperative blockade for at least 7 days. Choice and titration depend on BP, orthostasis, drug tolerance and team expertise rather than one universal regimen.

Add beta blockade for a defined indication only after adequate alpha blockade. Starting beta blockade first can worsen alpha-mediated vasoconstriction; beta blockade alone is not a preparation strategy.

Normal BP alone is not a reason to omit preparation in a biochemically functional tumor. Nonsecretory or atypical tumors need an expert individualized decision; they are not permission to skip the workup.

sections.title: Volume restoration without cardiac overload
bullets: Chronic vasoconstriction may contract intravascular volume. Restore volume as part of preparation, but do not blindly prescribe aggressive salt/fluid loading in heart failure, renal impairment or catecholamine cardiomyopathy.
Review orthostasis, ECG and cardiac function; echocardiography is useful when dysfunction is suspected. Establish vasoactive and fluid plans for the period after tumor removal.

sections.title: Before induction: access and rescue drugs
bullets: An arterial line before induction is generally appropriate for significant functional PPGL. Secure reliable IV access; central access and advanced cardiac monitoring depend on expected drug support and ventricular function.
Prepare titratable short-acting antihypertensive therapy and direct-acting vasopressors before starting. Agree on the trigger to stop manipulation and who announces adrenal-vein ligation.

sections.title: Induction, airway stimulation & medication cautions
bullets: Avoid abrupt sympathetic stimulation from anxiety, inadequate anesthesia, laryngoscopy and painful intervention. Choose a titratable induction based on cardiac reserve; no single drug is universally best for all PPGL patients.

Review agents capable of provoking catecholamine effects, including sympathomimetics and dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide. Avoid a reflex ketamine/ephedrine strategy; use the specialist plan rather than memorized drug lists without context.

sections.title: Tumor manipulation: hypertension and arrhythmia
bullets: Communicate with the surgeon, reduce or pause the provoking stimulus when possible, assess anesthetic depth and treat with titratable short-acting vasodilator/alpha-directed therapy. Nicardipine, nitroprusside and phentolamine are among reported options; select for patient physiology and local expertise.

Treat tachyarrhythmia in context, including ischemia and electrolyte disturbances, rather than giving beta blockade as the sole response to unopposed catecholamine vasoconstriction. Watch ventricular performance as well as arterial pressure.

sections.title: After ligation: abrupt hypotension
bullets: Catecholamine withdrawal, residual blockade and relative depletion can combine after removal. Stop or reduce antihypertensive infusions promptly as appropriate; assess blood loss and cardiac function alongside vasodilation.

Use measured volume replacement and direct-acting vasopressors titrated to perfusion; vasopressin may be considered in refractory vasodilatory hypotension. Persistent instability needs a broad assessment, not unlimited fluid administration.

Reassess preoperative insulin requirements after tumor removal and treat measured abnormalities. Do not rely on tachycardia or sweating to detect hypoglycemia in an anesthetized or beta-blocked patient.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Determine obstruction severity, location, object type and urgency; an asphyxiating object is not an elective bronchoscopy.
Flexible and rigid bronchoscopy have different retrieval and ventilation advantages; rigid backup may be needed.
Removal may require withdrawing the tube and object together, temporarily losing airway control.
Plan for displacement, complete obstruction, bleeding and airway trauma before the first extraction attempt.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)

sections.title: Object, location & physiologic urgency
bullets: Review onset, symptoms, imaging when available, oxygenation and the object’s size, shape and likely sharpness. Chronic retained objects may have granulation and infection rather than a dramatic choking history.
Do not delay urgent airway relief for a complete diagnostic workup when the object is asphyxiating. For stable cases, plan retrieval from the actual location and inspect for additional objects.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)

sections.title: Team, equipment & backup
bullets: Agree on flexible versus rigid bronchoscopy and have the equipment/operator needed for rescue. Rigid bronchoscopy is particularly useful with severe distress, difficult extraction, sharp objects or significant bleeding.

Plan who re-establishes ventilation if the airway device must be removed and what happens if the object lodges at the glottis. Surgical-airway and surgical-complication escalation must be immediately actionable.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)

sections.title: Sedation versus GA
bullets: A cooperative stable adult may undergo selected flexible retrieval with sedation; others need GA. Choose for object location, obstruction, reserve, expected technique and rescue feasibility.

Spontaneous breathing may help in some situations but can also allow airway collapse; positive pressure may assist ventilation but can move an object distally. Neither strategy is universally correct.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)

sections.title: Tube lumen & en-bloc removal
bullets: A foreign body may not fit through the tracheal tube. Anticipate removal of the tube, scope, retrieval device and object en bloc, with a period of unprotected or uncontrolled airway.
A supraglottic airway or rigid barrel may permit larger-object passage, but does not eliminate the possibility of en-bloc extraction. Match device geometry to the object and plan for reintubation.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)

sections.title: Ventilation during grasping and withdrawal
bullets: Coordinate any pause in positive-pressure or jet ventilation during object grasping and passage through the glottis. Continuously communicate oxygenation and the need to interrupt extraction.
If jet ventilation is used, ensure adequate expiration and monitor for gas trapping and barotrauma. Stop and reassess unexplained hypoxemia, pressure changes or circulatory deterioration.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)
StatPearls: airway for laser surgery (2022)

sections.title: Displacement & complete obstruction
bullets: Maintain visual control during withdrawal and avoid dislodging the object against airway structures. A newly central object can turn partial obstruction into complete obstruction.

If ventilation fails, immediately activate the agreed bronchoscopic/airway rescue plan. The experienced operator may need to reposition or retrieve the object; repeated blind manipulation can worsen obstruction or injury.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update

sections.title: Bleeding & airway injury
bullets: Granulation tissue can bleed during removal. Assess the ability to ventilate and clear the airway, not only estimated blood volume. Rigid bronchoscopy may facilitate suction, tamponade and control.
Major bleeding, suspected bronchial injury or persistent airway compromise warrants surgical escalation. Thermal hemostatic tools introduce their own airway-fire requirements.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)
StatPearls: airway for laser surgery (2022)

sections.title: Monitoring & access when the head is turned away
bullets: Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic depth, including continual assessment of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. For a tracheal or supraglottic airway, confirm placement and monitor exhaled CO₂; oxygen saturation alone does not establish adequate ventilation.

Before the table turns or drapes limit access, secure the airway/circuit and IV connections and agree how to regain access quickly. Recheck ventilation after positioning or changes in the operative field.

sections.title: Confirm removal & reassess the airway
bullets: After retrieval, the bronchoscopist should reassess for retained fragments, another object, bleeding or residual obstruction. A single extracted fragment does not establish that the entire problem is resolved.
Review persistent ventilation asymmetry or oxygenation difficulty for obstruction, trauma, atelectasis or another complication rather than assuming immediate full recovery after extraction.

sources.label: Adult airway foreign-body retrieval: clinical review (2017)

sections.title: Emergence & extubation readiness
bullets: Assess hemostasis, secretions, swelling and the difficulty of reintubation before removing airway support. Smooth emergence is desirable, but suppressing cough must not come at the expense of protective reflexes or ventilation in a contaminated or difficult airway.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. A visually detectable facial twitch or a short case does not establish full recovery.

Choose timing, location and assistance for extubation, with a specific reintubation plan when risk is elevated. Persistent edema, bleeding or inadequate ventilation may require delayed extubation rather than an obligatory operating-room extubation.

sections.title: Recovery monitoring & handoff
bullets: Continue appropriate monitoring during transfer and recovery, with assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature. Select postoperative observation for the patient’s airway risk, support needs and actual course.

Handoff should include the airway technique/difficulty, operation, bleeding or swelling concerns, packs remaining, analgesia/antiemetics and any rescue plan. New respiratory difficulty or progressive neck/oral swelling requires prompt escalation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Awake flexible-bronchoscopic intubation is one form of awake tracheal intubation; videolaryngoscopy is another option.
Use oxygen, tested topical anesthesia, an explicit backup plan and minimal carefully titrated sedation if needed.
DAS gives topical lidocaine 9 mg/kg lean body weight as a ceiling, not a target; account for every route and patient-specific limits.
Do not induce GA until visual confirmation and capnography establish correct tracheal tube placement.

sections.title: Indication & choice of awake technique
bullets: Consider awake intubation with predictors of difficult airway management, especially when ventilation, aspiration risk, apnea tolerance or invasive rescue would make induction unsafe.

Flexible bronchoscopy and awake videolaryngoscopy are options selected for anatomy, mouth opening, blood/secretions, cooperation and operator skill. The old small supraglottic-assisted case series is not a universal protocol.

sections.title: Consent, cooperation & explanation
bullets: Explain the purpose, sequence, expected sensations and communication signals while preserving the patient’s participation. Patient refusal is the absolute contraindication in DAS guidance; inability to cooperate requires reassessment of feasibility and alternatives.
Airway bleeding/soiling can make flexible visualization difficult and is a relative limitation rather than proof that every awake technique is impossible. Plan suction and alternative approaches.

sources.label: DAS adult awake-intubation guideline: full text

sections.title: Team briefing, position & equipment
bullets: Brief roles, primary technique, alternate device and emergency front-of-neck plan. Prepare oxygen, suction, tube, scope/device and topicalization before starting.
Use positioning suited to anatomy and breathing comfort. Arrange assistance and a more experienced operator before repeated attempts become necessary.

sources.label: DAS: awake tracheal intubation in adults (2019)

sections.title: Oxygenation & physiologic monitoring
bullets: Administer supplemental oxygen throughout ATI. Monitor ECG, pressure, oxygen saturation and ventilation/capnography where feasible; maintain awareness of sedation and respiratory effort.
Oxygenation does not guarantee ventilation or airway patency. Stop and reassess obstruction or oversedation rather than escalating sedation to force the procedure.

sources.label: DAS adult awake-intubation guideline: full text

sections.title: Topical anesthesia & cumulative lidocaine
bullets: Establish and test effective topicalization before advancing instruments. Sedation must not compensate for inadequate airway anesthesia.
The DAS maximum topical lidocaine dose is 9 mg/kg LEAN body weight, not actual body weight and not a target. Lower doses/limits may be appropriate for patient factors or local policy.

Count all topical, injected and other local-anesthetic exposure, document delivered dose and have LAST resources available. Do not interpret the ATI ceiling as a general infiltration-dose recommendation.

sources.label: DAS: awake tracheal intubation in adults (2019)

sections.title: Minimal sedation & independent attention
bullets: Minimal, cautious sedation can be useful, ideally administered by an independent practitioner. Preserve cooperation and spontaneous breathing; dose for reserve and response rather than a fixed recipe.
If oversedation occurs, stop/reverse as appropriate and restore oxygenation/ventilation. A deeper anesthetic plane may convert a controlled awake plan into an uncontrolled difficult airway.

sources.label: DAS: awake tracheal intubation in adults (2019)

sections.title: Oral versus nasal route
bullets: Choose route for anatomy, surgical access and nasal safety. For the nasal route, use appropriate vasoconstriction and gentle technique and reassess bleeding or significant resistance.
Consider tube diameter, length, compatibility with the scope/device and postoperative needs. Successful visualization is not the same as successful tube passage.

sources.label: DAS adult awake-intubation guideline: full text

sections.title: Two-point confirmation before induction
bullets: Confirm visually that the tube is in the trachea and obtain capnographic confirmation before inducing anesthesia. Do not rely solely on a view previously obtained before railroading the tube.
Secure the tube and reassess depth and ventilation after changing position or removing the scope/adjunct device.

sources.label: DAS: awake tracheal intubation in adults (2019)

sections.title: Attempts & unsuccessful ATI
bullets: Limit attempts to three, with one additional attempt by a more experienced operator (3 + 1). Change/optimize the approach between attempts rather than repeating the same failed maneuver.

After unsuccessful ATI, call for help, oxygenate, stop/reverse sedation if needed and prepare rescue. Postponement is the default when clinically feasible; essential urgent airway management requires an explicit expert-led alternative, potentially awake front-of-neck access.

Do not default automatically to routine induction after failed awake intubation. If high-risk GA is unavoidable, formulate an achievable rescue strategy and have the appropriate team immediately available.

bullets: Document indication, technique, route, topical drug/dose, attempts and complications. Communicate difficult-airway information to the patient and future clinicians.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A clear, motionless field is important near the orbit and skull base; plan airway security before access is restricted.
Assess OSA, asthma, aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, prior surgery and anticipated bleeding.

Before the table turns or drapes limit access, secure the airway/circuit and IV connections and agree how to regain access quickly. Recheck ventilation after positioning or changes in the operative field.

sections.title: Small tube & controlled ventilation
bullets: Use the smallest appropriate tube that still permits adequate ventilation and planned surgery; consider external diameter, resistance and the lesion. Avoid traumatizing the operative site during placement.

sections.title: Jet ventilation: expiration must remain possible
bullets: Jet ventilation requires a patent expiratory path, appropriate equipment and experienced operators. Obstruction or inadequate exhalation time can cause air trapping, barotrauma, pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum.

Assess chest movement, oxygenation and CO₂ with methods suited to the open system; standard end-tidal values may be limited. Longer cases may require additional CO₂ assessment. Predetermine when to stop surgery and switch to a secured airway.

sections.title: Apneic and spontaneous techniques
bullets: Intermittent apnea and high-flow oxygen may improve exposure but do not provide unlimited safe apnea or reliable CO₂ clearance. Set patient-specific limits and a prompt ventilation/reintubation plan rather than copying a published maximum time.
Spontaneous techniques preserve movement and may compromise surgical conditions or ventilation. Avoid calling any tubeless approach universally safer than a secured airway.

sections.title: Laser fire prevention
bullets: Agree on activation commands, lowest clinically feasible oxygen concentration, avoidance of nitrous oxide and oxidizer washout before laser use. If oxygenation requires escalation, stop the ignition source and reassess the plan.

Use a suitable laser-resistant tube when indicated and manage cuffs according to device/protocol instructions; saline with a visible dye is commonly recommended. Keep saline immediately available, protect exposed materials and use wavelength-specific eye protection.
Neither a low FiO₂ nor absence of a tracheal tube eliminates fire risk. Avoid treating experimental high-flow/laser combinations as permission for routine oxygen-rich laser work.

sections.title: Airway fire: coordinated immediate actions
bullets: Declare the fire and stop laser/ignition and oxidizer delivery while the team removes burning airway material and extinguishes with saline, following the institutional airway-fire protocol. These actions require rapid coordination, not a slow sequential checklist.

After extinction, re-establish oxygenation/ventilation, inspect the removed tube/material and assess the airway with appropriate endoscopy for injury or retained debris. Escalate to critical care and a definitive airway plan as indicated.

sections.title: Anesthesia, immobility & analgesia
bullets: TIVA may be useful when ventilation is interrupted or gas delivery is unreliable. Coordinate depth, immobility and any relaxant use with the chosen ventilation technique.

sections.title: Emergence & extubation readiness
bullets: Assess hemostasis, secretions, swelling and the difficulty of reintubation before removing airway support. Smooth emergence is desirable, but suppressing cough must not come at the expense of protective reflexes or ventilation in a contaminated or difficult airway.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. A visually detectable facial twitch or a short case does not establish full recovery.

Choose timing, location and assistance for extubation, with a specific reintubation plan when risk is elevated. Persistent edema, bleeding or inadequate ventilation may require delayed extubation rather than an obligatory operating-room extubation.

bullets: Review symptoms, prior airway records, mouth opening, neck movement and the actual lesion on available imaging/endoscopy. Prior surgery or radiation can reduce tissue mobility; apparently reassuring external anatomy does not exclude internal obstruction.

Consider awake airway management when anticipated difficult intubation is accompanied by difficult ventilation, aspiration risk, poor apnea tolerance or difficult emergency invasive access. Match technique and location to available expertise and an immediately usable rescue plan.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. A visually detectable facial twitch or a short case does not establish full recovery.

Choose timing, location and assistance for extubation, with a specific reintubation plan when risk is elevated. Persistent edema, bleeding or inadequate ventilation may require delayed extubation rather than an obligatory operating-room extubation.

bullets: This reference is adult-scoped: assess OSA, infection, bleeding risk and the actual tonsil/adenoid procedure.
Plan for a stimulated shared airway, mouth-gag placement and blood/secretions before emergence.
PROSPECT supports acetaminophen, an NSAID when appropriate and a single IV dexamethasone dose, with opioids reserved for rescue.

bullets: An oral RAE or other appropriate oral tracheal tube is commonly used, positioned to permit surgical access. Confirm depth, cuff integrity and ventilation after final head position and mouth-gag placement.

bullets: Routine anesthetist-inserted throat packs are not recommended by the adult DAS/BAOMS/ENT-UK consensus. If one is indicated, use an explicit insertion/removal record, reminder and handoff process; it is not a substitute for airway protection.

Account for removable packs/materials and suction blood, clots and debris before extubation. Distinguish a throat pack that must be removed from nasal packing intentionally left by the surgeon, and communicate the latter at handoff.

New or recurrent bleeding after discharge requires urgent assessment. If return to surgery is needed, reassess volume status, airway edema/contamination and aspiration risk; the previous easy anesthetic does not guarantee the same conditions now.

sections.title: Procedure-specific baseline analgesia
bullets: The PROSPECT guideline recommends acetaminophen plus an NSAID unless contraindicated, continued postoperatively, and a single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose for analgesic/antiemetic benefit. Individual renal, bleeding, gastrointestinal and other risks still matter.

Reviewed NSAID studies did not establish an increased bleeding signal sufficient to exclude the class routinely. This is not a claim of zero bleeding risk or permission to ignore an individual contraindication.

sections.title: Rescue opioids & adjunct limitations
bullets: Use opioids as rescue with attention to respiratory risk, especially OSA and concomitant sedatives. Avoid automatically adding sedating gabapentinoids to an opioid-containing recovery plan.

Routine local infiltration is not a simple low-risk substitute for systemic analgesia; the review describes limited-duration benefit and serious adverse events. Its ketamine recommendation as an alternative is pediatric-specific and is not adopted here as an adult routine.

sections.title: PONV, hydration & oral intake

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult epiglottitis/supraglottitis can deteriorate rapidly; assess severity and involve expert airway and ENT support early.
Not every adult requires intubation, but conservative care requires close monitoring and rapid access to airway intervention.
No single awake or anesthetized technique is proven best for every severity; prepare for failed intubation and front-of-neck rescue.
Medical therapy does not replace airway protection when obstruction or respiratory deterioration demands it.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)

sections.title: Severity & immediate priorities
bullets: Assess breathing effort, stridor, secretion handling, oxygenation, posture, trajectory and available airway information without provoking unnecessary distress. Severe disease can distort or obscure the laryngeal inlet.
Airway intervention is driven by severity, progression, reserve and available rescue, not a rule that every adult must be intubated or that a currently acceptable saturation makes the airway safe.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)

sections.title: Location, personnel & surgical backup
bullets: Use a location with expert anesthesia/ENT support and immediate rescue capability when time permits. A deteriorating patient may require intervention where they are; transfer must not delay lifesaving airway management.
Prepare for emergency front-of-neck access before attempting a high-risk airway. A difficult surgical airway may coexist with difficult laryngoscopy.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update

sections.title: Awake techniques: benefits and limits
bullets: Awake flexible intubation may suit a cooperative, sufficiently stable patient in experienced hands. The review’s high reported success came from selected less severe cases, not a randomized comparison proving universal superiority.

Severe obstruction, secretions, agitation or inadequate time can defeat an awake plan. Reassess feasibility and have an alternative rather than persisting because “awake is safest” was chosen initially.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)

sections.title: Anesthetized techniques & spontaneous breathing
bullets: Induction can worsen obstruction. Inhalational approaches preserving spontaneous breathing are described, but preservation of breathing is not a guarantee against airway loss.

Neuromuscular blockade remains a context-dependent decision in the evidence review; it is not established as universally required or universally prohibited. Choose an expert-led strategy with immediate backup.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)

sections.title: Visualization, tube passage & rescue
bullets: Edema and distorted anatomy can prevent both visualization and tube passage. Prepare suitable tube sizes and alternatives, but do not allow repeated attempts to consume the remaining oxygenation window.
Video or flexible instruments do not guarantee success when the inlet is obstructed or obscured. Prioritize oxygenation and timely rescue over repeated device changes without a coherent plan.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update

sections.title: Sedation, topicalization & tolerance
bullets: Avoid uncontrolled sedation that removes airway tone or cooperation before a definitive strategy is ready. If awake topicalization is used, dose and monitor it deliberately under the awake-airway pathway.
Do not force instrumentation through severe obstruction or assume that additional sedative will solve a poor view. Reassess anatomy, secretions and rescue options.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)
DAS adult awake-intubation guideline: full text

sections.title: Concurrent medical treatment
bullets: Coordinate treatment of the underlying infectious or noninfectious process with the treating team. Antibiotics, steroids and other adjuncts described in reports do not establish one universal regimen or remove the need for airway protection.
Do not postpone necessary airway intervention while waiting for medication response in a deteriorating patient.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)

sections.title: Failure & front-of-neck escalation
bullets: Recognize failure early and call for immediate help. The review documents significant failed-intubation risk and severe consequences of hypoxic deterioration.
Use the planned oxygenation and front-of-neck pathway when required; a second routine induction attempt is not a substitute for emergency rescue.

sources.label: BJA Open: adult epiglottitis airway systematic review (2024)

sections.title: After the airway is secured
bullets: Confirm tracheal placement with capnography, secure the tube and provide appropriate intensive monitoring and ongoing treatment. Avoid unnecessary tube displacement in a still-swollen airway.
Document the technique, degree of difficulty, airway findings and rescue plan so subsequent teams do not treat the airway as ordinary after initial stabilization.

sections.title: Resolution & planned extubation
bullets: Base extubation on improvement in edema/infection, respiratory status and protection, with specialist reassessment and reintubation readiness. Published median ventilation durations are not a timer for individual extubation.
A cuff leak alone cannot guarantee safety. Select personnel, setting and equipment for the residual airway risk.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Plan immobility and airway security for middle-ear repair with limited access to the head.
Avoid nitrous oxide-related pressure changes that can disturb the reconstruction.
Coordinate any facial nerve monitoring with neuromuscular-blocking drugs.
Prioritize PONV prevention and a smooth but safe emergence.

sections.title: Graft, ossicles & associated surgery
bullets: Confirm tympanic membrane repair alone versus ossicular reconstruction or combined mastoid work. This changes duration, operative sensitivity to movement and whether facial nerve monitoring is required.
Selected cooperative adults may have local anesthesia with sedation, but GA is frequently chosen for immobility, comfort and surgical preference.

sections.title: Preoperative hearing & communication
bullets: Establish how to communicate when hearing aids are removed, and document relevant baseline hearing, vertigo and facial function. Review prior ear operations and anesthetic/PONV history.
Choose technique for duration, cooperation, comorbidity and rescue access; a hearing impairment is not itself an indication for deep sedation.

sections.title: Airway and head positioning
bullets: A tracheal tube is often selected for prolonged surgery and controlled ventilation; a supraglottic airway may suit selected patients. Secure it before turning the head and restricting access.
Avoid excessive head rotation or pressure and recheck circuit/tube position. Movement during microsurgery can be consequential even when blood loss is small.

sections.title: Facial nerve monitoring & neuromuscular blockade
bullets: Confirm whether facial nerve EMG/stimulation is planned and when a usable signal is required. Neuromuscular blockade can suppress the motor response; agree on any induction dose, redosing and reversal strategy with the surgeon before giving additional relaxant.

Use quantitative peripheral neuromuscular monitoring to inform drug recovery, but do not equate an operative facial-nerve signal with readiness for extubation. A lost signal requires consideration of residual blockade, electrodes, stimulation and surgical causes.

sections.title: Middle-ear pressure & field quality
bullets: Nitrous oxide is generally avoided for middle-ear reconstruction because its uptake and subsequent washout can change cavity pressure and disturb repair or graft position. This concern is different from simply reducing PONV.

Optimize head position, venous drainage and stable ventilation with the surgeon. A dry field does not justify a universal low blood-pressure target; weigh any deliberate pressure reduction against organ perfusion and patient reserve.

sources.label: BJA Education: anesthesia for major middle-ear surgery (2019)

sections.title: Maintenance & surgical field
bullets: TIVA is frequently useful for immobility and PONV reduction. A volatile technique without nitrous oxide can also be appropriate; choose for the patient and the monitoring requirements.
Optimize ventilation and venous drainage before escalating deliberate hypotension. Minor field bleeding may be important surgically, but it does not justify compromising systemic perfusion.

sources.label: BJA Education: anesthesia for major middle-ear surgery (2019)

sections.title: Analgesia, vertigo & PONV
bullets: Middle-ear surgery has substantial nausea/vertigo potential. Use risk-based multimodal prophylaxis and consider propofol TIVA when appropriate; rescue persistent PONV with a suitable alternative class rather than repeating an ineffective regimen without reassessment.

Coordinate surgeon-administered local anesthesia with acetaminophen, an NSAID when appropriate and titrated rescue opioid. Avoid unnecessary sedation that obscures respiratory recovery or worsens dizziness.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: PFO and secundum ASD closure share catheter techniques but differ in indication and physiology; do not treat them as equivalent shunts.
For ASD, assess shunt burden, RV remodeling, pulmonary vascular disease and LV filling reserve before closure.
Eliminate air from IV/catheter systems and avoid avoidable increases in right-sided pressure; right-to-left flow permits paradoxical embolism.
TEE/GA or ICE/sedation depends on anatomy and expertise; assess device stability, residual shunt, rhythm and effusion afterward.

sources.label: ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)
AHA: 2025 ACHD guideline key points (summary only)
SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: PFO is not simply a small ASD
bullets: PFO closure is selected for an appropriate clinical indication after evaluation of competing causes; the presence of a PFO alone is not an indication. AF-associated stroke is not automatically treated by PFO closure.
A secundum ASD may cause meaningful left-to-right volume loading and RV enlargement. Confirm defect type and pulmonary venous anatomy; not all atrial defects suit device closure.

sources.label: ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)
SCAI ICE position statement (2025)
ESC AF guideline (2024)

sections.title: Pulmonary hypertension and closure suitability
bullets: Assess pulmonary vascular resistance and shunt direction with the congenital/structural team. Severe irreversible pulmonary vascular disease or Eisenmenger physiology can make closure harmful.

Avoid a single PVR cutoff presented as a complete eligibility rule. Treatment response, shunt magnitude, ventricular function and possible fenestration require current ACHD guideline and expert-center review.

sources.label: ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)
AHA: 2025 ACHD guideline key points (summary only)

sections.title: LV filling reserve after ASD closure
bullets: In impaired LV systolic/diastolic function, eliminating an atrial decompression route can increase filling pressures and precipitate HF.
Selected patients need balloon-occlusion hemodynamic assessment and a decision between complete, fenestrated or no closure; anesthesia loading conditions should be communicated.

sources.label: ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)

sections.title: Imaging and anesthesia choice
bullets: ICE can support selected PFO/ASD closure under sedation, while TEE may require deeper anesthesia or GA. Match technique to anatomy, patient tolerance and team experience.
Additional ICE access and intracardiac manipulation introduce their own vascular/perforation risks; absence of a TEE probe is not absence of procedural risk.

sources.label: SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: Air elimination and shunt physiology
bullets: Meticulously de-air all IV lines, injections and catheter systems. A right-to-left communication permits systemic embolization.
Maintain oxygenation, ventilation and hemodynamic stability; avoid excessive airway pressures or other preventable factors that increase right-sided pressure.

sources.label: ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)
SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: Device, rhythm and mechanical complications
bullets: Assess device position, residual shunt, obstruction and effusion before release/completion. New hypotension or hypoxemia needs prompt imaging and a procedural differential.
Watch for atrial arrhythmia and device-related complications; emergency retrieval/surgical capability should be coordinated with the intervention team.

sources.label: SCAI ICE position statement (2025)
ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)

sections.title: Recovery and follow-up
bullets: Document device and residual-shunt findings, rhythm, hemostasis and the individualized antiplatelet/anticoagulant instructions.
Arrange congenital/structural follow-up and imaging. Persistent or new dyspnea, chest pain, syncope or neurologic symptoms requires evaluation rather than presumed normal recovery.

sources.label: ESC adult congenital heart disease guideline (2020/2021)
SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: Room, airway access & team briefing
bullets: Apply operating-room standards to anesthesia in the EP/hybrid lab. Before draping, confirm oxygen, suction, airway equipment, emergency assistance, radiation protection and the route for urgent transfer or conversion.

Position the airway, breathing circuit, IV extensions and defibrillator connections so they remain accessible around the imaging equipment. Agree how the table and drapes will move if ventilation or resuscitation is required.

sources.label: ASA Statement on Nonoperating Room Anesthesia Services (2023)

sections.title: Monitoring & physiologic surveillance
bullets: For anesthesia care, continuously assess oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Use ECG, pulse oximetry and blood pressure/heart rate at least every five minutes; moderate/deep sedation requires exhaled CO₂ monitoring unless precluded or invalidated.

Choose invasive pressure monitoring and additional access for ventricular dysfunction, expected instability, repeated induced arrhythmia or major procedural risk, not simply because the case is in a cath lab. Confirm a perfusing pulse rather than relying on an ECG pacing spike.

bullets: Adult clinical-review draft for anesthesia professionals. This is not an individualized order set, pediatric/congenital dosing guide, device instruction manual or authorization to perform a procedure.

title: Atrial Fibrillation Ablation / Pulmonary Vein Isolation

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Left-atrial ablation combines transseptal access, anticoagulation and prolonged immobility; choose GA, deep sedation or conscious sedation with the EP team.
Plan airway access before draping and procedural heparinization; confirm anticoagulant adherence, thrombus assessment, ventricular function and the imaging strategy.
Distinguish RF thermal injury, cryoballoon phrenic-nerve monitoring and PFA-specific muscle contraction, coronary spasm and hemolysis/renal risk.
Treat unexpected hypotension as possible tamponade, bleeding, ischemia or arrhythmia; after recovery provide explicit delayed-complication and anticoagulation instructions.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)
PFA complications review (2026; registry and observational evidence)
AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Before induction: rhythm, function & thrombus
bullets: Review AF burden, prior ablation, LA/LV/RV function, heart failure, pulmonary disease/OSA and prior airway difficulty. Confirm whether TEE, ICE or delayed-phase CT will exclude atrial thrombus.
Therapeutic anticoagulation does not make thrombus impossible. Known left-atrial thrombus precludes elective catheter ablation until the specialist pathway resolves the risk.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)
ESC AF guideline (2024)

sections.title: Technique, airway & ventilation
bullets: GA gives controlled ventilation and immobility; deep or conscious sedation remains an option for selected patients and experienced teams. Anticipate obstruction or conversion when access to the head is limited.

Coordinate ventilation changes and apnea with mapping. Specialized high-frequency/low-volume approaches may improve stability but require expertise and CO₂/pressure surveillance; they are not default settings for every patient.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)
AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Anticoagulation, transseptal access & embolism
bullets: Verify the prescribed oral-anticoagulant plan, adherence and thrombus-exclusion strategy before left-atrial ablation. Do not independently stop or bridge anticoagulation; a secured airway does not imply the patient was previously unanticoagulated.

The 2024 AF consensus supports intraprocedural UFH adjusted to ACT at least 300 seconds, with initial heparin before transseptal puncture reasonable. Use the EP protocol for timing, repeat ACT, sheath management and reversal; do not import a cardiopulmonary-bypass ACT target.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)

sections.title: RF, cryoballoon and PFA are not interchangeable
bullets: RF near the posterior left atrium can injure the esophagus; cryoballoon techniques particularly require phrenic-nerve surveillance. Confirm the energy system, lesion set and operator protection strategy.
PFA is nonthermal electroporation with a different collateral-injury profile, not a guarantee of zero injury. It still carries vascular, perforation, embolic and anesthesia risks.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)
PFA complications review (2026; registry and observational evidence)

sections.title: Esophageal protection & delayed fistula
bullets: Coordinate temperature monitoring, cooling or other protection used by the center for thermal ablation. Temperature probes do not guarantee prevention; avoid presenting one probe threshold as a universal safe limit.

Delayed fever, chest pain, dysphagia, GI bleeding or neurologic symptoms after left-atrial thermal ablation require urgent assessment for esophageal injury/atrioesophageal fistula. Communicate the ablation history immediately and avoid routine esophageal instrumentation when fistula is suspected.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)

sections.title: Phrenic monitoring & neuromuscular blockade
bullets: If diaphragm response is required, agree on NMBA timing, recovery and any reversal before nerve stimulation. Paralysis can mask an important injury warning.
New dyspnea or reduced diaphragmatic movement after ablation deserves evaluation rather than being attributed automatically to residual sedation.

sources.label: EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS AF ablation consensus (2024)

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: An ILR is a small, leadless, subcutaneous device used for extended rhythm monitoring. Indications described include recurrent palpitations, unexplained syncope, and detecting occult atrial fibrillation after stroke.

Placement uses a small incision and a subcutaneous pocket on the left chest. Programming, recording and symptom-marking workflows are device-specific. Confirm the implanted model and follow electrophysiology/manufacturer instructions rather than assuming magnet activation.

For example, LINQ II patient guidance describes automatic data transmission and, when prescribed, symptom marking through its supported app/Patient Assistant workflow. Symptom marking is not a universal magnet-based activation instruction for all implantable loop recorders.

The source descriptions give different rib-level landmarks. Avoid treating either as a universal placement specification; the supplied evidence does not establish a single landmark for all devices or patients.

sections.title: Leaflet grasping and ventilation coordination

sections.title: Recovery and complication warnings
bullets: Assess hemostasis, neurologic status, rhythm/perfusion and effusion concern before discharge; same-day care is selective.
New dyspnea, syncope, chest symptoms or neurologic deficit requires urgent evaluation. A completed device release does not eliminate delayed bleeding or thromboembolic risk.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)
SCAI/HRS LAAO guideline (2025; corrected December 2025)

sections.title: Room, airway access & team briefing
bullets: Apply operating-room standards to anesthesia in the EP/hybrid lab. Before draping, confirm oxygen, suction, airway equipment, emergency assistance, radiation protection and the route for urgent transfer or conversion.

Position the airway, breathing circuit, IV extensions and defibrillator connections so they remain accessible around the imaging equipment. Agree how the table and drapes will move if ventilation or resuscitation is required.

sources.label: ASA Statement on Nonoperating Room Anesthesia Services (2023)
AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Monitoring & physiologic surveillance
bullets: For anesthesia care, continuously assess oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Use ECG, pulse oximetry and blood pressure/heart rate at least every five minutes; moderate/deep sedation requires exhaled CO₂ monitoring unless precluded or invalidated.

Choose invasive pressure monitoring and additional access for ventricular dysfunction, expected instability, repeated induced arrhythmia or major procedural risk, not simply because the case is in a cath lab. Confirm a perfusing pulse rather than relying on an ECG pacing spike.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical review
bullets: Adult clinical-review draft for anesthesia professionals. This is not an individualized order set, pediatric/congenital dosing guide, device instruction manual or authorization to perform a procedure.

Guidelines, position statements, narrative reviews and model-specific instructions have different evidence strength. Use the actual device instructions, heart-team plan and current local protocols; clinical signoff remains required.
