overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For a superficial cutaneous abscess in an immunocompetent patient without complicating risks, incision and drainage under local anesthetic is generally sufficient; the procedure is the accepted treatment.

Anorectal abscesses require prompt drainage. Small superficial cases may be managed in a clinic or emergency department with local infiltration; deep, extensive, or higher-risk cases warrant management under anesthesia.
Procedural pain is a major practical concern. In anorectal disease, assess for systemic sepsis and comorbidity; patient comfort during drainage helps permit thorough examination of the cavity.
Recovery priorities include reassessing the wound, providing wound-care instructions and adequate analgesia, and applying postanesthesia monitoring standards when anesthesia care has been provided.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For superficial cutaneous abscesses, drainage is the central treatment; local anesthetic is generally sufficient only for the population specified in the review: immunocompetent patients without confounding risks.

For anorectal abscesses, select the setting and anesthetic support according to depth, extent, sepsis severity, and patient risk. The anorectal review advises an examination under anesthesia before drainage when feasible; it does not establish a universal anesthetic technique.

For anorectal drainage, the approach is anatomy-specific. The source describes lateral decubitus or knee-elbow positioning for outpatient perianal or ischiorectal drainage, and lithotomy, Lloyd-Davies, or prone jackknife for larger/deeper cases or EUA.

The anorectal review advises adequate drainage while avoiding sphincter injury and generally avoiding probing the cavity to identify a fistula tract; inflammation can create false tracts and probing can risk sphincter injury.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For anorectal disease, assess sepsis severity and perform a disease-specific history and examination, including perineal and digital rectal examination. Relevant history includes sphincter function, prior anorectal procedures, blood-thinner use, and personal or family history of inflammatory bowel disease.

The anorectal source recommends laboratory assessment including CBC, creatinine, inflammatory markers, blood glucose, and HbA1c. Diabetes and other immunocompromised states are identified as risk modifiers; this is not an anesthesia-specific testing protocol.
Consider occult, recurrent, or complex disease and Crohn disease where clinically relevant; the source recommends selective imaging rather than routine imaging for all patients.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The sources do not define a procedure-specific room configuration. Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic actually provided; the ASA standard applies to general, regional, and monitored anesthesia care.

During anesthesia, qualified anesthesia personnel must remain present, and oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature must be continually evaluated. Blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the stated standard.
For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The available abscess sources do not specify an airway device or a comparative anesthetic technique. Airway management should therefore not be inferred from the procedure name alone; technique selection remains dependent on the individual case and the intended level of anesthesia.

If general anesthesia is used, assess ventilation continually; when an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, with quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis through transfer preparation as specified by the standard.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Plan for substantial procedural pain, particularly during cavity exploration and disruption of loculations. Local anesthetic can be less effective within the acidic abscess environment; the review describes perimeter infiltration as an advocated approach, not a proven universal regimen.

For anorectal drainage, the source describes saline irrigation and hemostasis by direct pressure, cautery, or lignocaine with adrenaline. These are reported procedural options, not an anesthesia-specific protocol.

Routine packing is not recommended by the anorectal source unless needed for hemostasis; it reports increased pain and no benefit in healing or fistula formation. The older superficial cutaneous review notes that evidence for packing is lacking, so do not treat its case-specific packing choice as a standard.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anorectal abscess may be associated with sepsis, perineal cellulitis, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, or Fournier gangrene. The source supports prompt recognition and severity-based timing, but does not provide an anesthesia resuscitation algorithm.

Postoperative anorectal complications include hemorrhage, urinary retention, surgical-site infection, sphincter-related incontinence, pudendal nerve injury, and anal stricture. Escalation and management details are not specified in the supplied source.

Fistula assessment requires caution: the source notes that probing amid inflammation and induration can create false tracts and risk sphincter injury; primary fistulotomy is described as controversial and dependent on anatomy and expertise.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The anorectal source describes local hemostatic measures but provides no fluid regimen, blood-loss thresholds, transfusion guidance, or intraoperative physiologic targets. No universal fluid or blood-management prescription can be derived from these sources.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local anesthesia is important to procedural comfort, but the evidence review found no randomized trials then evaluating optimal pain control for superficial cutaneous abscess I&D. Its cited local-anesthetic approaches are based on textbooks or expert opinion, not comparative proof.

After anorectal drainage, provide adequate analgesia and wound-care instructions; the source does not specify an analgesic drug or regimen. PONV prevention or treatment is not addressed in the abscess-specific sources.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The abscess sources do not establish emergence timing or a recovery-room protocol. After anesthesia care, use an appropriate postanesthesia-care area, transport monitoring/support appropriate to condition, and continual recovery evaluation.

During the initial phase of recovery from anesthesia, the ASA standard requires a quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry. Continue observation appropriate to the patient’s condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.
For anorectal wound care, the source advises absorbent dressings, hygiene, sitz baths, adequate analgesia, and follow-up until healing; it notes healing may take up to eight weeks.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The superficial cutaneous abscess article is an older evidence-based narrative review focused mainly on immunocompetent patients without confounding risks. It is not an anesthesia reference and reports no anesthesia-specific assessment or airway protocol.

The anorectal source is an educational review, not an anesthesia guideline; it supplies procedural and disease-management details but does not specify anesthetic regimens, monitoring standards, or emergence guidance. Its anorectal recommendations should not be generalized to all soft-tissue sites.

The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia-care sources provide general standards, not abscess-specific anesthetic choices. The supplied ERAS material concerns major gastrointestinal surgery and does not provide procedure-specific recommendations relevant to abscess I&D.
Comparative anesthetic technique, drug choice, airway strategy for complex cases, and PONV management are not established by the supplied abscess-specific evidence.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) for gastrointestinal surgery, part 2: consensus statement for anaesthesia practice

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Appendectomy may be performed laparoscopically or open. General anesthesia is commonly used for laparoscopy to support ventilation during CO₂ insufflation; neuraxial techniques have been reported in selected patients, but the available studies do not establish them as routine alternatives.

For laparoscopy, insufflation and positioning can alter pulmonary mechanics, CO₂ clearance, venous return, and hemodynamics. Priorities are appropriate ventilation and monitoring, attention to positioning, and prompt recognition of deterioration.

An endotracheal tube is preferred for laparoscopic surgery in the supplied educational review; insufflation and position changes can affect tube position, cuff pressure, and ventilation. Airway choice and ventilation should reflect the procedure and patient rather than a universal rule.

Recovery priorities include multimodal pain control, PONV prevention, appropriate PACU observation, and confirmation of adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: This reference covers adult appendectomy performed laparoscopically or open. The supplied material supports general anesthesia as a usual approach for laparoscopy; open appendectomy is also described under general or spinal anesthesia in a small cohort. These sources do not establish a preferred anesthetic for every patient or operative approach.

Neuraxial anesthesia has been studied or reported for appendectomy, but the laparoscopic randomized study was small and largely involved healthy patients. Its findings should not be generalized to complicated disease or higher-risk patients as proof of equivalent routine care.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study
Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the patient’s medical status and develop an anesthesia plan in context of the intended operation and the patient’s condition. The available sources do not provide an appendectomy-specific preoperative assessment protocol or a universal risk-stratification scheme.

Complicated appendicitis, obesity, and coexisting disease warrant particular attention when considering whether evidence from selected neuraxial studies applies. The laparoscopic study excluded patients with ASA status III or higher and had few perforated cases; it does not supply a validated aspiration-risk or urgency algorithm.
The cited laparoscopic appendectomy trial excluded pregnant patients; the supplied sources do not provide pregnancy-specific appendectomy anesthetic recommendations.

sources.label: Basic Standards for Preanesthesia Care
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For laparoscopic appendectomy, anticipate CO₂ insufflation. Positioning is not universal: the cited trial used Trendelenburg with a 15° turn, while other laparoscopic procedures may use different positions; insufflation and positioning can have hemodynamic and pulmonary effects.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring, including ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. For general anesthesia, the ASA standards specify continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart rate determination at least every five minutes, and continual ventilation evaluation.
Consider additional hemodynamic monitoring according to patient status and anticipated needs; the laparoscopic review gives examples but does not make invasive monitoring routine for appendectomy.

sources.label: Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The laparoscopic review describes general anesthesia as standard for ventilatory support and favors an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway. This supports a common approach, not a rule that every appendectomy or every patient requires intubation.

During insufflation or position changes, reassess ventilation and airway-device position as clinically indicated; the review describes possible endobronchial migration, increased cuff pressure, and atelectasis. Maintain expired CO₂ monitoring during general anesthesia unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment.

The review describes lung-protective ventilation and adjustment of minute ventilation for CO₂ absorption, but specific settings should be individualized to respiratory mechanics and clinical context rather than treated as appendectomy-specific targets.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation can increase systemic vascular resistance and cardiac filling pressures while IVC compression can reduce preload and venous return. Peritoneal stretch may provoke vagal bradyarrhythmias; hypercarbia may contribute to tachyarrhythmias and acidosis-related cardiovascular effects.

CO₂ absorption and cephalad diaphragmatic displacement can impair pulmonary compliance and promote ventilation/perfusion mismatch. Follow ventilation and oxygenation throughout insufflation and position changes, and communicate with the surgical team if physiology deteriorates.

The supplied material does not establish appendectomy-specific intraoperative targets or a universal insufflation-pressure strategy. Individualize management to physiology and coordinate changes in insufflation or positioning with the procedural team.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Potential laparoscopic hazards include vagal events at insufflation, impaired respiratory mechanics, airway-device changes, and access-related solid-organ injury or hemorrhage. Recognize evolving instability and coordinate prompt evaluation with the surgical team; the supplied review does not provide an appendectomy-specific rescue algorithm.

Subcutaneous emphysema or capnothorax may present with crepitus, rising airway pressures, hypoxemia, or hypercapnia. The review describes stopping insufflation as often followed by resolution in some cases and notes that significant cases may require further intervention; escalation depends on the clinical situation.

The case fields identify conversion to open surgery as a concern, but the supplied appendectomy study does not establish its frequency: all operations in that small study were completed laparoscopically. Be prepared to adapt the anesthetic to changes in operative approach without assuming conversion will occur.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The laparoscopic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, while warning that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg. Do not infer a fixed fluid volume for appendectomy from the supplied material.

Access-related hemorrhage is a recognized laparoscopic hazard, and limited visualization may make injury less apparent. Assess perfusion and suspected blood loss in context; the sources provide no appendectomy-specific transfusion threshold or hemorrhage protocol.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Laparoscopic pain may include somatic port-site pain and visceral pain from peritoneal stretch or tissue manipulation. The educational review describes multimodal nonopioid analgesia and port-site local anesthetic as options; tailor technique to the patient and operation.

PONV prevention is a relevant recovery priority in laparoscopy. The supplied material supports prophylactic antiemetic use but does not establish a single drug combination or regimen for all patients.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring when available and confirm adequate recovery before extubation; the cited ASA guideline overview recommends a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9. This does not apply to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide PACU or equivalent care after anesthesia, with continued assessment appropriate to the patient’s condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Handoff and documentation are part of the postanesthesia standards.

Monitor for pain, PONV, and residual neuromuscular weakness as applicable. The appendectomy sources report postoperative outcomes, but do not provide a universal discharge threshold or a procedure-specific PACU protocol.

sources.label: New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-specific laparoscopic anesthesia source is a small randomized study comparing general with combined spinal/epidural anesthesia in selected adults; its authors caution about limited perforated cases, obesity, complicated appendicitis, and generalizability. It is not a practice guideline.

The open-appendectomy comparison is a small, single-center, nonrandomized cohort restricted to adults with ASA I or II status and immediate recovery outcomes. Its observed comparisons do not establish a universal anesthetic choice.

The laparoscopic and robotic surgery review supplies general physiologic and perioperative context rather than appendectomy-specific recommendations; ASA standards support basic monitoring and postanesthesia care, while the neuromuscular-blockade source applies only when such drugs are used.

Appendicitis-specific decisions for perforation or sepsis, including aspiration-risk assessment, antimicrobial selection, and coordinated perioperative management, are not resolved by the supplied sources.

sources.label: Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The cited review addresses colorectal surgery and covers open and laparoscopic approaches, including laparoscopic-assisted surgery and possible conversion to open surgery. The supplied procedure-specific evidence is colorectal-focused; its applicability to small-bowel resection is not established.

Priorities include maintaining perfusion and oxygenation, individualized fluid and electrolyte management, and normothermia. Avoid assuming one fluid volume or a single anesthetic technique for all cases.

Obstruction, perforation, malnutrition, anemia, electrolyte disturbance, and comorbidity can materially alter perioperative risk. Routine mechanical bowel preparation is generally discouraged, with a reported rectal-resection/diverting-stoma exception.

Recovery priorities include opioid-sparing analgesia where appropriate, early feeding and mobilization within the care pathway, and surveillance for ileus, infection, respiratory complications, and anastomotic problems.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The available procedure-specific review addresses colorectal operations for malignant, inflammatory, ischemic, diverticular, traumatic, and obstructive conditions. It includes open and laparoscopic approaches; laparoscopy may require conversion to open surgery.

Stoma planning is relevant when a diverting or permanent stoma is anticipated; the review supports preoperative enterostomal education and site marking. The need for anastomosis, diversion, or other operative details is not established by these anesthesia sources.

Do not assume routine mechanical bowel preparation. The colorectal review discourages routine preparation; the rectal/pelvic review describes a qualified exception for rectal resection with diverting stoma, reflecting a procedure-specific unresolved issue.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess and address anemia, electrolyte imbalance, nutritional deficiency—particularly hypoalbuminemia—and weight loss when clinical urgency allows. Poor nutritional status is associated with increased postoperative complications.

For urgent obstruction or perforation, assess physiological deterioration and consider sepsis and hypovolemia; the review identifies history, examination, monitored parameters, blood gas analysis, and serum electrolytes as inputs to severity assessment.

Identify and optimize relevant comorbidities, including cardiac and respiratory disease; the colorectal review notes these are common. Elective fitness assessment may include functional reserve evaluation, but no single risk score or test is a universal requirement in the supplied sources.

For elective rectal/pelvic surgery, clear fluids are permitted up to 2 hours and solid food up to 6 hours before induction. A clear fluid containing complex carbohydrates 2 hours before anesthesia is recommended unless aspiration risk is increased, such as with bowel obstruction.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG is displayed during anesthesia, and blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every five minutes.

Position carefully and maintain positioning during laparoscopic surgery. The review notes reported brachial plexus injury and lower-limb compartment syndrome after laparoscopic large-bowel surgery; this supports attention to positioning, not a particular position or positioning device.

Maintain temperature monitoring and active thermoregulation as appropriate; normothermia is described as standard care in colon surgery. The sources do not establish a case-specific room configuration, vascular-access plan, or routine arterial-line indication.
Avoid routine nasogastric tube placement in colorectal surgery according to both perioperative reviews; this is not a prohibition when a clinical indication exists.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The supplied colorectal review does not specify an airway device or airway-management technique, and the rectal/pelvic review likewise gives no airway device or technique. Therefore, these sources do not establish routine intubation, rapid-sequence induction, or a ventilation regimen for every resection.

If general anesthesia is provided, follow applicable monitoring standards, including continual ventilation assessment and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. The source provides monitoring standards, not a bowel-resection ventilation prescription.

Aspiration risk is specifically raised for bowel obstruction in the rectal/pelvic review, but the supplied evidence does not define an induction method or thresholds for selecting one. Individual airway planning remains necessary.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The review's central anesthetic priorities are to minimize stress responses, maintain systemic and colonic blood flow and oxygenation, manage fluids and electrolytes carefully, provide multimodal analgesia, and limit postoperative gut dysfunction.

Hemodynamic optimization and goal-directed management are discussed as approaches associated with fewer gastrointestinal complications; the review describes a range of possible endpoints rather than a single target.

Prevent hypothermia with active thermoregulation in open and laparoscopic surgery. The review associates hypothermia with an exaggerated stress response and immune suppression; the rectal/pelvic review also links it with wound infection, cardiac ischemia, and bleeding.
No specific anesthetic agent is recommended by the colorectal review. Comparative findings are mixed and do not establish a preferred volatile or intravenous technique for routine practice.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Relevant postoperative concerns include ileus and impaired bowel function, infectious complications, and anastomotic leakage. These are risks to recognize and assess in context; the supplied reviews do not provide a case-specific diagnostic or treatment algorithm.

Opioids can inhibit bowel motility and contribute to nausea, vomiting, and constipation, potentially delaying bowel recovery and oral intake. Consider opioid-sparing strategies within the patient's surgical and analgesic context.
For laparoscopic cases, maintain positioning and remain alert to positioning-related injury; the cited reports establish a hazard, not its incidence or a specific prevention protocol.

In PACU or an equivalent recovery location, continually evaluate the patient, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Escalation should follow the patient's findings and local clinical pathways; no bowel-specific emergency algorithm is supplied.

sources.label: Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)
Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Individualize perioperative fluid therapy to maintenance needs, losses, and pathophysiological changes of major bowel surgery. The colorectal review explicitly gives no fixed fluid formula.

Optimize fluid balance and avoid fluid excess; the rectal/pelvic review describes targeting cardiac output and allowing vasopressors for arterial hypotension. This does not establish a universal fluid total or perfusion target.

The colorectal review describes restrictive postoperative fluid therapy as beneficial and cautions against excess fluid used solely to correct vasodilator-related hypotension. Interpret this alongside the need to maintain perfusion and individualize therapy.

Bowel surgery can involve fluid deficit in urgent presentations and changes in colonic blood flow related to volume status, hemorrhage, and sepsis. The sources provide no transfusion threshold, blood-loss estimate, or universal blood-preparation protocol.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For open colorectal surgery, thoracic epidural analgesia is recommended in the review and is associated with better gastrointestinal recovery. Its suitability depends on the patient, operation, and overall analgesic plan.

For laparoscopic surgery, evidence is insufficient to identify one preferred postoperative analgesic method. Epidural, systemic or intrathecal techniques, wound approaches, and TAP block are described, but the source reports limited or conflicting evidence for some comparisons.

Acetaminophen/paracetamol and NSAIDs are described as components of multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. The colorectal review notes concern about increased anastomotic-leak risk with COX-2 inhibitors; it does not justify treating all NSAIDs as interchangeable or universally appropriate.

Assess PONV risk and use prophylaxis according to risk. The rectal/pelvic review recommends prophylactic antiemetic treatment for patients with two or more identified risk factors; this is a review recommendation, not a universal regimen.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The colorectal review does not establish a specific extubation protocol. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site.

Provide postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent location, with appropriate monitoring and continuing evaluation. A qualified anesthesia-care-team member accompanies transport and gives a verbal handoff on arrival.

Recovery care should include attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard, subject to its stated exceptions.

Early oral feeding and mobilization are elements of enhanced recovery described in the rectal/pelvic review. Their application should follow the operative and patient-specific plan; the source does not define a universal pathway for all small- and large-bowel resections.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The main procedure-specific source is a clinical review of colorectal surgery, published in 2012; it is not a dedicated small-bowel resection guideline. The rectal/pelvic ERAS review addresses elective rectal/pelvic surgery, not every bowel-resection population.

For laparoscopic colorectal surgery, the review reports insufficient evidence to recommend a specific postoperative analgesic method. It also states that there is no evidence to recommend specific anesthetic or analgesic agents for colorectal surgery.

The bowel-preparation sources do not fully agree: routine preparation is discouraged generally, while the rectal/pelvic review describes a possible exception for rectal resection with diverting stoma and notes the need for further study.

Case-specific airway, ventilation, drug-selection, and extubation protocols are not established by the procedure-specific sources. The available ASA materials provide general monitoring, postanesthesia-care, and neuromuscular-blockade guidance rather than bowel-resection-specific anesthetic recipes.
Workflow limitation: case-specific targets and protocols are not established in the available sources.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The evidence covers image-guided needle sampling and localization as well as surgical excisional biopsy; it does not establish one anesthetic technique for the full range of breast operations. Excisional biopsy may be performed under local or general anesthesia.

Percutaneous biopsy is generally performed with local anesthesia. Bleeding, bruising, pain, infection, and vasovagal reactions are the relevant procedure-specific concerns described in the sources; these findings should not be assumed to quantify risk in larger operations.

For image-guided biopsy, positioning and access depend on the imaging modality and lesion. Do not infer routine operating-room positioning or airway management for lumpectomy or mastectomy from these percutaneous-procedure sources.

When anesthesia is given, apply general anesthesia monitoring and recovery standards as appropriate. The available sources do not establish a breast-surgery-specific fluid, analgesia, PONV, or recovery regimen.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Distinguish percutaneous sampling from surgical excision: image-guided FNS, CNB, and VAB sample tissue; excisional biopsy removes the lesion. Do not treat their anesthetic requirements as interchangeable.

Preoperative localization is used for nonpalpable lesions requiring surgery. The source describes wire localization, carbon marking, radiotracer injection, and radioactive or magnetic seeds; localization method and coordination are procedure-specific.

Percutaneous ultrasound-guided biopsy is performed supine or in a decubitus/lateral position; MRI-guided VAB is performed prone. These are image-guided procedure positions, not evidence for the position used in an operating-room breast operation.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Breast Biopsy Procedure Toolkit: Ultrasound, 2D Stereotactic, 3D Tomosynthesis, and MRI-Guided Procedures

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For percutaneous breast biopsy, explain the reason for the procedure, devices used, and possible adverse events, side effects, and complications; verify allergies to local anesthetic drugs. Local anesthesia is administered for CNB and VAB; it is optional for FNS.

Review bleeding history and antiplatelet or anticoagulant use for biopsy; decisions about interruption should be made with the prescribing physician and local guidance. The supplied sources do not establish a medication plan for breast surgery.

For MRI-guided biopsy, screen for MRI contraindications, relevant implants, prior contrast reactions, and renal impairment. This is specific to the MRI procedure and does not substitute for a broader anesthetic assessment.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For image-guided procedures, positioning and equipment depend on modality: mammography/tomosynthesis may use prone or upright systems, while MRI biopsy uses a dedicated breast coil and prone positioning. These descriptions do not establish operating-room setup for excision.

For any anesthetic, use appropriate monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ASA standards also require ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

When general anesthesia is delivered with an anesthesia machine, the cited ASA standard specifies oxygen analysis with a low-oxygen alarm and quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

bullets: For percutaneous core biopsy, tell the patient about the firing noise to reduce the chance of movement. The source describes sequential sampling for CNB and vacuum-assisted sampling without removing the needle for VAB.

Vasovagal reactions are a procedure-specific concern, reported more often with upright biopsy systems than dedicated prone tables. This evidence concerns biopsy positioning, not an anesthetic event rate for breast surgery.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For percutaneous biopsy, common reported effects include minor pain and bruising; larger hematoma or infection is uncommon in the cited review. Do not transfer these rates to excisional surgery.

Bleeding after biopsy is usually self-limited or managed with manual compression; severe bleeding requiring surgery is described as very rare. The source does not provide a surgical-mastectomy bleeding protocol.

A very rare chest-wall injury, including pneumothorax, is described with free-hand or ultrasound-guided biopsy; the source notes risk is practically null with mammography- or MRI-guided biopsy. This is a modality-specific hazard, not a general operative risk estimate.

bullets: The image-guided biopsy sources provide no IV-fluid regimen or intraoperative fluid-management guidance. They do not establish fluid volumes, blood-loss expectations, or transfusion criteria for lumpectomy or mastectomy.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Laparoscopic diagnostic procedures and adhesiolysis use abdominal insufflation; general anesthesia is the usual approach in the general laparoscopic-surgery reference, with an endotracheal tube preferred when higher ventilatory pressures or PEEP may be needed.

Prioritize ventilation and hemodynamic assessment as pneumoperitoneum and positioning can impair respiratory mechanics, alter venous return and filling pressures, and provoke hypercarbia-related effects.

Remain alert to access-related injury or hemorrhage, vagal bradyarrhythmia at insufflation, and respiratory or hemodynamic changes suggesting gas-related complications; escalate promptly when deterioration occurs.
Plan recovery around oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; address PONV and pain, and assess residual neuromuscular blockade before extubation if a blocker was used.

bullets: This reference concerns abdominal laparoscopy, including diagnostic procedures and possible adhesiolysis. The available general anesthesia source addresses laparoscopic and robotic surgery broadly, not this operation’s specific operative steps or adhesiolysis technique.

bullets: Assess patient-specific cardiopulmonary reserve and the anticipated effects of insufflation and position. The available general review identifies physiologic risks but does not supply procedure-specific selection criteria or a complete preoperative workup.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the patient and technique. For anesthesia, ECG display is continuous and blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standards.

Continually evaluate oxygenation and ventilation, including expired CO₂ monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment makes it invalid. When an ETT or LMA is in place, verify placement clinically and by expired CO₂.

Positioning varies with the operation. Trendelenburg and reverse Trendelenburg have distinct hemodynamic and respiratory effects; secure and protect the patient, and reassess airway and ventilation after position changes.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The broad laparoscopic-surgery reference describes general anesthesia as standard and prefers an ETT when higher pressures or PEEP may be required. This is not evidence that every short diagnostic procedure has an identical airway requirement.

Insufflation and cephalad diaphragmatic displacement can reduce compliance and functional residual capacity. Adjust ventilation to the patient’s mechanics and gas exchange; the review describes a commonly used lung-protective approach, not a mandatory case-specific prescription.
Reassess tube position and cuff pressure with insufflation or position changes; the review notes possible cephalad migration and changes in cuff pressure.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: At insufflation, anticipate changes in venous return, intrathoracic pressure, and cardiac filling pressures. Peritoneal stretch may trigger vagal bradyarrhythmia; monitor closely during initiation and respond to clinically significant instability.
CO₂ absorption can produce hypercarbia and acidosis, with cardiovascular effects; monitor ventilation and end-tidal CO₂ and reassess when the clinical trajectory is unexpected.

Pneumoperitoneum, lung compression, and Trendelenburg can worsen atelectasis and airway pressures. Interpret pressures in context of chest-wall and lung mechanics rather than treating a single pressure value as a universal target.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider access-related organ injury or hemorrhage when instability or unexpected findings arise; limited visualization can obscure injury. The sources do not give an adhesiolysis-specific injury or conversion protocol.

If airway pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, chest movement, or hemodynamics deteriorate, consider gas-related thoracic complications among the possibilities. The review lists findings and describes management ranging from observation to decompression or surgery depending on the case; it does not provide a universal response algorithm.
Recognize insufflation-associated vagal bradyarrhythmia and hypercarbia-related cardiovascular effects; promptly assess the patient and coordinate with the surgical team when instability develops.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The general laparoscopic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed administration; avoid assuming that a fixed volume is appropriate. Excess fluid may contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg.

Assess perfusion using the full clinical context; heart rate, blood pressure, central venous pressure, and urine output are described as poor surrogate predictors of intravascular volume during pneumoperitoneum.

Bleeding can accompany access injury despite the generally lower bleeding burden attributed to minimally invasive surgery. The available sources do not establish an operation-specific blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, or hemorrhage protocol.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Laparoscopic pain may be somatic at port sites and visceral from peritoneal stretch or abdominal tissue manipulation. The review describes multimodal analgesia, including acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and port-site local anesthetic, as opioid-sparing options rather than a mandatory regimen.
Laparoscopy is a PONV risk factor; consider prophylaxis based on the individual’s risk and clinical context. The sources do not establish one universal drug combination.

The diagnostic gynecologic case series reported postoperative nausea and vomiting, but its selected population and non-comparative design do not establish a general prophylaxis regimen or rate for adhesiolysis.

After anesthesia, recovery care should include ongoing evaluation appropriate to the patient’s condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Percutaneous feeding access may be placed into the stomach by PEG or an interventional-radiology approach, or into the jejunum; surgical jejunostomy has open, laparoscopic, and other approaches. The anesthetic technique depends on the approach and is not established as one standard by these sources.

Enteral access is considered when oral intake is inadequate or unsuitable. Relevant concerns include aspiration risk, anatomy that may make access difficult, coagulopathy, ascites, and prior gastric or abdominal surgery.

Important procedural hazards include bleeding, infection, and injury to adjacent organs; aspiration and tube-related complications also matter. Avoid assuming that transillumination, a particular airway technique, or general anesthesia applies to every approach.

Recovery priorities are appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and recognition of respiratory or procedural complications. The available material does not establish a case-specific anesthetic, airway, fluid, or analgesic regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Percutaneous enteral access places a tube through the skin into the stomach. Gastric access may be by PEG or image-guided IR; GJ tubes extend into the jejunum, while J tubes enter the jejunum directly.

Surgical jejunostomy approaches described include open, laparoscopic, needle-catheter, and percutaneous direct endoscopic techniques. Technique and positioning vary; the laparoscopic description starts supine and then uses reverse Trendelenburg.
Indications include inability to use the oral route and anticipated prolonged enteral nutrition; jejunostomy may be used when gastrostomy is contraindicated or proximal obstruction precludes it.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Femoral hernia repair may be open or laparoscopic. The available femoral-hernia sources describe open repair under local or epidural anesthesia and laparoscopic repair under general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; they do not establish one approach as routine for every patient.

For laparoscopy, prioritize the cardiovascular and respiratory effects of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum and positioning, including reduced compliance, hypercarbia, altered venous return, and possible vagal bradyarrhythmia.
Femoral-ring dissection and reduction can put femoral vessels and Corona Mortis vessels at risk; avoid implying a fixed approach or anesthetic response from these technical cautions.
Recovery priorities include condition-appropriate postanesthesia observation and, if neuromuscular blockers were used, quantitative confirmation of recovery before extubation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair generally combines reduction/mobilization, hiatal closure and fundoplication. A 360° Nissen is common, but motility findings can inform selection of a partial wrap.
General anesthesia with endotracheal intubation is described. Peritoneal stretch can trigger vagal bradyarrhythmias, and hypercarbia can cause tachyarrhythmias; pleural rupture is reported as common.
Recovery priorities include assessing swallowing and reflux-related symptoms, gas bloat and PONV. Dysphagia is common early after repair; Nissen may impair belching or vomiting.
The supplied sources do not establish a case-specific RSI, aspiration-prevention, drug, fluid-total or extubation protocol. Individualize these decisions to the patient and surgical circumstances.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The laparoscopic antireflux repair is built around adequate relaxed intra-abdominal esophageal length, hiatal closure and fundoplication. Large paraesophageal hernia repair may include sac excision; mesh reinforcement is described selectively, not as a universal step.

A short, loose 360° Nissen is commonly described. Toupet or Dor alternatives are also described; preoperative or intraoperative manometry may help guide wrap selection. This is a surgical choice, not an anesthesia prescription.
A bougie may be used to avoid excessive tightness during Nissen construction. Esophageal or gastric injury is a recognized hazard, particularly during reoperation.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm the indication and characterize hernia anatomy and reflux evidence. For operative candidates, the review describes barium esophagram and upper endoscopy as essential; pH testing and manometry are relevant when indicated by symptoms and operative planning.

Review dysphagia, respiratory or mechanical symptoms, prior repair and comorbidity/frailty. Large hernias may present with dysphagia, dyspnea, chest pain or obstruction; frailty and age are associated with greater perioperative morbidity in cited data.

Assess reflux and aspiration-related history as part of individualized anesthetic evaluation. The supplied sources do not establish a universal aspiration-risk protocol or mandate RSI for this operation.

sources.label: Hiatal Hernia – StatPearls
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Laparoscopic access and pneumoperitoneum are expected; an orogastric tube may be used for gastric decompression. The operation may involve a bougie passed by the surgical team, requiring clear communication about passage and removal.

Positioning is not consistent across the supplied procedure-specific account and general laparoscopic review: one describes 30-degree Trendelenburg, while reverse Trendelenburg is commonly used for upper gastrointestinal procedures. Confirm the intended position with the surgical team and protect pressure points.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature, including ECG, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and expired CO₂ monitoring during general anesthesia unless invalidated.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Hiatal Hernia – StatPearls
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedure-specific source describes general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. The laparoscopic surgery review favors an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway when higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP may be needed.

Pneumoperitoneum and position can reduce compliance and functional residual capacity, raise airway pressures and increase CO₂. Adjust ventilation to the observed physiology; the general review discusses lung-protective ventilation but does not establish a hiatal-repair-specific target.
Reassess tube position and cuff pressure after insufflation or position change, since cephalad carinal movement can cause endobronchial migration or increased cuff pressure.

sources.label: Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation can increase SVR and filling pressures, reduce venous return through IVC compression, and produce hypercarbia-related cardiovascular effects. The net response varies with position, volume status and patient factors.

Peritoneal stretch may cause a vagal response and bradyarrhythmia; hypercarbia can produce tachyarrhythmia and acidosis-related effects. Recognize a temporal relationship to insufflation or traction and communicate promptly with the surgeon.

Dissection around the hiatus and mediastinum places the pleura, esophagus, stomach, spleen and vagus nerve at risk. Surgical sources emphasize careful mobilization and protection of the vagus and spleen.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Capnothorax is a recognized laparoscopic antireflux complication. Consider it with rising airway pressure, hypoxemia or hypercapnia, unequal chest expansion or related signs; the general review describes a range of responses from observation to decompression or surgery according to severity.

Pleural rupture is described as common in the procedure-specific technical account, which says thoracic drainage is usually unnecessary and mentions positive-pressure lung recruitment at the end of surgery. This does not establish a universal response; assess the clinical effect and coordinate with the surgeon.

Bleeding or visceral injury may occur during access, reduction or fundus mobilization. Limited laparoscopic visualization can obscure access injury; surgical guidance emphasizes gentle dissection and prompt conversion for uncontrolled bleeding.

sources.label: Hiatal Hernia – StatPearls
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No hiatal-repair-specific fluid regimen, hemodynamic target or transfusion threshold is provided. The general laparoscopic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed administration, while cautioning that conventional measures such as urine output can be poor volume surrogates during pneumoperitoneum.

Expect generally limited blood loss but remain alert to splenic, hepatic or access-related injury; the procedure-specific source notes that uncontrolled bleeding may require conversion. There is no source-supported routine crossmatch or blood-loss estimate.

sources.label: Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Pain may arise from port sites and visceral manipulation. The general laparoscopic review describes multimodal analgesia, including acetaminophen, NSAIDs and port-site local anesthetic, as opioid-sparing options; the procedure-specific source reports pain is often mild but provides no regimen.

Laparoscopy increases PONV risk, so provide risk-informed prophylaxis and treatment. The available evidence does not support a mandatory number or specific combination of antiemetics for every patient.

Assess postoperative swallowing and bloating. Dysphagia is often transient; Nissen is associated with gas bloat and impaired ability to belch or vomit, which may affect counseling and symptom interpretation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH
Hiatal Hernia – StatPearls

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied procedure-specific sources do not define an emergence or extubation technique. Avoid presenting deep extubation, a particular drug, or a specific cough-suppression method as established case-specific practice.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, ASA guideline recommendations summarized by APSF support quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide monitored postanesthesia care with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature; assess for PONV, dysphagia, gas bloat and respiratory complications. Diet advancement is surgical-protocol dependent.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The procedure-specific 2016 article is a technical letter, not an anesthesia reference or comparative study; its brief anesthesia description cannot establish an anesthetic regimen or outcome.

StatPearls is an educational clinical review, not an anesthesia source. Its operative and postoperative discussion informs procedure context, but it explicitly lacks airway, anesthetic, fluid and emergence guidance.
The laparoscopic/robotic review provides general physiologic and anesthetic context, not hiatal-repair-specific targets. Its recommendations should not be mistaken for a procedure-specific protocol.

The provided sources do not resolve case-specific aspiration/RSI decisions, optimal positioning despite conflicting descriptions, or an emergence strategy. These remain individualized decisions rather than universal requirements.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open anterior repair may be performed under local, regional, or general anesthesia; local anesthesia is a supported option for open repair. Minimally invasive repair is generally performed under general anesthesia.
Approach selection depends on patient factors and surgical expertise. Laparoscopic approaches can assess and repair bilateral hernias and may be useful after a prior open repair.

For minimally invasive surgery, prioritize the physiologic effects of CO₂ insufflation and positioning: changes in ventilation and airway pressures, hemodynamics, and risks related to patient position.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, pain control, ambulation, and assessment for urinary retention; if neuromuscular blockade is used, confirm adequate recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open anterior repair is an option for local anesthesia; the review specifically encourages local anesthesia for open anterior repairs. General or regional anesthesia are also described options, without a complete protocol for any technique.

Laparoscopic TAPP and TEP are the described minimally invasive approaches; robotic-assisted repair follows similar principles and commonly uses a robotic TAPP approach. The supplied sources describe general anesthesia for minimally invasive repair.

Approach is a surgical-anesthetic decision informed by comorbidities, BMI, recurrence, bilaterality, and surgeon proficiency. Laparoscopy can access both sides and may use a different tissue plane after a prior open repair.

sources.label: Current options in inguinal hernia repair in adult patients
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess whether the patient can undergo general anesthesia and tolerate insufflation if minimally invasive repair is planned. Adhesions, prior radiation, ascites, large inguinoscrotal hernia, and incarcerated or strangulated hernia may increase difficulty or risk.

Clarify prior repair and planned approach. Recurrence after prior minimally invasive repair generally favors open repair in the cited review; approach remains dependent on surgical expertise and circumstances.

Incarceration or strangulation warrants heightened procedural planning: the review identifies these as factors that can complicate minimally invasive repair and lead to conversion. The supplied sources do not establish a universal aspiration or rapid-sequence induction protocol for this situation.

sources.label: Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For minimally invasive repair, prepare for laparoscopic or robotic equipment and coordinate positioning with the surgeon. The patient is described as supine; robotic-assisted repair uses Trendelenburg before docking.
Protect pressure points and the face, secure the patient against sliding, and account for restricted access after robotic docking. The table must not move while the robot is docked.

Use standard anesthesia monitoring. ASA standards call for ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

sources.label: Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is the described usual approach for minimally invasive repair. For laparoscopic and robotic surgery, an endotracheal tube is preferred over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; the hernia review itself does not specify an airway device.
Insufflation and position changes can alter respiratory mechanics and tube position. Reassess ventilation and airway pressures when these conditions change.

Ventilation may require adjustment for CO₂ absorption and reduced compliance during pneumoperitoneum. The general laparoscopic review describes a lung-protective approach and an end-tidal CO₂ goal, but these are not hernia-specific prescriptions and require clinical individualization.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Pneumoperitoneum can increase systemic vascular resistance and filling pressures while inferior vena cava compression may reduce venous return. Interpret hemodynamic changes in the context of insufflation and position.

CO₂ absorption and diaphragmatic displacement reduce pulmonary compliance and functional residual capacity; atelectasis and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may follow. Trendelenburg can worsen these effects.

Be alert to bradyarrhythmia at insufflation onset from vagal response and tachyarrhythmia with hypercarbia. Recognize a significant change and escalate with the surgical team; the available sources do not establish a case-specific treatment algorithm.

Surgical hazards include injury to vessels, nerves, bladder, or bowel during access, dissection, or reduction. The minimally invasive review emphasizes careful dissection and avoidance of nerve- and vessel-containing regions.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider airway or pulmonary complications when airway pressures rise, oxygenation worsens, or ventilation changes after insufflation or repositioning; the laparoscopic review describes endobronchial migration, tube obstruction, and atelectasis.

Subcutaneous emphysema and capnothorax are recognized insufflation-related hazards. The source describes crepitus and respiratory or hemodynamic changes as warning features; significant cases require close monitoring and escalation.

Vascular or visceral injury may be difficult to identify because access and limited visualization can obscure bleeding. Conversion to open surgery may be required for injury or difficult dissection, including incarceration or strangulation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The laparoscopic review supports balanced crystalloid and goal-directed administration, while cautioning that excess fluid may contribute to facial, pharyngeal, or laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg.

Potential hemorrhage includes injury during needle or port access; assess perfusion in context because common bedside measures may be unreliable during pneumoperitoneum. The supplied sources do not establish a hernia-specific fluid total or transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For open repair, local anesthesia is described as suitable. Local and regional anesthesia are described as providing preemptive analgesia and a more comfortable postoperative period; patients receiving either are reported to require fewer postoperative analgesics than those receiving general anesthesia. The review provides no complete anesthetic protocol.

For laparoscopic approaches, pain may arise from port sites and visceral tissue manipulation. A multimodal strategy and port-site local anesthetic are described options; the supplied review gives no specific drug doses.
Laparoscopy is an independent PONV risk factor; prophylactic antiemetic administration is recommended in the general laparoscopic review.

sources.label: Current options in inguinal hernia repair in adult patients
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

After anesthesia, provide postanesthesia care with monitoring appropriate to the patient's condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard, subject to its stated exceptions.

Assess pain, ambulation, and urinary retention during recovery; urinary retention is specifically associated with spinal anesthesia in the hernia review. No case-specific discharge criteria are provided.

title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Toe / Foot / BKA / AKA)
aliases: Lower Extremity Amputation (Toe / Foot / BKA / AKA)

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lower-extremity amputation may be performed under general or regional anesthesia; the choice is individualized. Regional techniques include neuraxial anesthesia and peripheral nerve blocks, but the available sources do not establish a single preferred technique for every patient or amputation level.

The dominant risk context is substantial comorbidity—particularly peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, cardiac disease, renal impairment, and infection. Assess physiologic reserve and the urgency of source control when selecting an anesthetic approach.

Regional anesthesia can support analgesia and may reduce some perioperative morbidity, but comparative findings are mixed and do not establish a mortality benefit. Consider block coverage, tourniquet use, contraindications, and the risk of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity.

Recovery priorities include adequate acute stump pain control, surveillance for hemodynamic and wound complications, and attention to phantom limb pain. Use postanesthesia monitoring and handoff appropriate to the patient’s condition.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Amputation level and staging depend on tissue viability, infection, and whether adequate bone coverage can be obtained. A staged open amputation may be used for source control in septic shock; a single-stage operation may be suitable when the patient and soft tissues permit.

The reviewed regional approaches are level- and coverage-dependent. For BKA, adductor-canal saphenous and popliteal sciatic blocks are described; the review cautions that tourniquet ischemic pain and discomfort limit their use as the sole anesthetic.

For AKA, comprehensive peripheral block coverage may involve femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, sciatic, and obturator nerves. The review notes added time, local-anesthetic exposure, and toxicity risk with multiple blocks; these descriptions are not a universal technique recommendation.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary, and functional reserve, and account for diabetes and preoperative infection as relevant comorbidities and risk factors in major lower-extremity amputation.

For diabetes and suspected infection, consider glycemic optimization and early antibiotic treatment as part of preoperative care. In PVD, the indication and level relate to nonhealing tissue when blood-flow restoration is not an option; assess healing potential and tissue condition rather than relying on one measure alone.

Review anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy and evaluate for coagulopathy or systemic infection before considering neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques. The review describes circumstances in urgent cases where neuraxial anesthesia may be avoided; it does not provide medication interruption intervals.

For traumatic injury, evaluate for concomitant life-threatening injuries, bleeding, and resuscitation needs. Discuss likely functional outcome and the risks of major amputation with the patient or designated advocates when circumstances allow.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The chapter describes supine positioning and use of an appropriately sized tourniquet when appropriate. Some patients have no vascular inflow, in which case a tourniquet is not necessary; protect the skin before application.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards call for continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes; temperature monitoring is required when clinically significant change is intended, anticipated, or suspected.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General or regional anesthesia are described options. The available procedure-specific sources do not establish an airway device, ventilation strategy, or universal sedation approach; select these according to the planned anesthetic and patient condition.

For general anesthesia, ASA monitoring standards require ongoing ventilation assessment and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by patient, procedure, or equipment. Verify endotracheal-tube or laryngeal-mask position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide when used.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect a high-risk cardiovascular population. One observational study summarized in the review found less intraoperative hypotension and vasopressor administration with regional anesthesia than with alternative modalities, but the regional group combined spinal anesthesia and peripheral blocks; this does not establish a technique-specific effect.

Consider tourniquet-related discomfort and ischemic pain when selecting regional coverage. The evidence describes stable hemodynamics in a small high-risk BKA study without a tourniquet, but does not establish that result for other patients or tourniquet conditions.
The surgical approach may be staged in unstable or septic patients to obtain source control; coordinate timing and anesthetic decisions with the surgical team as clinical status evolves.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Major concerns include cardiopulmonary complications, wound infection, prolonged ICU care, and revision. Risk context includes cardiac disease, renal impairment, infection, and proximal amputation; reported mortality varies by population and should not be treated as an individual prediction.

If stump pain persists, consider non-anesthetic causes as well as inadequate analgesia, including infection, wound dehiscence, reduced blood flow, osteomyelitis, hematoma, or inadequate tissue coverage.

Peripheral blocks require attention to coverage and local-anesthetic toxicity risk, especially when multiple nerves or substantial volumes are involved. The review’s case reports do not establish routine management for patients with sepsis, thrombocytopenia, or respiratory infection.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The sources do not establish a procedure-specific fluid regimen, transfusion threshold, or blood-ordering rule. Assess bleeding and resuscitation needs in the clinical context; the chapter specifically identifies hemostasis and adequate resuscitation for traumatic injuries.

The review summarizes studies associating regional anesthesia with reduced blood loss or transfusion in some settings, but the comparative evidence is mixed and does not provide a patient-specific estimate or mandate an anesthetic technique.
Perfusion and tissue viability inform level selection and healing potential; TcPO₂ may contribute to assessment but does not capture the whole patient or limb condition.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan acute stump analgesia before the anesthetic or block regresses. The review favors regional anesthesia for acute stump pain and describes multimodal planning, while noting that opioids alone may be insufficient; the sources do not establish one universal drug regimen.

For BKA, combined saphenous/adductor-canal and sciatic coverage is described for perioperative pain; continuous catheters may extend analgesia. Evidence for long-term prevention of phantom limb pain remains limited.

Discuss phantom limb pain and residual limb pain as distinct but potentially overlapping recovery problems. Early acute-pain-service involvement and a preemptive approach are emphasized in the review; no intervention is guaranteed to prevent chronic pain.

A retrospective BKA comparison reported lower pain scores, opioid use, and postoperative nausea and vomiting with combined femoral and sciatic blocks than with general anesthesia; this observational finding does not establish a universal technique choice.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure-specific sources do not specify emergence or extubation criteria. For general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, apply quantitative recovery guidance; do not impose that requirement on cases without blockade.

After anesthesia, use PACU or equivalent care, including ICU when appropriate. Continue condition-appropriate monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; evaluate pain and the operative wound.

Provide a structured handoff covering the preoperative condition, surgical and anesthetic course, adverse events, blood loss and resuscitative measures, and the planned destination. A receiving clinician should accept responsibility before anesthesia-team departure.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthesia review is a narrative review focused on major lower-extremity amputation and regional anesthesia, especially peripheral nerve blocks; it is not a guideline or meta-analysis. Its summarized studies vary in design and population.

Comparative outcome evidence is unresolved: studies report possible morbidity advantages with regional techniques, while mortality findings are controversial. Many studies combine neuraxial and peripheral techniques, limiting technique-specific conclusions.

The StatPearls chapter is an educational surgical review rather than an anesthesia reference. ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards provide general requirements, not amputation-specific anesthetic plans.

The available sources do not resolve individualized airway/ventilation planning, anesthetic technique selection for a particular patient, or perioperative anticoagulant management for regional procedures.
The procedure-specific chapter does not specify vascular-access strategy or monitoring standards.
