overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: This is emergency abdominal surgery for a potentially life-threatening intra-abdominal condition such as perforation. The operative approach is pathology- and patient-dependent; consider laparoscopy when appropriate rather than assuming an open operation.

Priorities are to recognize physiologic instability and sepsis, assess electrolyte and acid–base derangements, and anticipate regurgitation and aspiration risk associated with emergency abdominal disease.

When general anesthesia is required, manage the airway with the elevated aspiration risk in mind and select induction drugs to maintain hemodynamic stability. The sources do not establish a single mandatory induction drug or a universal RSI rule for every patient.

Recovery planning starts intraoperatively: maintain normothermia, reassess extubation suitability with the multidisciplinary team, and select postoperative care according to instability and ongoing support needs; ICU care is likely appropriate for many emergency-laparotomy patients.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The emergency-laparotomy guidance covers non-elective, potentially life-threatening intra-abdominal conditions, including perforation. It does not prescribe a single operation or surgical approach.

Approach selection is individualized to patient factors, pathology, imaging, and surgical expertise. Laparoscopy may be considered when appropriate; evidence associating it with better outcomes is largely observational and susceptible to confounding.

For critically ill patients unlikely to tolerate prolonged definitive surgery, damage-control strategies may control sepsis or hemorrhage and defer definitive management. Decisions are individualized; the guideline notes limited evidence and potential burdens of multiple operations and prolonged ICU care.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess for electrolyte and acid–base disturbances: the perforation-peritonitis source describes hypokalemia with chloride loss, hyperkalemia in hypotensive metabolic acidosis or renal insufficiency, and metabolic acidosis related to shock or reduced renal function. It identifies blood-gas and electrolyte assessment with correction as important.

Treat suspected or established sepsis and physiologic instability as major anesthetic risk modifiers. Emergency abdominal patients also have elevated aspiration risk associated with obstruction or distension, sepsis, opioids, and emergency surgery.
Consider intra-abdominal fungal infection in the clinical assessment; the perforation-peritonitis letter describes poor prognosis and advises early recognition, while noting nonspecific presentation.

The available sources do not provide a complete perforation-specific preoperative assessment or resuscitation protocol. Use clinical assessment and applicable local pathways rather than inferring required tests or a fixed optimization interval from this reference.

sources.label: Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis
Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Consider early arterial and/or central venous pressure catheters for physiologic assessment and titration or delivery of fluids and vasopressors; the guideline does not make either line universal.

Follow basic anesthetic monitoring standards: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; display ECG and assess blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.
Measure core temperature and use active warming and warmed IV fluids to maintain normothermia. Record fluid balance during and after surgery.
The supplied sources do not specify a patient position or procedure-specific room arrangement; select these with the surgical team and the planned approach.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Emergency-laparotomy patients are at increased risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Where rapid-sequence induction/intubation is chosen, the consensus guideline supports a fast-acting neuromuscular blocker; it does not establish that RSI is mandatory for every individual or specify one induction agent.
If using controlled ventilation, the guideline recommends tidal volume based on predicted body weight and initial PEEP, with subsequent titration to flow-volume loops and clinical evaluation.

For general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify its position by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas; continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis until extubation/removal or initiation of transfer to postoperative care.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Induction and ongoing anesthesia require attention to hemodynamic stability in patients with sepsis or other physiologic derangement. The sources advise selecting induction drugs to maintain stability but do not establish ketamine or another agent as universally preferred.

In sepsis present or suspected during emergency laparotomy, the guideline describes norepinephrine as the first-choice vasopressor to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; epinephrine or vasopressin 0.03 U/min may be added to norepinephrine. Apply this guidance in context rather than as an automatic drug sequence.

Correct electrolyte disturbances throughout the perioperative period. The perforation-peritonitis letter links metabolic and electrolyte disturbances to arrhythmia, hemodynamic disturbance, and delayed recovery.

Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within the guideline's pre-incision interval unless appropriate therapy is already underway; select and continue therapy according to local or national guidance, pathology, and operative contamination.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Maintain vigilance for aspiration and hemodynamic instability; if instability occurs, assess the patient's physiology and escalate support according to local emergency practice. The sources do not provide a perforation-specific collapse-resuscitation algorithm.
Consider acid–base and electrolyte derangements when evaluating arrhythmia or hemodynamic disturbance; shock and reduced renal function are described contributors to metabolic acidosis.

Prevent and detect hypothermia with temperature monitoring and active warming. At the end of surgery, evaluate extubation suitability in light of blood loss, ventilatory needs, acid–base status, temperature, and ongoing support requirements.
Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring when a neuromuscular blocker is used, and confirm adequate recovery before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: For emergency laparotomy, prefer balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline for resuscitation and intravascular volume maintenance; the guideline grades this as a weak recommendation based on low evidence and notes that evidence is inferred from other populations.

Individualize fluid boluses using objective measures of hypovolemia and avoid both volume overload and inadequate perfusion. The available guidance does not establish a fixed fluid volume for perforation cases.

Use a restrictive red-cell transfusion approach as the guideline recommends, with exceptions based on individual clinical status and comorbidities. Do not treat an unsupported fixed hemoglobin target as routine.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use an individualized multimodal analgesic plan, including acetaminophen and NSAIDs when not contraindicated; consider wound catheters or abdominal-wall blocks to reduce opioid demand.

Assess sepsis and coagulation abnormalities before considering thoracic epidural or spinal techniques. The emergency-laparotomy guideline advises individualized assessment rather than routine neuraxial placement.
Treat emergency-laparotomy patients as high risk for PONV and use multimodal prevention while minimizing triggers and opioid exposure.

To reduce ileus burden, consider opioid-sparing analgesia as part of a broader recovery strategy. The perforation-peritonitis letter also discusses epidural analgesia, but does not establish an emergent epidural as appropriate for every patient.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Make extubation a multidisciplinary end-of-surgery decision. Consider respiratory status, blood loss, temperature, acid–base condition, and ongoing fluid or hemodynamic support rather than relying on a single criterion.

Choose postoperative destination using preoperative risk, procedure impact, instability, and ongoing therapeutic or supportive needs. ICU care may be appropriate for many patients, but is not a universal disposition.

For postanesthesia transfer, provide appropriate monitoring and support, communicate the anesthetic and surgical course, and continue observation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature in the receiving area.
Consider nasogastric tubes individually, reassess their need daily, and remove as early as possible; routine postoperative use is not supported by the perforation-peritonitis letter.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pilonidal surgery ranges from drainage of an acute abscess to definitive treatment of chronic disease. The operative approach matters: these sources describe local anesthesia for selected drainage and pit-picking procedures, and general anesthesia for the reviewed modified cleft-lift technique.
For definitive excision and closure, the review supports off-midline techniques over midline closure; it reports no evidence that one off-midline method is superior to the others.

Prone positioning is reported for the reviewed cleft-lift operation, but the surgical reviews provide no anesthesia-specific airway technique, physiologic targets, or complication-management protocol. Do not infer a routine airway or anesthetic recipe from them.

Recovery priorities in the available evidence are surgical wound healing and follow-up: open wounds can require prolonged healing and frequent dressing changes, while dehiscence and recurrence are reported after closure procedures.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Acute abscess management is distinct from definitive treatment of chronic sinus disease. The surgical review favors simple incision and drainage for an acute abscess; complete excision during acute swelling may create a very large wound defect.

Definitive options include excision with healing by secondary intention or closure. Midline primary suture is not recommended in the reviewed guidelines; off-midline closure options include Karydakis, cleft lift, and Limberg flap.

For the authors’ modified Bascom cleft lift, the described workflow uses general anesthesia and prone positioning with moderate waist flexion. This is a description of that technique, not a universal anesthetic requirement for pilonidal procedures.

bullets: Clarify whether the planned procedure is acute abscess drainage, a minimally invasive intervention, or definitive excision and closure; these are distinct approaches, and the sources do not provide one anesthesia plan applicable to all of them.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Port placement is typically performed through venous access using a Seldinger technique, with the catheter connected to a subcutaneous pocket; removal is mentioned in the evidence, but its technique is not described.

Anesthesia varies: local anesthesia or superficial cervical plexus block with intravenous sedoanalgesia has been studied, while another cohort reports general anesthesia. These sources do not establish one preferred technique.
Key procedural hazards include arterial puncture, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, and catheter malposition; guidewire and catheter position need attention during placement.
Recovery priorities include monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic, assessment for access-related complications, and confirmation of recovery status before discharge from postanesthesia care.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Robotic cholecystectomy is a minimally invasive upper-abdominal operation. General anesthesia with tracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is commonly described; robotic docking makes access and patient movement more constrained.

Key physiologic concerns are CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, impaired respiratory mechanics and hypercarbia, and reduced venous return in reverse Trendelenburg. Coordinate positioning, ventilation, and insufflation with the surgeon.

Plan access and escalation before docking, including a team-practiced robotic-cart removal drill. If neuromuscular blockade is used, coordinate its maintenance and reversal with the surgical team and assess recovery quantitatively before extubation.
Prioritize multimodal analgesia and PONV prevention, then monitor recovery for oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, nausea, and shoulder or port-site pain.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess history, examination, functional status, and relevant cardiopulmonary and metabolic disease; optimize conditions where possible and plan airway and access before draping or docking restricts them.

Significant cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease warrants careful assessment and team judgment. The review identifies increased intracranial pressure as a reason to avoid laparoscopic surgery; these are general review statements, not a robotic-cholecystectomy selection rule.
Pregnancy requires individualized maternal and surgical assessment; the supplied review discusses laparoscopic cholecystectomy in pregnancy but does not establish a trimester-based rule.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Reverse Trendelenburg is commonly used for cholecystectomy. Anticipate reduced venous return and hypotension, particularly if intravascular volume is low; agree positioning and access arrangements with the surgeon before docking.
Pad pressure points and protect the face; robot arms and a docked system can restrict access, and the table should not be moved while docked.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring, including ECG, blood pressure, oxygenation, and capnography; monitor neuromuscular blockade when used. Consider advanced hemodynamic monitoring according to patient risk and procedure needs, not routinely.

bullets: General anesthesia with tracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is the approach described for laparoscopic surgery; an endotracheal tube is preferred in the educational reference to permit higher ventilation pressures and PEEP.

Pneumoperitoneum and positioning can impair compliance and increase ventilation requirements. Track ventilation and end-tidal CO₂; consider arterial CO₂ assessment when clinical circumstances make end-tidal values unreliable.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation can cause vagal bradycardia from peritoneal stretch; hypercarbia and acidosis may contribute to tachyarrhythmia or impaired cardiac function. Communicate abrupt changes promptly with the surgeon and reassess insufflation and patient physiology.

Pneumoperitoneum and reverse Trendelenburg can reduce venous return while raising airway pressures and impairing respiratory mechanics. Follow gas exchange and hemodynamics through insufflation, position changes, and desufflation.

For robotic cases, immobility and timing of reversal require coordination with the surgeon. The sources differ on routine depth/continuation of blockade; use clinical judgment and quantitative monitoring if blockade is administered.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider tube migration, atelectasis, or impaired compliance with rising airway pressures or hypoxemia. Reassess airway position, ventilation, and surgical position with the team.

Gas-related complications include subcutaneous emphysema and capnothorax. Recognize signs such as crepitus, increased airway pressure, hypoxemia, or hypercapnia; alert the surgeon and assess for airway or hemodynamic compromise.

Vascular injury, gas embolism, or sudden cardiovascular collapse require immediate team escalation and surgical coordination. A docked robot can impede access; follow the locally rehearsed undocking response rather than assuming access is immediate.

Bleeding may follow port or needle access injury and can be difficult to recognize when visualization is limited. Heart rate, blood pressure, CVP, and urine output are imperfect volume surrogates during pneumoperitoneum; interpret them in context.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Robotic ventral or incisional hernia repair is generally performed under general anesthesia with CO₂ pneumoperitoneum; mesh is placed in a preperitoneal or retromuscular plane, with the approach determined by defect and tissue characteristics.

Key physiologic stresses include raised intra-abdominal pressure and CO₂ absorption, with potential cardiovascular effects, reduced pulmonary compliance, hypercarbia, and position-related edema or pressure injury. Assess the patient and operative conditions rather than assuming one uniform response.

Before docking, establish safe patient access and protect the face, ventilation tubing, and pressure points. Maintain complete neuromuscular blockade while the robotic platform is docked. Do not move the operating-room table while docked.

Recovery priorities include assessing ventilation and oxygenation, residual neuromuscular block when applicable, pain, PONV, and position-related facial or airway edema. Use an appropriate postanesthesia care setting and ongoing assessment.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Robotic ventral/incisional repairs use a minimally invasive sublay approach. Described options include preperitoneal repair (r-TAPP), retromuscular approaches (including r-TARM and r-E-TEP), and robotic transversus abdominis release (RoboTAR). These are surgical options, not interchangeable anesthesia protocols.

Approach depends on hernia location, size, prior operations, tissue planes, and the need for component separation. The technique review describes TAPP as dependent on a robust preperitoneal layer and RoboTAR for selected medium- or large-sized incisional hernias requiring component separation.

For expected intestinal adhesions, the technique review advises considering direct-vision transabdominal adhesiolysis before E-TEP to reduce bowel-injury risk during sac or posterior-element dissection.
The supplied hernia-specific sources address ventral and incisional repairs; they do not establish an anesthesia approach specific to robotic inguinal hernia repair.

bullets: Assess the defect and prior abdominal operations with the surgical team; prior operations and anticipated adhesions may affect access and the operative dissection plan.

bullets: The described ventral/incisional procedures use supine positioning. Table flexion, or legs-down positioning with slight Trendelenburg if hip flexion is unavailable, may be used to improve working geometry; choose positioning with attention to patient comfort and operative access.

Plan arm positioning and protect the face, airway tubing, and pressure points before docking. Robot arms can create pressure or accidental-extubation hazards, and access to the patient is constrained while docked.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards call for continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.

Keep the operating table stationary while the robot is docked. Make an access and communication plan for any urgent need to reach the patient; the provided sources do not supply a procedure-specific undocking algorithm.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is reported for the described robotic hernia procedures. A general laparoscopic/robotic anesthesia review favors an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; airway choice remains dependent on the procedure and patient.

Pneumoperitoneum and position can reduce pulmonary compliance and promote atelectasis; CO₂ absorption can increase carbon dioxide. Reassess ventilation after insufflation and position changes rather than assuming unchanged mechanics.

For laparoscopic and robotic surgery, a commonly used lung-protective strategy is 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight with PEEP 5–10 cm H₂O, titrated according to driving pressure and respiratory compliance; these are not hernia-specific targets.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify correct positioning by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation or removal, or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location, continually analyze end-tidal CO₂ using a quantitative method.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation may increase systemic vascular resistance and filling pressures, while inferior vena cava compression can reduce venous return. Peritoneal stretch may cause vagal bradyarrhythmia; hypercarbia may contribute to tachyarrhythmia or acidosis.

Reduced compliance, atelectasis, increased airway pressures, and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may accompany insufflation and Trendelenburg. Interpret airway pressures in context and reassess after operative or position changes.
Surgical descriptions use CO₂ pneumoperitoneum and report reducing pressure during selected closure steps. Those operative technique details do not define a universal anesthetic pressure target.
Maintain adequate neuromuscular relaxation through docking when blockade is used, and coordinate the end of blockade with undocking and the operative phase.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: At insufflation onset, a pronounced vagal response can produce bradyarrhythmia and, rarely, cardiac arrest. Recognize the temporal association and promptly coordinate assessment with the surgical team; the supplied review does not provide a case-specific rescue algorithm.

Position or insufflation can be associated with endobronchial intubation, tube obstruction, or atelectasis. Reassess airway position and ventilation when airway pressures, oxygenation, or ventilation change.

Consider subcutaneous emphysema or capnothorax when crepitus, rising airway pressure, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or asymmetric chest movement occurs. The review notes that these may resolve after insufflation is stopped, but significant cases require close monitoring and assessment for airway or hemodynamic compromise.

Bowel injury during adhesiolysis and trocar or access-related bleeding are surgical hazards. Limited visualization can obscure access injury; coordinate prompt evaluation with the surgeon when suspected.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The general laparoscopic/robotic review describes balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration. It cautions that heart rate, blood pressure, central venous pressure, and urine output are poor surrogates for intravascular volume during pneumoperitoneum.
Avoid assuming that minimally invasive access eliminates hemorrhage risk. Solid-organ injury during Veress needle or port access is described, and limited visualization may delay recognition.

Excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg. Individualize fluid administration to clinical circumstances; the hernia-specific cohort provides no fluid or blood-loss regimen.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Pain may be somatic at port sites and visceral from peritoneal stretch or abdominal tissue manipulation. A multimodal approach including acetaminophen and NSAIDs is described in the general review to limit opioid use; selection should reflect patient and procedure factors.
TAP blocks are described as an option for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches, not as a required component of every robotic repair. The hernia cohort does not specify an analgesic regimen.
Laparoscopy is identified as an independent PONV risk factor; prophylactic antiemetic administration is recommended by the educational review. It does not specify a hernia-specific regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred to clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Assess for facial, pharyngeal, or laryngopharyngeal edema after substantial Trendelenburg exposure, especially alongside fluid-related edema risk. The supplied hernia sources do not establish a routine delayed-extubation protocol.

After anesthesia, use a PACU or equivalent care area, with continuing assessment appropriate to the patient's condition and attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Evaluate pain, PONV, and bowel transit in recovery; the hernia cohort reported unscheduled presentations for pain and delayed intestinal transit, but these observations do not define a routine treatment protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Soft-tissue mass excision ranges from a localized excision under local anesthesia to larger or complex procedures; the available procedure study reports local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia, but does not establish which patients need which technique.

Priorities supported by the procedure sources are careful dissection near neurovascular structures, hemostasis, and limiting traction or thermal injury; reported complications include seroma, hematoma, and nerve injury.

Do not assume general anesthesia, an advanced airway, or neuromuscular blockade for a small superficial mass; the supplied sources do not define case-specific selection criteria or an anesthesia regimen.
Recovery should include assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and patient condition; the procedure literature does not define a specific emergence, analgesic, or PACU protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operative approach depends on lesion site and extent. Excision may be diagnostic as well as therapeutic when complete tissue architecture is needed; the supplied sources do not specify a single approach for all soft-tissue masses.

For lipomas, one described limited-incision method uses circumferential dissection, full mobilization before delivery, meticulous hemostasis, irrigation, and layered closure. This is a reported technique, not a universal standard.

For a rapidly growing presumed lipoma, the source describes radiologic evaluation to help distinguish it from malignant neoplasms. The available material does not establish a sarcoma staging, margin, or frozen-section protocol.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify lesion location, depth, size, vascularity, and proximity to neurovascular structures with the surgical team; these factors affect planning, but the sources provide no universal anesthesia-selection rule.

Consider whether complete excision is appropriate or whether a diagnostic alternative is needed for a large or complex lesion near vital structures. This is a source-described concern, not a fixed contraindication to excision.
Assess patient-specific medical status and develop the anesthesia plan; the provided standards identify this responsibility but do not supply a procedure-specific assessment protocol.

bullets: Positioning and room setup are site-dependent. A cutaneous excision reference calls for comfortable positioning, appropriate surgical lighting, and a setup at the surgeon’s appropriate height; it does not establish positioning for every deep mass.
For MAC or general anesthesia, apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.
The supplied sources do not support routine invasive monitoring or a particular vascular-access plan for this procedure.

bullets: The lipoma series includes local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia but gives no regimen or criteria for choosing between them. Do not infer that all excisions require general anesthesia or an airway device.
Airway device selection, general-anesthetic technique, and ventilation strategy are not addressed by the procedure-specific evidence.

bullets: For local infiltration in the described lipoma technique, the authors emphasize allowing time for epinephrine vasoconstriction and using hydrodissection to facilitate dissection and reduce bleeding. These are technique details from a retrospective series, not an anesthesia protocol.
Avoid unnecessary traction and thermal injury during limited-incision dissection; the source describes careful mobilization and preference for scissors or forceps over electrocautery for dissection.
No procedure-specific physiologic targets or phase-based anesthetic management are established in the supplied evidence.

bullets: Relevant reported procedural complications include seroma, hematoma, and nerve injury. In the single retrospective lipoma series, the nerve injury occurred in a large mass and resolved spontaneously; these data do not establish general rates for all soft-tissue excisions.

Maintain attention to bleeding and potential hematoma. The excisional-biopsy reference identifies bleeding as the most common intraoperative concern and notes that persistent bleeding may require further local control.

For expanding, tense postoperative hematoma, the reference describes prompt evacuation and wound-bed re-exploration to reduce risk of tissue ischemia, infection, and edge necrosis; this is procedural guidance, not an anesthetic algorithm.

bullets: Postanesthesia care applies after general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care. During transport, the patient should be evaluated and treated with monitoring and support appropriate to condition; on PACU arrival, reassessment and handoff are required.
During the initial recovery phase, the postanesthesia standard requires a quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry; ongoing observation should reflect the patient’s condition.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended and recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 should be confirmed before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Splenectomy may be open, laparoscopic, or robotic; minimally invasive approaches are favored for scheduled procedures, particularly for hematologic conditions. The approach and position are surgical decisions, with open surgery described supine.
Prioritize anticipation and recognition of hemorrhage, especially with splenomegaly or portal hypertension, and protect the pancreas and other adjacent structures during dissection.
For laparoscopic surgery, insufflation and position can impair respiratory mechanics and alter venous return and hemodynamics; monitor and respond to the individual patient's physiology.
Recovery priorities include surveillance for bleeding, pancreatic complications, thromboembolism, and infection; vaccination and ongoing infection-prevention measures matter after splenectomy.

Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Splenectomy removes the spleen and can be open, laparoscopic, or robotic-assisted. The review describes minimally invasive approaches as favored over open surgery, especially for scheduled hematologic procedures; this does not establish that a particular approach suits every patient.

For laparoscopic cases, positioning is not settled: right lateral decubitus can facilitate posterior and hilar dissection, while other positions offer different operative access. Selection depends on surgeon preference and the likelihood of conversion.
Open surgery is described supine. Laparoscopic access and dissection vary; the review describes open cutdown as preferred when splenomegaly makes access more hazardous.

sources.label: Splenectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess spleen size and relevant comorbidity. For elective laparoscopic splenectomy, the review calls for preoperative abdominal ultrasonography; it notes CT assessment for accessory spleens in patients with ITP or malignancy.

Splenomegaly can restrict operative space and complicate dissection or extraction; it is associated with more blood loss and conversion. Portal hypertension also increases bleeding and conversion concerns.

Review vaccination status and optimize relevant anemia, nutritional deficiencies, comorbidities, and clotting or bleeding abnormalities. Elective vaccination against encapsulated organisms is recommended approximately two weeks before surgery in the cited review.

sources.label: Splenectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Positioning for laparoscopic splenectomy is technique-dependent; right lateral decubitus is one described option, not a universal requirement. Open surgery is described supine.

The procedure review lists arterial line, Foley catheter, gastric tube, and sequential compression devices for open and laparoscopic procedures. It gives no individualized criteria or monitoring targets; select invasive monitoring according to the case and patient.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.

sources.label: Splenectomy

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is described for laparoscopic and robotic procedures; endotracheal intubation is specified for open surgery in the procedure review and was used in the reported laparoscopic series. The laparoscopic-surgery reference describes an endotracheal tube as preferred to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP.

With pneumoperitoneum, reduced lung compliance and functional residual capacity, atelectasis, and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may complicate ventilation. The general laparoscopy reference describes increasing minute ventilation to compensate for CO₂ absorption; no splenectomy-specific ventilatory target is established here.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For laparoscopy, insufflation and positioning can affect preload, venous return, airway pressures, and gas exchange. Monitor for clinically important changes during insufflation and position changes rather than assuming a uniform response.

Dissection and mobilization are bleeding-risk phases; the review identifies splenic capsule or short-gastric-vessel injury as common sources of intraoperative bleeding. Adequate hemostasis and readiness to change approach are central priorities.

Hilar dissection requires attention to the pancreatic tail and neighboring organs. The procedure review describes laparoscopic hilar division with a vascular-load stapler, with clips or hemostatic agents for staple-line bleeding; it does not establish an anesthetic-specific intervention.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Hemorrhage may follow mobilization or splenomegaly and portal hypertension. If bleeding is not controlled promptly, the procedure review supports considering conversion; it supplies no anesthesia-specific hemorrhage algorithm.

Pancreatic injury can lead to pancreatitis, fluid collection, or pancreatic fistula; stomach and colon are also among commonly injured structures. Suspected pancreatic injury warrants surgical assessment; the review describes drain placement when injury is suspected.

Laparoscopic access and insufflation can cause solid-organ injury or hemorrhage that is obscured by limited visualization; gas-related thoracic complications are also described in the general laparoscopy reference. Recognize unexpected hemodynamic or respiratory deterioration and escalate evaluation with the surgical team.

Postoperative concerns include venous thromboembolism, infection including overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, and intra-abdominal abscess. The review describes lifelong preventive measures and monitoring after splenectomy.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The procedure-specific review provides no fluid, blood-product, or hemodynamic management protocol. Anticipate blood loss in higher-risk anatomy and tailor access and product availability to the clinical context rather than applying a fixed volume or transfusion rule.

For laparoscopic procedures, the general reference supports balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, and cautions that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, especially with Trendelenburg.
The cited retrospective laparoscopic series reports a local intraoperative blood-salvage protocol, but it does not establish a general transfusion strategy or threshold for splenectomy.

bullets: The splenectomy review provides no specific analgesia regimen. The general laparoscopy reference describes multimodal analgesia, including acetaminophen and NSAIDs, with local anesthetic at port sites as options to reduce opioid use; select according to patient and procedure factors.
A transversus abdominis plane block may be offered for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches; the general laparoscopy reference does not make neuraxial anesthesia routine.
Laparoscopy is an independent PONV risk factor; the general reference recommends prophylactic antiemetic administration, without specifying a splenectomy-specific regimen.

bullets: The splenectomy review gives no specific emergence, extubation, or recovery-room protocol. Recovery planning should reflect the operative course and patient status; the source does not establish routine ICU disposition for all cases.

After anesthesia, patients should receive postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent location, with ongoing assessment appropriate to their condition and particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Provide ongoing surveillance for bleeding, pancreatic complications, infection, and thrombosis. The splenectomy review describes vaccination and often antibiotic prophylaxis as longer-term prevention measures, not substitutes for immediate postoperative assessment.

bullets: The procedure-specific review is a general surgical review, not an anesthesia reference; it does not provide anesthetic drug regimens, fluid or transfusion protocols, analgesia, emergence instructions, or monitoring targets.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Plan around thyroid function and airway compression, not gland size alone; positional symptoms or substernal extension can change induction and rescue options.
Coordinate the EMG tube and neuromuscular-blocker strategy when recurrent laryngeal nerve monitoring is planned.
Expanding neck hematoma with airway compromise is an immediate emergency; recognize early swallowing, swelling and breathing changes.
After surgery, distinguish hematoma, bilateral vocal-cord dysfunction, edema, hypocalcemia and rare tracheomalacia rather than calling all stridor laryngospasm.

sections.title: Extent, neck dissection & substernal disease
bullets: Clarify lobectomy versus total/completion thyroidectomy, cancer-related nodal dissection, reoperation and any substernal component. Extensive dissection changes airway, nerve and parathyroid risks.

Review imaging when compression or retrosternal extension is suspected, including level/extent of tracheal narrowing. Establish whether positioning worsens symptoms and whether specialist airway or thoracic backup is needed.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Thyroid state & elective optimization
bullets: Review thyroid function, symptoms, rate/rhythm, heart failure and antithyroid or replacement treatment. Aim to control significant overt hyperthyroidism before elective surgery; avoid assuming an apparently calm patient is biochemically optimized.

Severe hypothyroidism can affect cardiac function, ventilation, drug sensitivity and recovery. Coordinate endocrine optimization and the urgency decision rather than using one abnormal TSH result as a universal cancellation rule.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
Thyroid surgery anesthesia review (2013; historical narrative review)

sections.title: Compressive goiter & induction strategy
bullets: Assess voice, dysphagia, stridor, orthopnea, supine intolerance and neck mobility; review prior vocal-cord assessment. Tracheal deviation alone does not mandate awake intubation, but symptoms and meaningful compression warrant a deliberate plan.

For an anticipated difficult airway or intolerance of apnea, consider awake intubation with appropriate oxygenation, topicalization and skilled backup. Confirm tracheal placement visually and with capnography before induction; do not assume maintaining spontaneous breathing guarantees safety.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

BJA Education: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery (2024)
OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024)
Pheochromocytoma perioperative review (2025)

sections.title: Positioning, airway access & exposure
bullets: Check cervical mobility before extending the neck. Pad pressure points, protect eyes, secure the airway and IVs, and recheck ventilation after final positioning and draping. Avoid forcing extension in cervical disease.

Account for restricted airway access after the table turns. Extensive central/lateral neck dissection, reoperation or substernal disease changes the duration and airway plan; it is not interchangeable with a small focused operation.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Nerve-monitoring tube & neuromuscular blockade
bullets: If laryngeal EMG monitoring is planned, position the tube electrodes correctly at the vocal cords and verify contact after neck positioning. Tube movement, electrode contact and residual blockade can cause poor signals; loss of signal is not automatically surgical nerve injury.

Coordinate adequate intubating conditions with recovery before stimulation. Neuromuscular blockers suppress EMG amplitude, so agree on the induction/reversal strategy and any additional doses rather than applying an indiscriminate “never use relaxant” rule.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring; a usable surgical EMG signal is not proof of complete systemic recovery. When blockade was used, confirm adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: neuromuscular blockade guideline summary (2023)

sections.title: Thyroid storm or unexplained instability
bullets: Unexplained tachyarrhythmia, hyperthermia and cardiovascular deterioration should raise concern for thyroid storm in the appropriate setting, while also evaluating other causes. Altered mental status and gastrointestinal findings may be unavailable under anesthesia.

Stop provoking stimulation where feasible, call for help and initiate the local thyroid-storm pathway with supportive cooling, hemodynamic care, endocrine-directed antithyroid therapy and glucocorticoids. Rate-control drugs require caution in decompensated cardiac failure; a beta blocker is not the whole treatment.

sources.label: Thyroid surgery anesthesia review (2013; historical narrative review)

sections.title: Analgesia, nausea & smooth recovery
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia with acetaminophen, local infiltration or a selected superficial cervical plexus technique, and NSAID/COX-2 therapy when renal, bleeding and other risks permit. Reserve titrated opioids for additional need, particularly with OSA or airway concerns.

Plan risk-based PONV prevention and prompt treatment. Aim for a controlled emergence without severe coughing or retching, but do not sacrifice ventilation or airway protection merely to suppress the response.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Extubation & postoperative voice/airway
bullets: Plan extubation from the preoperative airway and operative course. Significant compression, difficult intubation, swelling or nerve concerns may require delayed extubation or a staged specialist plan rather than routine immediate removal.

Bilateral RLN dysfunction can cause acute stridor and airway obstruction; unilateral dysfunction may cause hoarseness or impaired airway protection. Escalate new voice or respiratory changes, and do not use a reassuring nerve-monitor trace as a substitute for clinical assessment.

Tracheomalacia is an uncommon consideration after longstanding compression, not an assumed finding in every large goiter. A cuff-leak assessment cannot by itself rule out every cause of extubation failure.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update
Thyroid surgery anesthesia review (2013; historical narrative review)

sections.title: Neck hematoma: recognize & act
bullets: Look for DESATS: difficulty swallowing/discomfort, rising early-warning score, swelling, anxiety, tachypnea/difficulty breathing and stridor. Stridor may be late; a small hematoma can still produce dangerous airway compression and venous congestion.

Call surgical and senior anesthesia help, give oxygen and assess the airway with the patient head-up. Rapidly expanding swelling or airway compromise requires immediate emergency management; do not delay decompression for imaging or routine transfer.

For airway compromise from suspected hematoma, trained clinicians should open and evacuate the wound using the local emergency protocol. SCOOP means skin exposure, cut sutures, open skin, open muscles including the strap layer, and pack the wound. Merely opening superficial skin may not decompress the deeper collection.

If compromise persists, proceed with expert airway management, limited attempts and immediate front-of-neck rescue capability. Definitive surgical hemostasis and close monitored care are still required after initial decompression. The thyroid consensus is the direct source; adapt through the local neck-surgery pathway for parathyroid cases.

sources.label: DAS/BAETS/ENT-UK: thyroid hematoma consensus guideline (2021)
StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Hypocalcemia & hormone replacement
bullets: Monitor postoperative calcium/PTH according to extent of surgery and local protocol. Paresthesia, muscle spasm, tetany, QT prolongation or laryngospasm can signal hypocalcemia; severe symptomatic cases require monitored urgent treatment.

Total thyroidectomy requires thyroid-hormone replacement; after partial surgery assess residual function rather than assuming the same regimen for everyone. Document endocrine follow-up and any calcium/calcitriol plan at discharge.

sections.title: Observation & discharge safeguards
bullets: Ensure staff can recognize hematoma and access emergency neck-opening equipment. The DAS consensus recommends at least hourly observations initially for 6 hours after thyroid surgery, with subsequent frequency and discharge individualized to risk and local policy.
Provide explicit emergency advice for neck swelling, swallowing/breathing difficulty and hypocalcemic symptoms. An uneventful PACU period does not eliminate later hematoma risk.

Guidelines, narrative reviews and device/procedure-specific evidence are not interchangeable. Hormone status, organ reserve and postoperative trends determine the plan; a tumor label alone does not establish safe anesthesia or discharge.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Tracheostomy establishes an airway through the anterior tracheal wall by an open surgical or percutaneous approach. Open procedures are usually performed in an operating room; percutaneous placement is commonly performed at the bedside in an ICU.

The key anesthetic priorities are coordinated airway transition, reliable confirmation of tracheostomy-tube position, and avoidance of loss of ventilation or airway access. End-tidal carbon dioxide and, for percutaneous placement, bronchoscopic visualization support confirmation.

Important hazards include operative bleeding, false passage or airway loss during tube exchange, posterior-wall injury, and rare airway fire when electrocautery is used in an oxygen-enriched environment.

Recovery planning centers on a secured, patent tracheostomy airway, surveillance for bleeding, obstruction or displacement, and appropriate postanesthesia or ICU care. The source does not establish a specific anesthetic emergence or analgesia regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Tracheostomy creates an opening in the anterior tracheal wall, usually between the second and third rings. The approaches described are open surgery and percutaneous placement using a modified Seldinger technique.

Open tracheostomy is traditionally performed in the operating room; selected cases may be performed under local anesthesia. Percutaneous placement is usually performed at the ICU bedside, though it may also be done in the operating room.

The choice of approach depends on the clinical situation, anatomy, procedural expertise and setting. In the COVID-era review, evidence did not establish superiority of open over percutaneous technique; that review’s infection-control context should not be treated as a general approach mandate.
Initial placement generally uses a cuffed, nonfenestrated tracheostomy tube. The operative technique and airway plan should be coordinated between the proceduralist and airway operator.

Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify the indication and whether the patient is already intubated; assess current airway access, neck anatomy, prior surgery or radiation, and coagulation status. These factors can affect approach and procedural difficulty.

For a planned case, review whether the patient can tolerate the brief ventilation interruption that may be needed during tracheal entry or dilation. The available sources do not establish a universal threshold for tolerance.

In life-threatening airway emergencies, the source states that no condition is an absolute contraindication to tracheostomy; management remains dependent on the emergency and available airway options.

The COVID-era review recommends multidisciplinary discussion for its population and describes infectious-risk planning. Those recommendations are specific to COVID-19-era practice and do not establish routine timing or testing requirements for other patients.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For neck access, supine positioning with neck extension is described; a shoulder roll or chest bump can improve anterior tracheal access. Individualize positioning when neck mobility or anatomy limits extension.

Have tracheostomy equipment and appropriate tube options available. For percutaneous placement, the described technique uses flexible bronchoscopy to visualize needle and guidewire placement and confirm tube position.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature; for general anesthesia, expired carbon dioxide monitoring is continued unless invalidated by the patient, procedure or equipment.

For a transmissible respiratory pathogen or other aerosol-risk context, use infection precautions and room controls appropriate to the circumstance and local policy; the COVID-era review describes negative-pressure rooms when available.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Open procedures are usually performed under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, but selected upper-airway-compromise cases may be managed awake under local anesthesia with spontaneous breathing. Percutaneous procedures are typically performed in intubated, sedated patients, with or without neuromuscular blockade.

For percutaneous placement, the described conventional technique withdraws the ETT under bronchoscopic guidance before needle entry; coordinate ETT movement and tracheal access with the proceduralist. The precise airway sequence may vary by approach.

Ventilation may be interrupted briefly during tracheal entry or percutaneous dilation if clinically feasible. Once the tracheostomy tube is inserted, confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and reconfirm ventilation.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation is conditional on blockade use; it does not impose paralysis for every tracheostomy.

Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The airway transition is a critical phase: coordinate ETT withdrawal, tracheal entry, tracheostomy-tube insertion and connection to the breathing circuit. Confirm tube position and ventilation after the transition.

Bleeding can obscure the operative field or impede bronchoscopy. The source emphasizes correction of coagulopathy when possible and meticulous hemostasis; it does not supply a universal fluid or transfusion regimen for this reference.

When electrocautery is used, coordinate with the surgical team to reduce airway-fire risk from oxygen and ignition sources. The supplied sources do not establish a universal inspired-oxygen threshold for all tracheostomies.
Tracheostomy may reduce airway resistance and facilitate ventilator weaning, but the source does not provide case-specific physiologic targets or a ventilation prescription.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anticipate bleeding, false passage, tube obstruction, displacement and loss of airway access. Tube displacement into soft tissue or a false passage may require airway re-establishment; the source identifies flexible-laryngoscopic guidance as preferable for reintubation when required.
Posterior-wall disruption, false passage or apical injury can lead to pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. Bronchoscopy can help prevent posterior-wall injury during percutaneous placement.

If airway fire occurs, the source describes immediate circuit removal, mask ventilation and airway inspection for thermal injury. This is a source-reported response, not a substitute for local emergency protocols.

Early tube changes are discouraged unless necessary because the immature tract increases the risk of false passage and airway compromise. The source describes the initial tube change as typically occurring on postoperative days 5 to 7; this is not a universal timing instruction for an individual patient.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Bleeding is identified as the most common intraoperative complication. Assess and manage hemostasis in the context of the patient’s coagulation status and procedural findings.

The tracheostomy overview provides no fluid regimen or specific fluid-management guidance. Fluid administration and perfusion goals therefore remain patient- and context-dependent rather than fixed by these sources.

The COVID-era review likewise does not specify fluid-management regimens, blood-product thresholds or transfusion practice; its discussion of anticoagulation is specific to COVID-associated illness and does not define a general perioperative anticoagulation protocol.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The tracheostomy source provides no analgesic regimen or specific postoperative pain-management recommendation. It therefore does not support a standard drug or dose for this procedure.

The supplied sources do not provide a procedure-specific PONV assessment or prophylaxis regimen; manage these issues according to the patient and applicable practice guidance rather than infer a tracheostomy-specific protocol.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure establishes a tracheostomy airway, which is connected to the ventilator as appropriate. Confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and reassess ventilation; the source does not specify when or how anesthesia should be discontinued or the ETT removed.

Plan recovery in a PACU or equivalent area such as an ICU, with transport monitoring and handoff appropriate to the patient’s condition. The ASA postanesthesia standards call for attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature.

Postprocedure surveillance includes tube patency and position, bleeding, and subcutaneous air. Humidified gas, suctioning and routine stoma or cannula care are described as measures to reduce obstruction risk.

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure source is a clinical overview, not an anesthesia-specific guideline or formal systematic review. It describes approaches, airway considerations and complications but does not provide detailed anesthetic emergence, analgesia or fluid protocols.

The second procedure source concerns COVID-19-associated respiratory failure and is a narrative review combining prior outbreak literature with institutional experience. Its timing and infection-control discussion should not be generalized as routine practice outside its scope.

ASA basic monitoring, postanesthesia-care and neuromuscular-blockade sources support general monitoring and recovery principles, not a tracheostomy-specific anesthetic plan. The supplied ERAS sources concern gastrointestinal surgery and provide no tracheostomy recommendations.

A specific cuff-pressure target is not adopted here: the tracheostomy overview gives discordant pressure statements in different sections and uses different units. Case-specific anesthetic targets and an analgesia or emergence protocol are not established by the available procedure sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adult primary umbilical hernia repair, open surgery may be performed with local anesthesia plus monitored anesthesia care (LA + MAC); laparoscopic and robotic approaches are also described. The anesthetic approach depends on the patient, operation, resources, and preference.

For laparoscopic or robotic abdominal surgery, general anesthesia is described as standard; an endotracheal tube is preferred over a supraglottic airway to support ventilation when insufflation raises ventilatory demands.

With abdominal insufflation, prioritize assessment of ventilation and hemodynamics: CO₂ absorption, altered respiratory mechanics, pressure effects, and positioning can all affect physiology. Adapt support to the operation and observed response.

Plan recovery around pain and PONV, and assess for residual neuromuscular blockade if a blocker was used. Quantitative confirmation of recovery applies to NMB cases, not to every local or neuraxial technique.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The hernia-specific source addresses elective repair of primary adult umbilical hernias and distinguishes these from incisional umbilical hernias. It describes open repair, laparoscopic repair, and several robotic approaches; it does not establish one approach as universally preferred.

For open primary umbilical repair, LA + MAC is a described option, particularly for older patients with substantial comorbidity. Regional anesthesia is also discussed as an approach in settings where resources or general anesthesia are limited. Neither is established here as a universal regimen.

The general laparoscopic/robotic review supplies relevant anesthesia considerations but is not a hernia-specific protocol. Do not infer a required anesthetic technique for every repair from approach alone.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the patient’s comorbidities and preferences alongside the planned approach and local expertise/resources. The source describes LA + MAC as an option, not a default; in the authors’ practice, patient preference was the stated contraindication to offering it for most open repairs.

For hernia decision-making, the source discusses obesity, smoking, hernia size, and infection risk. It recommends counseling about smoking and weight loss but says repair should not be denied solely because a patient cannot or adamantly refuses to make those changes.

Acute incarceration with strangulation may require urgent or emergent treatment; bowel-containing hernias warrant more cautious management than those incarcerated with fat. The source does not provide an anesthesia-specific induction protocol for these circumstances.
The supplied hernia source concerns primary umbilical hernia, so its selection and risk discussion does not resolve assessment for ventral or prior-incisional repairs.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For laparoscopic or robotic surgery, the general review recommends standard ASA monitors. Consider additional hemodynamic monitoring only when patient or procedural circumstances warrant it; the source does not prescribe routine arterial access.

Potential laparoscopic/robotic positions include Trendelenburg, reverse Trendelenburg, lateral decubitus, lithotomy, and flexed position. Position-related venous return changes and pressure injury are relevant; protect pressure points and coordinate table movement when a robot is docked.

Basic monitoring standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes. These standards apply across anesthetic techniques, including MAC.
The supplied sources do not establish hernia-specific room equipment, warming, urinary-catheter use, or access requirements.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Open repair may be performed under LA + MAC in selected patients; this evidence does not justify imposing intubation or neuromuscular blockade on local-anesthetic cases. During moderate or deep sedation, ventilation assessment includes clinical observation and expired CO₂ monitoring unless precluded or invalidated.

For laparoscopic/robotic surgery, general anesthesia is described as standard; the review prefers an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP. This is approach-specific guidance, not a mandate for open minimal-anesthetic repair.

Insufflation and position changes can alter airway pressures and tube position; the review notes possible endobronchial migration and increased cuff pressure. Reassess ventilation and airway status as the operation and position evolve.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: At insufflation, pneumoperitoneum can increase intrathoracic pressure and cardiac filling pressures; inferior vena cava compression may reduce preload and venous return. Interpret hemodynamic changes in the context of insufflation, position, and the patient’s response.

CO₂ absorption and altered respiratory mechanics can increase CO₂ and airway pressures, while reduced compliance, atelectasis, and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may develop. The review describes increasing minute ventilation to compensate for CO₂ absorption; exact ventilator settings must reflect the individual case.

Insufflation onset can produce a pronounced vagal response and bradyarrhythmias; hypercarbia can contribute to tachyarrhythmias. Recognize abrupt changes and coordinate promptly with the surgical team regarding the operative stimulus and insufflation.
The supplied sources do not characterize abdominal-wall closure physiology or closure-related ventilation changes specifically for hernia repair.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For laparoscopic access, solid-organ injury and hemorrhage may be obscured by limited visualization. Keep access-related injury in the differential when physiology changes unexpectedly and communicate concerns with the surgeon.

CO₂-related complications described include subcutaneous emphysema and capnothorax. Findings may include crepitus, increased airway pressure, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or unequal chest expansion; monitor for airway compromise and significant hemodynamic change and escalate for assessment.

Residual neuromuscular blockade is associated with upper-airway obstruction, reintubation, atelectasis, pneumonia, and prolonged PACU stay. If NMB is used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; the guideline favors adductor pollicis monitoring and confirmation of recovery before extubation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The laparoscopic/robotic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, and cautions that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, worsened by Trendelenburg. This is general MIS guidance, not a hernia-specific fluid prescription.

During pneumoperitoneum, heart rate, blood pressure, central venous pressure, and urine output are described as poor surrogate predictors of intravascular volume. Interpret these measures alongside the operative and physiologic context rather than as isolated volume indicators.

MIS is associated with less bleeding and reduced transfusion need, but access-related hemorrhage remains possible. The supplied evidence gives no hernia-specific blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, or fluid total.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For laparoscopic procedures, the review describes multimodal analgesia including acetaminophen and NSAIDs to limit opioid use, with local anesthetic at port sites as an option. It does not establish a hernia-specific drug regimen.
TAP blocks are described as an option for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches. The source does not establish a TAP block as mandatory or as a universal technique for open hernia repair.

Laparoscopy is identified as an independent PONV risk factor, and the review recommends prophylactic antiemetic administration. The supplied evidence does not specify an individualized prophylaxis regimen.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: If neuromuscular blockers were administered, use quantitative monitoring to confirm adequate recovery before extubation. The cited guideline recommends TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 and the adductor pollicis monitoring site; these recommendations do not apply to cases without NMB.

After anesthesia, patients should receive postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent unless specifically ordered otherwise by the responsible anesthesiologist. Continue appropriate observation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

During transport to the PACU, a knowledgeable Anesthesia Care Team member must accompany the patient and provide monitoring and support appropriate to the patient’s condition. Re-evaluate the patient on arrival and provide a verbal report to the responsible nurse. The hernia-specific article does not provide detailed emergence or postoperative-care instructions.

sources.label: New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The hernia-specific article is a perspective/review, not an anesthesia guideline or randomized anesthesia trial. It reports no randomized trials comparing LA + MAC with general or regional anesthesia for umbilical hernia repair; its institutional feasibility cohort included 53 veteran patients, limiting generalizability.

The hernia-specific source addresses primary umbilical hernias exclusively; the general MIS review supports contextual laparoscopic/robotic considerations but does not establish hernia-specific management. Evidence for ventral and incisional hernia anesthesia is therefore not resolved by these sources.
The ERAS sources concern major abdominal or gastrointestinal surgery and provide broad principles or consensus context in the supplied material, not detailed hernia-specific recommendations.

Case-specific anesthetic management for ventral/incisional repair, including closure-related respiratory effects and approach-specific airway, fluid, and recovery guidance, is not established in the supplied evidence.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Debridement ranges from bedside sharp removal to surgical excision in the operating room. Surgical debridement removes nonviable tissue down to intact structures; the extent and method depend on the wound and patient.

For surgical cases, plan adequate anesthesia and account for pain and bleeding. Tissue and vessel injury with bleeding are common during surgical debridement; wound-care sources do not establish an anesthetic technique for a particular patient or wound.

Choose the anesthetic and monitoring to fit the planned procedure and patient; available sources do not establish a default airway, ventilation strategy, invasive monitoring plan, or fluid regimen for debridement.

After anesthesia, use an appropriate postanesthesia-care setting and monitor recovery according to the patient's condition. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited guideline supports quantitative confirmation of recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Debridement removes adherent dead tissue, scabs, or foreign bodies; the selected method should reflect the wound and patient rather than assume one technique is suitable for all cases. Debridement supports wound assessment and healing, but repeated, unselected surgical removal may impair healing.

Sharp debridement may be performed on an outpatient basis and can leave nonviable tissue behind. Surgical debridement is more extensive and, in the cited wound primer, is performed in the operating room; pronounced findings warrant adequate anesthesia in an operating room in the position paper.

The wound primer notes that surgical debridement often requires general anesthesia or local infiltrate. The position paper advises discussing general anesthesia as an option; neither source establishes a universal anesthetic technique.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify wound extent, the proposed method and setting, patient comorbidities, pain, and the patient's overall condition. The cited position paper also identifies available resources and clinician competencies as factors in method selection.

Assess bleeding risk before surgical debridement, including coagulation disorders and anticoagulant treatment, and incorporate findings into procedural planning. The source identifies significant bleeding as a particular complication but gives no thresholds or medication-interruption schedule.

Assess pain and consider individualized, adequate analgesia. Pyoderma gangrenosum during its inflammatory phase is identified as a condition in which debridement may worsen disease through pathergy; the source says medically controlled inflammation changes that consideration.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For pronounced findings requiring surgical debridement, the wound-care position paper recommends an operating-room setting with adequate anesthesia. It does not provide positioning, access, warming, or room-equipment specifications.

Apply the relevant basic anesthesia monitoring standards for the anesthetic delivered: oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature are continually evaluated, with blood pressure and heart rate assessed at least every five minutes.

Do not infer that an arterial line is routinely required for this procedure. The monitoring standard describes intra-arterial pressure as one possible means of continually evaluating circulation during general anesthesia, not a debridement-specific indication.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The provided wound-debridement sources do not specify airway choice, induction, ventilation, or criteria for general versus local anesthesia beyond noting that surgical debridement may require general anesthesia or local infiltrate. Select technique for the individual procedure and patient; no routine intubation or paralysis is established here.

For general anesthesia, follow the basic ventilation-monitoring standard, including continual evaluation of ventilation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the standard's stated exceptions apply.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to local-anesthetic or other cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Surgical debridement may involve removal down to intact tissue, with tissue and vessel injury and bleeding commonly occurring. The supplied wound sources do not define physiologic targets or procedure-specific critical phases.
After surgical debridement, the position paper describes hemostasis by manual compression or hemostatic wound dressings and recommends a short-term clinical check that bleeding is controlled.

The primer notes that sharp or surgical debridement often causes bleeding; it provides no bleeding rate or quantified complication risk. Avoid extrapolating this observation to an expected blood loss for an individual case.
