sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Bleeding is a recognized complication of surgical debridement. Reassess hemostasis clinically after the procedure; the wound position paper does not supply a blood-loss threshold or a transfusion algorithm.
Consider pathergy in susceptible wounds, particularly pyoderma gangrenosum during active inflammation. The source advises that debridement can be performed when inflammation is medically controlled.
Worsening wound findings may include increased exudate, pain, odor, bleeding, and tissue friability.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Individualize fluid and blood-product planning to the patient, wound, and observed losses. The supplied sources do not establish a fluid volume, transfusion threshold, or blood-product preparation rule for debridement.

Account for bleeding risk before the procedure and assess hemostasis after surgical debridement. The wound paper describes clinical bleeding control rather than a quantitative perfusion or blood-loss endpoint.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Assess pain regularly with an appropriate instrument and plan analgesia individually. The position paper gives visual analog and numeric rating scales as examples.
For minor procedures, topical lidocaine–prilocaine cream may be sufficient; the position paper specifies an adequate application time of not less than 30–60 minutes.
Discuss general anesthesia as an option for surgical debridement when appropriate. No PONV prevention or treatment regimen is supplied for this procedure.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied debridement sources do not provide emergence criteria or procedure-specific postoperative anesthesia care. Use the appropriate postanesthesia-care setting unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise.

During recovery, evaluate the patient continually with monitoring appropriate to medical condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. A quantitative oxygenation method such as pulse oximetry is required in the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation as described in the cited guideline overview. The source does not establish a debridement-specific discharge or extubation protocol.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-relevant source is an ICW professional-society position paper on chronic-wound debridement nomenclature and wound-care practice, not an anesthesia reference. It supports debridement-method selection, analgesia considerations, bleeding risk, and clinical bleeding checks, but does not provide an anesthetic plan.

The second wound source is a primer/review covering acute and chronic wounds; it describes debridement approaches but supplies no anesthesia-specific recommendations. Neither wound source specifies an adult-only population.

ASA sources provide general standards for monitoring, preanesthesia responsibility, and postanesthesia care, not debridement-specific technique or risk management. The neuromuscular-blockade source is an overview of ASA guidance and applies only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Diagnostic EGD is usually performed with conscious sedation; deeper sedation may be used when clinically selected. The endoscope creates a shared airway and can partially obstruct it.

Prioritize airway access, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring, and readiness to rescue deeper-than-intended sedation. Positioning and oxygen-delivery choices must account for limited airway access.
Assess aspiration and cardiopulmonary risk before the procedure; consider a protected airway when aspiration risk is especially high or the procedure is prolonged or technically challenging.
Recovery priorities are ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and consciousness, with monitoring for sedation or instrumentation complications and use of discharge criteria.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: EGD (also termed OGD in the sources) provides direct visualization and mucosal sampling for diagnosis, therapy and surveillance of upper-GI symptoms. The procedure and intended sedation level should be agreed with the patient as part of consent.

Most diagnostic examinations use conscious sedation; unsedated examination with topical pharyngeal anesthetic is also described. Sedation practice varies, and the sources do not establish one regimen as the routine choice for every adult EGD.

This is a shared-airway procedure with reduced airway access. The scope is a foreign body in the aerodigestive tract and may cause partial obstruction; stimulation and required sedation depth can change during the examination.

sources.label: Complications of diagnostic upper Gastrointestinal endoscopy: common and rare – recognition, assessment and management
Guidelines for sedation and anesthesia in GI endoscopy
Hypoxia During Upper GI Endoscopy: There is Still Room for Improvement

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review prior adverse reactions to sedation, medications and interactions, cardiopulmonary disease, sleep apnea, neuromuscular or swallowing impairment, obesity, airway features, baseline consciousness and recent oral intake. Consider ASA class as one risk modifier; ASA III or above is associated with increased adverse-event risk in GI endoscopy.

Review the last oral intake and assess for impaired gastric emptying or esophageal motility disorders. A review describes minimum fasting periods of 2 hours for clear liquids and 6 hours for food, extended to at least 12 hours for known or suspected delayed gastric emptying or motility disorders and 48 hours in achalasia. The ASGE guideline reports no direct evidence linking fasting duration to pulmonary-aspiration risk and no universally accepted practice standard; it cites ASA guidance of at least 2 hours after clear liquids and 6 hours after light meals.

Reflux, dysphagia, food impaction, GI bleeding and anemia are identified as airway-related risk modifiers; obesity, pulmonary disease, reduced cardiac output and fever may increase vulnerability to rapid desaturation during apnea. Pregnancy testing is recommended in the appropriate clinical setting for women of childbearing age; the sources do not make pregnancy a universal contraindication.

sources.label: Complications of diagnostic upper Gastrointestinal endoscopy: common and rare – recognition, assessment and management
Guidelines for sedation and anesthesia in GI endoscopy
Hypoxia During Upper GI Endoscopy: There is Still Room for Improvement

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Expect lateral, semi-prone or prone positioning and plan for restricted access to the airway. Position is not standardized in the supplied sources; select it with the endoscopist while preserving feasible airway access.

Have appropriate airway and resuscitation equipment immediately available, and ensure the team can communicate and respond despite endoscopist access needs. Bite blocks can dislodge teeth; assess dentition and use appropriate protection.

For moderate or deep sedation, monitor oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, pulse, blood pressure and responsiveness. ASA standards call for at least every-five-minute blood pressure and heart-rate assessment during anesthesia; consider capnography particularly for deep sedation, without treating its benefit in moderate sedation as established.

Supplemental oxygen is required by the ASGE guideline when deep sedation is targeted and should be administered if hypoxemia is anticipated or develops. The sources do not establish one optimal oxygen-delivery device for EGD.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan for partial obstruction from the endoscope and sedation-related loss of upper-airway tone, compounded by limited access in common positions. The airway plan should be chosen for the patient and intended sedation depth rather than assumed to be a natural airway in every case.

Maintain the ability to rescue deeper-than-intended sedation. The ASGE guideline identifies chin lift, jaw thrust and oral or nasal airway insertion as potential rescue interventions; it does not establish one maneuver as universally most effective for EGD.

During moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation continuously by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure or equipment precludes or invalidates it. Pulse oximetry alone does not substitute for ventilation assessment.

Consider general anesthesia, with or without endotracheal intubation, when aspiration risk is especially high or the examination is likely to be prolonged or technically challenging. This is a consideration, not a universal EGD airway technique.

bullets: The initial insertion can provoke gagging, coughing or laryngospasm, while required sedation depth can change as stimulation changes. Titrate sedation cautiously to the lowest effective dose, particularly in elderly or comorbid patients.

Apnea or hypoventilation can lead to rapid desaturation, especially in patients with limited oxygen-loading capacity or increased oxygen demand. Vigilance and timely recognition are priorities; the supplied sources do not prescribe a procedure-specific intervention algorithm.

Cardiopulmonary events include hypoxia, hypotension, vasovagal episodes and dysrhythmias. A vagal response is possible during instrumentation, but the sources do not establish a specific EGD treatment regimen.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: The principal sedation-related hazards are oversedation with respiratory depression or hypoxia, airway compromise, laryngospasm, aspiration and hemodynamic events. Maintain readiness to recognize deterioration and escalate airway or resuscitation support.

Dental trauma can occur, particularly with poor dentition or loose teeth. Temporomandibular-joint dislocation is rare; new jaw pain or inability to close the mouth after the procedure warrants assessment.

Perforation is uncommon but potentially serious. Disproportionate or persistent chest or abdominal pain, distension, dysphagia, shortness of breath, voice change or systemic deterioration after EGD should prompt urgent evaluation and appropriate multidisciplinary escalation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ERCP combines upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and x-rays to diagnose and treat disease involving the bile ducts, pancreatic ducts, ampulla, and related structures. The anesthetic approach ranges from monitored sedation with spontaneous breathing to general anesthesia with an airway device; no single approach is established as superior.

Priorities are maintaining immobility and adequate oxygenation and ventilation while accommodating procedural complexity and position. ERCP may be performed prone or semi-prone, which can limit airway access and affect cardiopulmonary physiology.

Respiratory depression, airway obstruction, hypoxemia, and aspiration are important sedation-related hazards. Select airway support and monitoring according to patient risk, anticipated procedure, and position rather than treating intubation as mandatory for every ERCP.

Recovery requires observation for sedation- and instrumentation-related adverse effects, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness. The supplied sources do not establish an ERCP-specific postoperative monitoring protocol or discharge criteria.

bullets: ERCP combines upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and x-ray imaging for diagnosis and treatment of pancreatobiliary and related disease. Therapeutic procedures vary substantially in complexity and duration.

Respiratory-risk modifiers identified in the ERCP review include higher ASA class, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, advanced age, Mallampati III–IV, and heavy alcohol use. Consider these with the procedure plan rather than applying a fixed airway rule.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate the position, endoscope access, airway approach, and team before starting. ERCP is often semi-prone; moving an intubated patient from supine to prone requires coordinated staff and equipment.

For general anesthesia, apply basic anesthetic monitoring: continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes. For a secured airway, monitor exhaled carbon dioxide continually.

During moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation continuously by clinical observation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment makes it invalid or impractical. sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose among spontaneous ventilation, a supraglottic airway, and tracheal intubation using patient-specific aspiration and respiratory risks, procedural complexity, position, and access. Available evidence does not establish one approach as universally superior.

Consider a secured airway for high aspiration or major bleeding risk, concurrent gastric outlet obstruction, transluminal access or drainage, and prolonged or highly complex procedures. A cuffed endotracheal tube provides stable ventilation access and protection from aspirated gastric contents or blood.

A supraglottic airway may facilitate ventilation without tracheal intubation, but seal, displacement, and aspiration remain considerations. In prone positioning, LMA manipulation requires care and it does not protect against aspiration of gastric fluid.

For spontaneously breathing patients, supplemental oxygen and respiratory support should be matched to risk. High-flow nasal oxygen can reduce hypoxia in some studies, but effectiveness in obese and other high-risk patients and effects on hypercarbia remain uncertain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Transvaginal cerclage is the usual approach. When appropriate, regional anesthesia is commonly favored over general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; either technique may be used when carefully selected.

Priorities include confirming the indication and excluding labor, ruptured membranes, and infection; pregnancy-related aspiration risk and aortocaval compression should inform anesthetic and positioning decisions.

Lithotomy, with Trendelenburg when needed to reduce bulging membranes, is described for transvaginal placement. Fetal heart rate is assessed before and after; continuous intraoperative fetal monitoring is generally not performed.

Recovery priorities are obstetric reassessment and observation for contractions, bleeding, membrane rupture, infection, and neuraxial-block resolution; pain is often limited and acetaminophen is commonly used.

bullets: Uterine perforation is identified as the most common immediate complication in pregnant or nonpregnant patients; the source lists postpartum hemorrhage, postmenopausal status, nulliparity, and retroverted uterus as risk factors.
Suspected bowel injury, significant hemorrhage, or suspected lateral uterine-wall perforation may require direct visualization or laparoscopy, according to the procedural review.

Cervical lacerations are associated with excessive traction or manipulation. The source describes pressure, topical agents, and occasionally suture ligation; persistent endocervical injury may require further evaluation and escalation of care.

Pregnancy-related hemorrhage may reflect retained products, uterine atony, abnormal placentation, or cervical or uterine injury; management should address the underlying cause. Hemorrhage is described as extremely rare in nonpregnant patients.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Endometrial ablation destroys functional endometrium to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding. Second-generation devices use different energy sources and generally do not require hysteroscopic surgical skills; the approach depends on the device and uterine cavity.

Many second-generation procedures are performed as outpatient procedures under local anesthesia, sometimes with minimal conscious sedation. General anesthesia is an alternative setting, not an approach established as necessary for every ablation.
Priorities include confirming suitability, reviewing uterine anatomy and endometrial assessment, and counseling about alternatives, outcomes, contraception, and the intended anesthetic setting.

Recognize pain, vasovagal symptoms during cervical instrumentation, uterine perforation, and hemorrhage as relevant concerns. Recovery planning should account for pain, nausea/vomiting, and the patient's readiness for discharge.

bullets: The objective is to reduce menstrual blood loss by destroying functional endometrium; ablation may reduce bleeding without eliminating it.
First-generation techniques require hysteroscopic visualization and operator expertise. Second-generation devices use varied energy sources; selection and conduct are device-specific.

bullets: Use a multimodal, opioid-sparing strategy. Regular acetaminophen plus an NSAID is recommended unless contraindicated; the guideline also describes gabapentin as an option but does not establish its optimal dose or timing.

For major oncologic surgery specifically, thoracic epidural analgesia is only a weak, low-evidence consideration; hypotension and supplemental IV opioid requirements may occur. IV PCA is an alternative described by the guideline.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Hysteroscopy directly visualizes the uterine cavity for diagnosis and, in selected cases, treatment. Office diagnostic hysteroscopy commonly uses vaginoscopy, without a speculum or tenaculum; sedation is not routine.

The principal physiologic hazard is absorption of distension fluid, which can cause fluid overload and electrolyte or plasma disturbances, including hyponatremia with hypotonic solutions. Monitor fluid status and communicate concerns with the procedural team.

Procedure-related priorities include minimizing pain and excessive distension, recognizing vasovagal events, and identifying possible uterine perforation or gas embolism. The anesthetic approach depends on whether the procedure is diagnostic or operative and its setting.
Available sources do not establish a routine airway device, general-anesthetic regimen, or emergence protocol for hysteroscopy. Do not infer these from the procedure name alone.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Hysteroscopy provides direct visualization of the vagina, cervix, and uterine cavity. Office procedures are used mainly for abnormal uterine bleeding and may also diagnose or treat selected intrauterine lesions.

Office procedures may include sampling, adhesiolysis, and removal of polyps, small leiomyomas, retained products, or intrauterine devices. The planned intervention affects procedural extent; sources do not define a universal anesthetic technique for each.

Vaginoscopy is the recommended standard outpatient diagnostic technique: the scope passes through the vagina and cervix without a speculum or tenaculum. It may reduce procedural pain with similar efficacy to conventional hysteroscopy.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify diagnostic versus operative intent, anticipated procedural extent, expected discomfort, and patient preferences. Counsel on goals and anticipated discomfort; the office guideline recommends verbal reassurance during the procedure.

Relevant history includes medical conditions, chronic pain, prior cervical procedures, and sexual-abuse history. Consider pain tolerance and cervical stenosis when assessing whether an office procedure under local anesthesia is appropriate.

The office guideline advises ruling out pregnancy or timing the procedure immediately after menstruation, and postponing hysteroscopy during active pelvic or genital infection until treatment. These are procedure-selection considerations, not an anesthesia regimen.

For patients with cardiac or pulmonary comorbidities that compromise hemodynamic stability, the office guideline advises considering earlier termination at specified fluid deficits; these are qualified recommendations, not universal thresholds.

bullets: Use the minimum distension pressure needed for adequate visualization; excessive distension may cause pain. Smaller-diameter scopes generally cause less discomfort and require less cervical dilation.

Avoid routine cervical dilation in outpatient procedures when feasible: it is unnecessary for most and is associated with pain, vasovagal reactions, and uterine trauma. Avoid overdilation because it can increase distension-fluid leakage.

bullets: Fluid absorption can cause overload, hyponatremia, and cerebral edema; possible manifestations include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, shortness of breath, or headache. Hypotonic electrolyte-free solutions are particularly associated with hyponatremia and cerebral edema.

Uterine perforation is a recognized diagnostic and operative complication, with greater risk when resection extends into the myometrium. The supplied sources do not establish a universal anesthesia response pathway.

Gas embolism is chiefly associated with surgical hysteroscopy. If suspected, the source advises stopping the procedure, removing the causative gas or solvent to reduce cavity expansion, and notifying the anesthesia team immediately.

bullets: Total laparoscopic hysterectomy removes the uterus and cervix; laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy removes the upper uterus while preserving the cervix. For laparoscopic hysterectomy, the usual described anesthetic is general anesthesia with neuromuscular relaxation, tracheal intubation, and controlled ventilation.

Pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg can impair respiratory mechanics and increase airway pressures; CO₂ absorption can cause hypercarbia. Priorities include adapting ventilation and monitoring to changing conditions.

bullets: TLH removes the uterus and cervix; LSH preserves the cervix. Hysterectomy indications include bleeding or pain not managed with other treatments, fibroids, prolapse, endometriosis, adenomyosis, and uterine or cervical malignancy or premalignant abnormalities.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Vaginal pelvic organ prolapse repair may be performed with anterior/posterior repair, with or without vaginal hysterectomy. Both spinal and general anesthesia have been used; the available comparative evidence does not establish a preferred technique.

Spinal anesthesia is one documented option; in a gynecologic enhanced-recovery pathway, sedation or light general anesthesia was left to the anesthesiologist. Select the technique to the patient, procedure, and team rather than treating either as routine.

Postoperative bladder management deserves explicit planning: catheter reinsertion occurred in both anesthesia groups in a comparative cohort, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant. This does not support describing retention as universal.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Postpartum tubal ligation is commonly performed through an infraumbilical mini-laparotomy; the enlarged postpartum uterus can bring the tubes within reach of the incision.

When feasible, consider neuraxial anesthesia, including a functional labor epidural; individualize technique and timing to the patient’s condition and preferences. The evidence does not establish a universally superior technique.

Key perioperative concerns include aspiration risk, postpartum hemodynamic status and blood loss, and the possibility that labor epidural anesthesia may be inadequate or fail as time from delivery increases.

After anesthesia, admit the patient to the PACU or an equivalent area unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Re-evaluate the patient on arrival and continually in recovery; monitor according to the patient’s medical condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature. Use a quantitative method of assessing oxygenation, such as pulse oximetry, during the initial phase of recovery.

bullets: Insufflation and steep Trendelenburg can compound respiratory and cardiovascular effects: reduced lung volumes and compliance, increased airway pressure, hypercarbia, and altered venous return. Facial, conjunctival, tongue, or laryngopharyngeal edema may signal airway risk. If concern is present, assess the airway before extubation and consider delayed extubation or other airway-protection measures based on the clinical findings.

bullets: Sacrocolpopexy suspends the vaginal apex to the sacral promontory using mesh; the supplied sources describe open abdominal and laparoscopic approaches, and discuss robotic assistance.

For minimally invasive pelvic surgery, anticipate positioning and pneumoperitoneum-related respiratory and cardiovascular effects; protect pressure points and secure the patient before robotic docking.

bullets: The operation supports the vaginal vault by securing mesh to the vagina and the anterior longitudinal ligament at the sacral promontory. Open abdominal repair is described through a Pfannenstiel or low midline incision; laparoscopic repair uses a minimally invasive abdominal approach.

Robotic assistance is described as an option for intracorporeal suturing. The available robotic series report variable operative times and complications; they do not establish a preferred approach or a routine anesthesia protocol.

Surgical exposure may involve dissection of the promontory and adjacent vaginal spaces. The source describes identifying the ureter and major vessels before promontory dissection and avoiding excessive lateral or leftward dissection.

bullets: Assess comorbidities and the planned approach, including ability to tolerate general anesthesia, pneumoperitoneum, and the required position. The procedure cohort reports approach selection influenced by BMI and comorbidities, but does not define a general selection rule.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, the procedural source describes general anesthesia in modified lithotomy, with vaginal and rectal access. Pelvic MIS may use Trendelenburg; the precise position and degree should follow the operative approach and patient tolerance.

Plan padding and securement before docking; protect the face from robot arms and avoid moving the table while the robot is docked. Position-related nerve injury, pressure injury, and edema are described concerns.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. The ASA standard calls for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.
A urinary catheter is part of the described laparoscopic setup; the source notes that it can also permit bladder filling to help identify bladder margins or lesions.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy procedural review specifies general anesthesia but does not state an airway device or ventilation plan. A general laparoscopic/robotic reference prefers an endotracheal tube to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; apply this as approach-level context, not a sacrocolpopexy-specific protocol.

Pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg can reduce pulmonary compliance and functional residual capacity, increase airway pressures, and promote atelectasis. The generic MIS source describes lung-protective ventilation as commonly used, with settings titrated to mechanics rather than a case-specific target.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not imply paralysis is required for every approach.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During insufflation, anticipate changes in preload, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac filling pressures, and rhythm; Trendelenburg can further alter venous return and filling pressures. Reassess when position or insufflation changes.

CO₂ absorption and restricted respiratory mechanics may produce hypercarbia and increased airway pressures. The general MIS reference describes increasing minute ventilation to compensate for CO₂ absorption and notes permissive hypercapnia may be acceptable to avoid barotrauma; no sacrocolpopexy-specific targets are established.

Promontory dissection is a critical phase for presacral or median sacral vessel bleeding and potential injury to nearby major vessels or ureter. Maintain communication with the surgeon if bleeding or unexpected anatomy compromises exposure.

Position and insufflation can also affect renal perfusion and urine output; the generic MIS review describes reduced renal perfusion with parenchymal compression. Interpret urine output in the operative context rather than as a stand-alone measure of intravascular volume.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Presacral hemorrhage is a high-consequence hazard. A retrospective cohort reports two presacral-vein hemorrhages, controlled surgically with a Z-suture and warm-sponge pressure; this describes study events, not a universal response protocol.

Potential operative injuries include bowel or rectum, bladder, ureter, and vessels. If injury or major bleeding is suspected, coordinate promptly with the surgeon and support assessment and management according to the evolving clinical situation; the supplied procedure sources do not provide an anesthesia-specific rescue algorithm.

During robotic surgery, limited access after docking makes advance communication about undocking and access to the patient important. The generic robotic reference identifies accidental extubation and face pressure injury from robot arms as hazards.

After steep Trendelenburg, assess for airway or facial edema, visual symptoms, and position-related nerve injury. The source describes these as potential complications, not as an indication for a particular routine extubation test.

bullets: The general MIS reference describes balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, cautioning that excess fluid may worsen facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema in Trendelenburg. It provides no procedure-specific volume or transfusion protocol.

In a prospective series of 132 laparoscopic sacrocolpopexies beyond the learning curve, reported blood loss was 185 mL (SD 124). bullets: Salpingectomy removes the affected fallopian tube. The strongest procedure-specific evidence here concerns urgent surgery for acute ruptured ectopic pregnancy, principally laparotomy; it does not establish a routine approach for other salpingectomy indications.

Laparoscopy is described in a single ruptured-pregnancy report, with conversion to laparotomy when bleeding impaired visualization. This illustrates a possible need for conversion, not a standard approach or conversion threshold.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Rapidly establish clinical stability and whether rupture or ongoing hemorrhage is suspected; an initially reassuring appearance may not exclude substantial blood loss. Do not let further optimization displace necessary definitive surgery.

Assess airway and aspiration risk, hemodynamic status, hemoglobin, and available blood products; obtain large-bore IV access. The source gives practical access advice, but the necessary resources depend on presentation and setting.

Treat the patient as potentially having a full stomach when aspiration risk is present. Pregnancy, pain, or vomiting may inform assessment, but the supplied evidence does not establish a universal airway technique for every salpingectomy.
Coordinate with the surgical team and assemble senior assistance when instability or hemorrhage is possible; use local emergency and blood-management pathways.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Hemorrhagic shock is the principal time-critical threat. Recognize poor response to initial resuscitation or worsening instability and escalate urgently with the surgical team rather than relying on anesthetic support alone.
Significant blood loss may lead to coagulopathy and progression to complex shock. Reassess the clinical course and laboratory results as available, and involve local hemorrhage resources when needed.

Aspiration risk and failed intubation require preparation for oxygenation and ventilation alternatives. The source prioritizes adequate ventilation and oxygenation rather than intubation at all costs.

Consider antifibrinolytic therapy and blood-conservation options within the applicable local protocol and clinical context. The source discusses TXA during massive hemorrhage and low-technology autotransfusion where appropriate; these are not universal instructions.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH) is an open abdominal operation. General anesthesia is represented in procedure-specific evidence, while neuraxial and regional techniques are options rather than universal requirements.
Priorities include preoperative anemia and VTE risk assessment, maintaining euvolemia and normothermia, and limiting opioid-related effects through multimodal care.
Recovery planning should address pain and PONV, early mobilization, urinary-catheter removal when appropriate, and thromboprophylaxis tailored to the patient and operation.

bullets: TAH is an open approach to hysterectomy. The supplied guidance discusses abdominal hysterectomy alongside vaginal and minimally invasive procedures; approach selection is not prescribed for an individual patient.

bullets: Use judicious opioids when appropriate and emphasize stepwise, multimodal, nonopioid strategies. For women undergoing TAH, preemptive acetaminophen, gabapentin, NSAIDs, and COX-2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce total narcotic requirements and improve pain and satisfaction.

For open gynecologic surgery, postoperative spinal or thoracic epidural analgesia may be considered. Neuraxial techniques are not feasible or appropriate for every procedure and can limit mobilization.

TAP blocks are an option, but findings are mixed. A small randomized TAH trial found lower 24-hour morphine use in its TAP group than in its epidural and parenteral groups; its protocol and population do not establish a universal preferred technique.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Vaginal hysterectomy removes the uterus through the vaginal canal without abdominal incisions; it is often preferred for benign disease when feasible, especially uterine prolapse and favorable pelvic anatomy.

Do not assume a single anesthetic technique: general anesthesia is common for hysterectomy, while spinal or epidural anesthesia may be appropriate for selected vaginal procedures; the available sources give no selection criteria or regimen.

Prioritize hemodynamic and blood-loss surveillance, and maintain awareness of bladder and ureter injury risk. The supplied sources do not establish vaginal-hysterectomy-specific anesthetic targets or a standard intraoperative fluid or transfusion protocol.

Plan recovery around multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia, early oral intake and mobilization when appropriate, and timely urinary-catheter removal; monitor for pain, urinary dysfunction, bleeding, and other complications.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The vaginal route provides access through the vaginal canal and avoids abdominal incisions. For benign conditions, it is often preferred when anatomy and other factors make it feasible, particularly with uterine prolapse.

Route selection is individualized. Consider the indication, uterine size and mobility, pelvic anatomy, prior surgery, comorbidities, surgeon expertise, available resources, and patient preference; a large uterus or adhesions may affect feasibility or prompt consideration of another approach.

Vaginal access does not generally require abdominal laparoscopic or robotic equipment unless a combined procedure is planned. The sources do not provide a procedure-specific operative sequence for anesthesia planning.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the indication, uterine size and mobility, pelvic anatomy, prior pelvic or abdominal surgery, comorbidities, and patient preferences as they bear on route and anesthetic planning.

Evaluate medical fitness and optimize relevant conditions. Significant cardiopulmonary disease warrants particular consideration; obesity, prior surgery and adhesions, and large uterine size are relative considerations, not automatic exclusions.

Review relevant imaging and pathology, assess cardiopulmonary status when indicated, and coordinate anticoagulant management with the appropriate specialists. The supplied sources do not provide a vaginal-hysterectomy-specific risk score or anticoagulant interruption schedule.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For any anesthetic, qualified anesthesia personnel should remain present and continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Apply monitoring appropriate to the selected technique and patient.

ASA basic standards include continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes during anesthesia. For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is common across hysterectomy procedures, but spinal or epidural anesthesia may be appropriate for specific vaginal procedures. The sources do not establish a preferred technique for vaginal hysterectomy or provide selection criteria.

Choose airway management and ventilation according to the anesthetic technique and individual clinical circumstances. The supplied procedure-specific review does not give an airway protocol for vaginal hysterectomy.

If general anesthesia is used, continually evaluate ventilation; ASA standards call for expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. Confirm airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide when an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain awareness of blood loss and hemodynamic status during dissection and control of uterine and other pelvic vessels. The source identifies potential bleeding sites but does not supply a vaginal-hysterectomy-specific sequence or blood-loss target.

Bladder and ureter injury are relevant surgical hazards. The source highlights the ureter’s proximity to uterine arteries and cardinal ligaments; it does not specify an anesthetic intervention to prevent injury.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Significant blood loss may require transfusion, conversion from minimally invasive to open surgery, or further intervention. No transfusion thresholds or blood-product protocols are provided.

Bladder or ureter injury may be recognized intraoperatively or present later. The source describes delayed ureteral injury symptoms including flank pain, fever, urinary leakage, hydronephrosis, or impaired renal function; these warrant clinical evaluation.

Postoperative surveillance should include hemorrhage, infection, urinary retention or dysfunction, ileus, venous thromboembolism, and vaginal cuff complications. Escalate new or worsening clinical concerns; the supplied sources do not provide a VH-specific rescue algorithm.

bullets: Assess fluid administration against perfusion, blood loss, comorbidities, and the anticipated postoperative course. The supplied evidence does not establish a fixed intraoperative fluid total for vaginal hysterectomy.

ERAS guidance favors balanced crystalloid over normal saline when IV fluids are required and recommends oral fluids and food on the day of surgery whenever possible. In uncomplicated recovery, postoperative IV fluids beyond 12–24 hours are rarely needed once oral intake and analgesia are tolerated.

Blood availability and transfusion decisions should reflect the clinical context and anticipated risk. The sources do not define a vaginal-hysterectomy-specific blood-ordering practice or transfusion threshold.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal, opioid-sparing postoperative analgesia. ERAS recommends regular acetaminophen and an NSAID together unless contraindicated; opioids should be oral when the patient can tolerate diet, with IV PCA an option when diet cannot be tolerated.

For vaginal hysterectomy specifically, paracervical nerve block or intrathecal morphine may reduce pain and opioid consumption, with a reported small benefit; local anesthetic infiltration may reduce early postoperative pain and opioid use. These are weak recommendations based on low-level evidence, not mandatory techniques.

Anticipate pain as neuraxial analgesia regresses if that technique is used, and assess PONV and opioid-related adverse effects during recovery. The available sources do not support a single drug regimen or dose for this procedure.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Use postanesthesia care appropriate to the anesthetic received. During initial recovery, use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry; continue evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This applies when blockade is used, not to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

Monitor for pain, hemorrhage, and urinary retention. ERAS recommends short-duration postoperative bladder drainage, preferably less than 24 hours; the guideline notes limited gynecologic-surgery evidence.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For a felon with abscess, tension, or fluctuance, the source-supported procedure is incision and drainage; cellulitis without abscess is managed differently.
A digital block before I&D is the only anesthetic technique specifically described for felon drainage; a finger tourniquet may aid visualization.
Prioritize complete drainage while protecting digital neurovascular structures, flexor tendon sheath, and nail matrix; edema and pus can compromise perfusion.
Aftercare described for felon includes wound packing and splinting, followed by reassessment; the available procedure source does not establish an airway or general-anesthetic plan.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For felon with abscess formation, tension, or fluctuance, drain the infected material. Cellulitis without abscess is not described as an I&D indication in this source.

The described approach targets maximal volar swelling and tenderness. Deep felon drainage uses a lateral incision with specified separation from the DIP joint and nail plate; superficial felon may use a volar longitudinal incision.

Bluntly separate fingertip septae as needed for complete drainage, irrigate, and pack and splint the wound. The source discourages fish-mouth, hockey-stick, and transverse palmar incisions because of reported injury and scarring.
This approach is supported for felon only; it should not be treated as a procedure description for flexor tendon sheath infection or palmar-space abscess.

bullets: For general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or monitored anesthesia care, ASA basic standards call for ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with the specified monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and circumstances.
The ASA standards specify ECG display and blood-pressure and heart-rate assessment during anesthesia care. They do not supply a tendon-repair-specific monitoring protocol.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The supplied sources do not establish a tendon-repair-specific airway technique or ventilation plan. Do not infer a need for an airway device from the operation alone.
The survey reports use preferences across regional, general, and WALANT techniques, but does not report airway assessment or airway management. Technique selection remains patient- and team-specific.
When moderate or deep sedation is provided, ASA standards call for continual clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the stated exceptions apply.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: If WALANT is chosen, active movement provides the surgeon an opportunity to assess tendon excursion and repair integrity during the operation. It is not a substitute for the anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the care provided.

The review describes reinforcing observed gapping and adjusting pulley release or reconstruction when gliding is impaired. These are surgical decisions informed by movement testing, not anesthesia instructions.
No tendon-repair-specific physiologic targets or anesthetic critical-phase protocol are established in the supplied evidence.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Repair gapping and rupture are relevant surgical concerns. The flexor-tendon review links intraoperative movement testing and reinforcement of observed gapping with rupture-risk reduction; it does not provide an anesthesia rescue algorithm.

Adhesions are a significant postoperative concern in the review, particularly with accompanying bone or severe soft-tissue injuries. The surgeon and therapy team address these risks through operative and rehabilitation decisions.

With local anesthetic exposure, recognize possible LAST; the supplied review lists early neurologic symptoms and severe neurologic or respiratory effects. It does not establish a tendon-case-specific monitoring or treatment protocol.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The tendon-repair sources do not provide a fluid-management plan or blood-loss guidance; neither a routine fluid total nor a procedure-specific target is established here.

The flexor-tendon review describes avoiding cautery near tendons and using local measures to manage minor bleeding in its WALANT approach. This is a reported surgical technique, not a general hemostasis standard.

A hand-anesthesia review describes epinephrine-related vasoconstriction as potentially limiting blood loss and advises caution with compromised circulation; it does not specifically validate a tendon-repair regimen.

bullets: The survey likewise reports no postoperative analgesic regimen. The supplied evidence does not establish a tendon-repair-specific PONV approach.

Catheter-based peripheral nerve blocks are discussed in a general hand-anesthesia review as a way to prolong postoperative anesthesia, but the source does not make them a tendon-repair recommendation.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care, ASA postanesthesia standards call for appropriate recovery-area care, handoff, and continuing assessment; the specific destination and discharge decision depend on the applicable care arrangements.

Flexor-tendon postoperative care described in the review emphasizes splint protection and staged, therapist-supervised movement. The reported protocol is not established as a universal adult rehabilitation schedule.
The supplied sources do not establish a tendon-repair-specific emergence or PACU checklist; evaluate recovery and discharge according to the anesthetic delivered and applicable standards.

bullets: The principal surgical source is a clinical review informed by literature and author experience, not an anesthesia guideline or trial; it does not state that its population is exclusively adult.

The anesthesia-preference evidence is a survey of surgeons’ reported practice, with a directly acknowledged conflict between its Results section and table; it cannot resolve comparative effectiveness or individual selection.

The general hand-anesthesia review covers bedside procedures and blocks but does not prescribe a particular anesthetic technique for each operation. Case-specific adult anesthesia selection and regimen therefore remain unresolved by these sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Hepatic resection removes part of the liver for benign or malignant lesions; it may be performed open or by a minimally invasive approach.
General anaesthesia with tracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is usual. Tailor invasive access and monitoring to patient risk, resection extent, approach, and duration.

The major intraoperative hazards are sudden, substantial bleeding—particularly hepatic-vein backflow during transection—and hemodynamic instability during vascular occlusion or release. Balance venous-pressure reduction against perfusion and air-embolism risk.
After resection, watch for bleeding, bile leak, metabolic disturbance, and post-hepatectomy liver failure (PHLF); extent of resection and clinical condition guide the level of postoperative care.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Resection is used for benign lesions and primary or secondary malignancy; colorectal liver metastases are identified as the main indication in the review.

Laparoscopic and robotic approaches share the indications of open surgery. Approach selection should account for the possibility of conversion and the need for prompt vascular control if bleeding occurs.
The review reports less blood loss, pain, wound infection, and length of stay with minimally invasive resection than open surgery, while noting that complication types and incidence are similar.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess underlying liver disease, functional reserve, comorbidities, frailty, anaemia, and nutrition. Cirrhosis and chemotherapy-associated liver injury increase PHLF risk; no single test reliably predicts postoperative liver dysfunction.

CT or MRI can estimate future liver remnant (FLR) volume; interpret it alongside liver function and post-hepatectomy liver failure risk. The review cites minimum FLR volumes of 20% with normal liver function, 30–40% with severe steatohepatitis or prior hepatotoxic chemotherapy, and at least 50% with cirrhosis.

CTP class, MELD, and ICG retention may inform multidisciplinary selection, but none should be treated as a stand-alone clearance rule. PVE and other augmentation strategies may be considered when FLR is inadequate.
Optimize relevant comorbidities and consider chemotherapy-related hepatic and cardiac effects; the review states surgery should be delayed until 4–6 weeks after neoadjuvant treatment.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Ensure large-bore IV access and ready access to blood products because hemorrhage may be sudden and catastrophic. Decide on arterial and central access according to patient, procedure, and monitoring needs rather than treating either line as universal.

Use standard anaesthetic monitoring and add invasive haemodynamic monitoring when justified. Avoid hypothermia; temperature and coagulation effects matter in a procedure with substantial bleeding potential.
Trendelenburg is one reported means of lowering CVP, not a mandatory position. During minimally invasive surgery, pneumoperitoneum can make CVP readings unreliable.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anaesthesia with a tracheal tube and controlled ventilation is the usual technique described for hepatic resection.

For laparoscopic or robotic cases, assess tolerance of prolonged CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, particularly with cardiac or respiratory dysfunction. Standard laparoscopy sources describe altered respiratory mechanics and increased ventilatory requirements during insufflation.
Use appropriate capnography and verify tracheal-tube position. The supplied sources do not establish a liver-resection-specific ventilator prescription.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During parenchymal transection, hepatic-vein backflow is a major bleeding source. Venous-pressure reduction is used to limit bleeding, but must be balanced against systemic perfusion and organ blood flow.

Pringle manoeuvre interrupts hepatic arterial and portal inflow and can alter venous return and systemic vascular resistance. Communicate with the surgeon at clamp and release, anticipating hemodynamic change.

Occlusion strategy and duration depend on liver condition and surgical circumstances. The review describes intermittent clamping with reperfusion intervals; prolonged continuous inflow interruption risks ischaemia–reperfusion injury.
Total vascular exclusion can produce profound volume shifts and is reserved in the review for selected situations, including persistent major hepatic-vein bleeding or required IVC resection.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Be prepared for abrupt major haemorrhage, including from hepatic-vein injury. In minimally invasive surgery, rapid vascular control may be difficult; escalate promptly with the surgical team when bleeding is suspected.

Consider venous air embolism when sudden haemodynamic or end-tidal CO₂ changes occur, particularly during low-CVP transection or reperfusion. Source-described signs include a fall in end-tidal CO₂, oxygenation changes, and arrhythmias; use local emergency escalation and surgical coordination.
Monitor for PHLF, bile leak, postoperative haemorrhage, renal dysfunction, and metabolic disturbance. The review describes PHLF by rising INR and bilirubin on or after postoperative day 5.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: ERAS guidance summarized in the review recommends balanced crystalloids, low CVP during resection, and euvolaemia after resection. Avoid carrying restrictive intraoperative fluid practice into recovery once hemostasis is achieved.

Low-CVP practice is debated: evidence summarized in the source suggests reduced blood loss and transfusion but not improved clinical outcomes, and another analysis found CVP monitoring did not affect blood loss. Individualize the strategy and preserve end-organ perfusion.
Do not treat CVP as a stand-alone volume measure during pneumoperitoneum. After transection, assess and restore circulating volume according to bleeding, hemodynamics, and perfusion needs.
Use blood-conservation and transfusion decisions in the context of actual blood loss, physiology, and coagulation assessment; the supplied sources do not establish a universal transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia tailored to open versus minimally invasive surgery. The ERAS review does not recommend routine thoracic epidural analgesia for open liver resection; it identifies intrathecal opioids and peri-incisional catheters as alternatives.
Paracetamol and NSAIDs may be components when appropriate to liver function, renal function, and other contraindications; the source urges caution with extensive resection and liver disease.
Use multimodal PONV prevention; the ERAS guidance summarized recommends two antiemetics.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Postoperative destination should reflect resection extent, approach, and patient condition. More extensive or open resections generally need closer monitoring than smaller minimally invasive resections.

Do not apply a fixed extubation rule based only on resection category: the source material provides no standardized liver-resection emergence or extubation criteria. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative TOF recovery before extubation.

Recovery care should include surveillance for bleeding, bile leak, glucose disturbance, and evolving PHLF; early oral intake and mobilization are included in the ERAS recommendations summarized by the review.
Postanaesthesia monitoring must address oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with an appropriate PACU or equivalent care location.

bullets: The principal procedure-specific source is an educational perioperative review, not a trial. Its summary of ERAS recommendations and low-CVP evidence should be interpreted with the stated debate and limits on demonstrated clinical outcomes.
The vascular-control source is an older narrative review and does not establish an optimal anaesthetic technique; some reported evidence comes from small studies or nonclinical populations.

Case-specific targets and standardized rescue or extubation protocols are not established across the supplied evidence; decisions remain individualized to procedure, patient physiology, and local practice.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Liver transplantation is a major operation conducted under general anesthesia. The anesthetic course is organized around dissection, anhepatic, and graft-reperfusion phases, each with changing hemodynamic and coagulation demands.

Priorities include anticipating dissection-related bleeding, managing preload changes during caval clamping when used, and preparing for abrupt cardiovascular instability at reperfusion, including arrhythmia and right-heart stress.

An arterial line and central access are usual components of monitoring and access; additional cardiac monitoring and bypass resources depend on the patient's physiology, operative approach, and local practice.

Most recipients proceed to ICU care for ongoing hemodynamic and hematologic monitoring. Extubation is individualized; when neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative recovery should be confirmed before extubation.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Liver transplantation is a treatment for end-stage liver disease and also addresses selected cases of acute liver failure and hepatic malignancy. Selection and allocation depend on clinical criteria; the supplied review describes MELD-based allocation and Milan criteria for primary liver tumours.

The operative phases are hepatectomy (dissection), anhepatic, and reperfusion (neohepatic). In classic transplantation, caval clamping affects preload and venovenous bypass may be used; the piggyback approach may have less hemodynamic fluctuation.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess disease severity and allocation context, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal function, encephalopathy, ascites, and the patient's coagulation profile. MELD incorporates creatinine, bilirubin, INR, and sodium; acute liver failure prioritization is described separately from MELD.

Cirrhosis may produce low SVR with compensatory high cardiac output, while pulmonary hypertension, cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, hepatopulmonary syndrome, and hepatorenal syndrome can materially alter anesthetic risk and monitoring needs.

Coagulation abnormalities may include hypocoagulability, hypercoagulability, or DIC; do not infer bleeding risk from a single conventional test in isolation. Review notes that severe anemia is also usual in the described cirrhotic population.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan reliable large-bore access, central access, rapid fluid-delivery capability, warming equipment, infusion pumps, and immediate defibrillation capability according to anticipated needs. The supplied review identifies an arterial line and central line for every recipient.

Choose cardiac monitoring with the patient's risks and local expertise in mind. One source describes TEE as standard of care, while another says it is not routine; PA catheter monitoring is specifically indicated in the supplied material for portopulmonary hypertension.

Use frequent blood sampling and point-of-care testing for acid-base status, electrolytes, hemoglobin, and coagulation, including viscoelastic testing where available. Positioning details are not provided in the transplant sources.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is the described technique. RSI is usually preferred in the review because delayed gastric emptying and related aspiration risks are common considerations; selection and conduct should account for hemodynamics and the individual presentation rather than presume a universal indication.

Titrate induction agents carefully to avoid further reduction in SVR. The review identifies intravenous propofol and etomidate as preferred short-acting induction agents and notes agent-specific hemodynamic and pharmacokinetic considerations.

Maintain standard anesthetic monitoring, including continual ventilation assessment and quantitative expired CO₂ monitoring for general anesthesia, subject to the stated standard's exceptions. The transplant sources do not establish a case-specific ventilation prescription.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During dissection, hemorrhage and instability can follow manipulation of the diseased liver, caval compression, or vascular torque. Optimize circulating volume and support perfusion while preparing for the hemodynamic changes of the next phase.

During the anhepatic phase, caval clamping in classic transplantation can reduce preload and cardiac output; acidosis and coagulopathy may worsen. Follow potassium and ionized calcium and coordinate phase-specific volume and hemodynamic management with the surgical team.

Reperfusion may abruptly reduce SVR and contractility while increasing pulmonary pressures; returning cold, acidotic, hyperkalemic blood and preservation-solution contents can precipitate dysrhythmia or right-heart dysfunction. Confirm readiness and communicate closely with the surgical team before graft flow is restored.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: In liver transplantation, post-reperfusion syndrome is defined as a 30% decrease in MAP for at least one minute within the first five minutes after graft reperfusion; it can cause severe arrhythmias or asystole.

Consider pulmonary hypertension and right-heart dysfunction when instability occurs around reperfusion: severely cold or acidotic reperfused blood, or excess volume returning to the right heart, can raise pulmonary pressures and cause right-heart dysfunction. TEE may help evaluate cardiovascular collapse, including pulmonary hypertension, hypovolemia, myocardial depression, clot, or air embolism.

Persistent bleeding may reflect surgical sources, coagulopathy, or hyperfibrinolysis; distinguish these before targeted correction. Graft dysfunction and ongoing hemorrhage require close postoperative surveillance and may prompt further intervention.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use repeated volume and perfusion assessment; avoid assuming either liberal or restrictive fluid therapy is universally appropriate. The review reports risks from excessive fluid, including pulmonary or graft edema, and renal-failure risk with restrictive therapy; it states that no ideal fluid prescription or monitoring system is established.

Manage bleeding and coagulation with clinical assessment and viscoelastic testing where available. Sources conflict on some transfusion strategies: one describes avoiding plasma and lowering CVP in the pre-anhepatic phase, while another describes PRBC and FFP replacement; these do not support a universal ratio or empiric transfusion rule.

Anticipate citrate-associated hypocalcemia during blood-product administration and changing potassium and acid-base status across phases; monitor and respond to measured values and clinical context. Avoid excess transfusion because congestion may impair graft function.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use a multimodal analgesic approach appropriate to graft function, renal status, bleeding risk, and recovery goals. The supplied ERAS review recommends multimodal analgesia for transplantation but does not provide a transplant-specific drug regimen.

Neuraxial epidural analgesia is not recommended in the supplied transplant ERAS table because of bleeding risk. If systemic analgesia is used, account for renal and hepatic dysfunction; the sources do not establish a universal postoperative opioid or NSAID plan.
The ERAS review recommends dual antiemetic therapy, with an additional agent if required; individual contraindications and the patient's risk profile still apply.

sources.label: A review of the current ERAS guidelines for liver resection, liver transplantation and pancreatoduodenectomy
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Plan postoperative ICU care for ongoing hemodynamic and hematologic monitoring. Extubation at the conclusion of surgery may be considered in selected patients, but the sources do not establish universal criteria or a fixed timing protocol.

When a neuromuscular blocking drug has been used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Transfer and recovery should include appropriate monitoring, handoff, and reassessment in the receiving ICU or equivalent care area; recovery standards require continued attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The transplant-specific sources are an educational clinical summary and a narrative review, not formal procedure-specific anesthesia guidelines; neither provides evidence grading or a systematic review method.

Monitoring and fluid practices are not fully settled in the supplied evidence. TEE use and some fluid/transfusion approaches differ between sources; clinical claims above retain this uncertainty rather than presenting one approach as universal.

The sources do not specify positioning, a universal setup configuration, case-specific fluid targets, or a detailed extubation protocol. These details require local expertise and individual clinical judgment; their absence does not establish that a fixed target should exist.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open cholecystectomy may be planned or converted from a laparoscopic operation; the described approaches are a right subcostal (Kocher) or upper midline incision. General anesthesia is the usual technique described for the operation.

The dominant procedural hazards are uncertain or variable biliary anatomy, bile duct injury, bleeding, and liver injury during exposure. Careful identification of anatomy and inspection of the gallbladder bed are central surgical priorities.

In critically ill patients, an open approach may avoid the cardiovascular and ventilatory effects of pneumoperitoneum; the supplied sources do not establish a procedure-specific anesthetic response or target.

The larger incision is usually more painful than laparoscopic surgery and is associated with more wound complications. Recovery requires postanesthesia assessment and monitoring appropriate to the patient's condition.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open surgery may be selected in advance or used after conversion from laparoscopy. Reasons for conversion include unclear anatomy, extensive inflammation or adhesions, anatomical variation, bile duct injury, retained duct stones, uncontrolled bleeding, or need for duct exploration.

Planned open surgery is described for cirrhosis, gallbladder cancer, extensive upper abdominal adhesions, selected comorbidities, and critically ill patients. These are source-described selection contexts, not a complete set of indications or contraindications.
Exposure is through a right subcostal (Kocher) or upper midline incision, using packs and retractors. The source emphasizes avoiding liver injury from retraction.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review the indication, prior upper abdominal operations and adhesions, comorbidities, and whether the planned approach is open or may convert. The surgical workup described includes ultrasound, with CT, HIDA scanning, blood work, and history and examination as appropriate.

Assess and optimize hemodynamic status before surgery; the source specifies stabilization and resuscitation when needed. It also describes possible antibiotics and thrombosis prophylaxis as elements of standard surgical preparation, without giving an individualized anesthetic protocol.
Planned open surgery may be used for patients with cirrhosis; the source does not specify how cirrhosis-related conditions should alter anesthetic management.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use an operating room equipped for open abdominal surgery. The surgical source describes packs and retractors and recommends that cholangiography equipment be available when intraoperative cholangiography is needed.

The supplied open-cholecystectomy source does not specify patient positioning, vascular access, or a procedure-specific monitoring package. Select access and monitoring according to the patient's condition and anticipated operative course rather than assuming routine arterial or central venous lines.

For anesthesia, continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ASA basic standards include ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedure source describes general anesthesia but does not establish an airway device, induction method, or ventilation targets for open cholecystectomy. Airway and ventilation planning therefore require individual clinical judgment; no universal rapid-sequence technique is supported by these sources.

When general anesthesia is used, assess ventilation continually; verify endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, and continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide monitoring through the specified intraoperative period.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Critical surgical steps include exposure and identification of the gallbladder, Calot triangle, and bile ducts, followed by cystic duct and artery division and separation of the gallbladder from the liver bed. The source stresses obtaining a critical view before division.

Anatomical variation is a material surgical hazard: the source reports altered biliary anatomy and describes potential common bile duct misidentification and right hepatic artery injury. This supports careful communication around difficult anatomy, not an anesthesia-specific intervention.

An open approach may avoid pneumoperitoneum-related decreases in cardiac return and increases in ventilation pressures in critically ill patients. The source does not provide ventilation or hemodynamic targets for this operation.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Relevant operative complications include bleeding, liver injury, bile leak, bile duct injury, and retained duct stones. The surgeon inspects the liver bed for bleeding and bile leakage; anesthesia should maintain communication with the surgical team if these concerns arise.

The source reports more wound infection, hematoma, and hernia with open than routine laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and a higher overall complication rate in a cited study. These observations identify recovery concerns but are not individualized risk estimates.

During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, bile duct injury or uncontrolled bleeding may prompt conversion to open surgery; the source does not provide an anesthesia-specific complication-management protocol.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Patients should be hemodynamically stabilized and resuscitated if needed before surgery. The source does not specify an intraoperative fluid-management regimen.

Uncontrolled bleeding is a stated reason to convert to open surgery, and the liver bed is inspected for bleeding and bile leaks. The source does not specify an anesthesia-specific blood-product or blood-loss strategy.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Open cholecystectomy is usually more painful than laparoscopic surgery. The supplied procedure source does not specify an analgesic regimen, and the available evidence does not establish thoracic epidural analgesia as a universal standard for this operation.

A two-patient report describes thoracic paravertebral block in selected high-risk adults, but its authors identify the small case number as a limitation. It cannot establish routine analgesic or anesthetic practice. The supplied procedure source gives no PONV regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The open-cholecystectomy source does not specify an emergence or extubation approach. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation.

After anesthesia, admission to a PACU or equivalent is expected except by specific anesthesiologist order. During initial recovery, use quantitative oxygenation assessment and monitor according to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

The open operation's larger incision makes wound infection and hematoma relevant postoperative concerns; assess the surgical wound and clinical status during recovery. No procedure-specific PACU schedule or discharge criteria are supplied.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure source is an educational narrative review of open cholecystectomy, not an anesthesia protocol. It explicitly leaves airway, positioning, monitoring, anesthetic drugs, ventilation, fluid management, and emergence unspecified.

The paravertebral-block source is a two-patient case report in selected adults; it cannot define routine technique. Liver and pancreatic ERAS or anesthesia sources address different operations and are not used here to prescribe open-cholecystectomy management.

General ASA monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade sources support applicable monitoring and recovery principles; they do not supply a procedure-specific anesthetic plan. Case-specific targets and choices remain dependent on clinical assessment.

bullets: Adjacent HPB case, not strictly endocrine: major pancreatic/duodenal resection may treat adenocarcinoma or a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.
Assess nutrition, jaundice/infection, coagulation, glucose and gastric-emptying/obstruction risk before a prolonged abdominal operation.
Plan blood access, warming, physiology-guided fluids and analgesia without treating epidural-related vasodilation automatically with fluid loading.
Recovery priorities include hemorrhage, pancreatic fistula/infection, delayed gastric emptying, respiratory problems and glucose/nutritional needs.

sections.title: What is removed and reconstructed?
bullets: Pancreaticoduodenectomy removes the pancreatic head and duodenum with biliary resection; reconstruction restores pancreatic, biliary and gastric/intestinal drainage. Standard and pylorus-preserving variants differ, so confirm the actual operation rather than assuming a uniform stomach resection.
Clarify open versus minimally invasive access, vascular resection and the indication. A hormone-secreting tumor adds its syndrome-specific preparation to the major abdominal plan.

sections.title: Frailty, weight loss and nutritional reserve
bullets: Assess weight loss, intake, frailty and nutritional deficits before surgery. ERAS emphasizes intervention for severe nutritional risk; this is not simply a preoperative fasting problem.
Arrange support with the pancreatic team and dietitian, accounting for obstruction, malabsorption and diabetes. Do not prescribe routine parenteral nutrition when oral/enteral intake is feasible.
