sections.title: Jaundice, cholangitis and coagulation
bullets: Review biliary obstruction/stents, infection, renal function, coagulation and platelets. These affect antimicrobial planning, bleeding preparation and suitability for neuraxial analgesia.

Routine preoperative biliary drainage is not an automatic ERAS requirement. Drainage decisions depend on cholangitis, treatment timing and surgical context; anesthesia should know what was done and any culture/antibiotic implications.

sections.title: Gastric-emptying risk and induction
bullets: Assess vomiting, gastric/duodenal obstruction and delayed emptying rather than relying on a reported fasting interval. Standard elective fasting or carbohydrate drinks are not appropriate by default in an obstructed patient.

Use an airway strategy appropriate to aspiration and cardiopulmonary risk, usually general anesthesia with a secured tracheal tube for major resection. Plan decompression with the surgeon and avoid assumptions about retained gastric contents.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

BJA Education: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery (2024)

sections.title: Vascular dissection and hemorrhage preparation
bullets: Dissection around the portal/mesenteric vessels and any planned vascular resection can produce substantial bleeding. Agree on blood availability, reliable large-bore access and invasive monitoring suited to the patient and extent.
Track the phase of resection/reconstruction, measured loss, laboratory trends and perfusion. No fixed blood-loss or fluid-total estimate is safe for every Whipple.

Pancreatic surgery anesthesia editorial (2014; older background)

sections.title: Position, lung protection and warming
bullets: Secure airway and access before positioning/draping or robot docking. Use lung-protective ventilation appropriate to physiology; adjust for pneumoperitoneum and position if minimally invasive surgery is used.
Actively maintain normothermia during long exposure and fluid/blood administration. Avoiding hypothermia is a high-evidence ERAS element.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024)
ERAS pancreatoduodenectomy recommendations 2019 (published 2020; abstract)

sections.title: Perfusion without overload or rigid restriction
bullets: Individualize balanced crystalloid, blood and vasoactive therapy using perfusion and responsiveness rather than a fixed restrictive/liberal label. Both depletion and salt/water overload can impair recovery.

Epidural-related hypotension can reflect vasodilation, not just fluid loss. Assess bleeding, preload and cardiac function and use vasoactive support when appropriate rather than repeatedly flooding the patient with fluid.

sources.label: ERAS pancreatoduodenectomy recommendations (2012/2013; earlier guideline)

sections.title: Glucose and endocrine function
bullets: Measure glucose through surgery and recovery and titrate insulin/dextrose to the institutional pathway. Avoid both hypoglycemia and substantial hyperglycemia rather than interpreting older “tight control” wording as a universal narrow target.
If the indication is insulinoma or another functional PanNET, add its hormone-specific monitoring plan. Pancreatic resection extent and pre-existing diabetes affect subsequent treatment needs.

Pancreatic surgery anesthesia editorial (2014; older background)

Insulinoma and anaesthetic implications (2012; narrative review)

sections.title: Epidural and regional alternatives
bullets: Thoracic epidural can provide effective analgesia for open surgery but is not mandatory for every patient. Coagulation, anticoagulation timing, hemodynamic effects, failure risk and local expertise all matter.

The updated ERAS recommendations recognize wound catheters as an alternative to epidural analgesia. Other regional/local techniques and systemic multimodal analgesia should match approach and institutional capability; no single block replaces every component of major abdominal analgesia.

Pancreatic surgery anesthesia editorial (2014; older background)
ERAS pancreatoduodenectomy recommendations 2019 (published 2020; abstract)
Review of ERAS recommendations: pancreatoduodenectomy

sections.title: NG/OG tubes and early nutrition
bullets: Routine prolonged postoperative nasogastric decompression is not recommended in ERAS pathways, although decompression may be needed for a specific indication. Coordinate tube insertion/removal with the surgical team and reconstruction.

Support early oral/enteral intake as tolerated through the surgical pathway. Persistent vomiting or delayed gastric emptying requires reassessment for intra-abdominal complications, not simply indefinite fasting without a nutrition plan.

sources.label: ERAS pancreatoduodenectomy recommendations (2012/2013; earlier guideline)
Review of ERAS recommendations: pancreatoduodenectomy

sections.title: Fistula, bleeding and delayed deterioration
bullets: Pancreatic fistula, intra-abdominal infection, hemorrhage and delayed gastric emptying are important postoperative problems. New hemodynamic instability, bleeding or sepsis signs require prompt surgical evaluation.
Follow respiratory, renal, metabolic and coagulation status in addition to the abdomen. Do not use early extubation or initial stability as proof that the major-complication risk has passed.

sources.label: Pancreatic surgery anesthesia editorial (2014; older background)

sections.title: Extubation, observation and thromboprophylaxis
bullets: Extubate only when ventilation, temperature, neuromuscular recovery, hemodynamics and bleeding permit. Plan monitored postoperative care according to support needs; routine ICU admission is center-specific, not a universal requirement established here.
Use the procedure’s antimicrobial, VTE-prevention, mobilization and nutrition pathway. Coordinate pharmacologic prophylaxis with any epidural catheter and bleeding risk.

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical review
bullets: Adult clinical-review draft for anesthesia professionals, not an individualized order set. Use current institutional protocols, the actual surgical plan and endocrinology input; software checks do not constitute clinical signoff.

Guidelines, narrative reviews and device/procedure-specific evidence are not interchangeable. Hormone status, organ reserve and postoperative trends determine the plan; a tumor label alone does not establish safe anesthesia or discharge.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The supplied adult ACDF evidence describes elective procedures under general anesthesia. Cervical plexus block is discussed as an adjunct; sole-block approaches are described as uncommon and not established as routine.

Treat anesthesia duration as a risk-assessment consideration, not a modifiable target or proof of causation: longer duration was associated with higher adjusted odds of selected adverse outcomes in an observational cohort.
Cervical plexus block may improve analgesia and reduce opioid requirements when used with general anesthesia, but the review does not establish a preferred universal technique or regimen.

Recovery priorities supported by general standards are ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature; when neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sources.label: Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ACDF is the anterior cervical discectomy and fusion procedure represented in the supplied elective adult cohort. The available cohort evidence concerns general anesthesia; it does not define surgical indications, levels, approach details or a preferred anesthetic technique.

Cervical plexus block has been described as an adjunct to general anesthesia for cervical spine surgery. The regional-anesthesia review favors superficial or intermediate approaches and cautions that deep cervical block can have serious complications; this does not establish a routine ACDF block protocol.

sources.label: Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Apply the adult scope of the available ACDF cohort and perform individualized preanesthetic assessment. The general ASA preanesthesia standard assigns the anesthesiologist responsibility for determining medical status and developing the anesthesia-care plan; it does not supply ACDF-specific selection criteria.

Consider duration in overall risk assessment, especially alongside patient and procedural factors. The reported association is observational and should not be interpreted as a reason to avoid a lengthy procedure or as evidence that a particular anesthetic change prevents complications.

sources.label: Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF
Basic Standards for Preanesthesia Care

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring and maintain qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout anesthesia. The supplied ACDF study and regional review do not provide a procedure-specific positioning, access or enhanced-monitoring protocol.

During anesthesia, continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature, with ECG displayed and blood pressure and heart rate assessed at least every five minutes under the basic monitoring standard.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. When an endotracheal tube is inserted, verify its position by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From tube placement until extubation or initiation of transfer, perform continual quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The adult observational cohort found higher adjusted odds of any complication and return to the operating room in its longest anesthesia-time group versus its shortest. Interpret this as an association subject to study limitations, not a causal mechanism or an instruction to shorten necessary care.

sources.label: Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: In the cohort, the longest anesthesia-time group had higher observed rates of pulmonary complications, transfusion, sepsis, wound complications, prolonged stay and return to the operating room than the shortest group. The study did not test a management strategy for preventing these events.

If a cervical plexus block is chosen, recognize the block-specific hazards reported in the review, including systemic local-anesthetic toxicity and possible nerve damage after intraneural injection. The source does not provide an ACDF-specific rescue algorithm.

sources.label: Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No ACDF-specific fluid regimen, blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold or perfusion target is supplied. Individualize these decisions; the available study explicitly did not capture blood-loss volume and did not test fluid or bleeding protocols.

sources.label: Anesthesia Duration as an Independent Risk Factor for Early Postoperative Complications in Adults Undergoing Elective ACDF

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: A cervical plexus block may be considered as an adjunct for analgesia and opioid sparing, with technique and suitability discussed in context. The review reports benefit but does not establish optimal dosing or a universal block regimen.

One ACDF trial summarized in a narrative review reported less nausea and vomiting with local anesthesia using cervical plexus blocks, but also greater pain and higher patient satisfaction with general anesthesia. These comparative findings do not establish a routine anesthetic or PONV-prevention regimen.

Awake spine surgery: An eye-opening movement

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Postanesthesia care should include continual assessment appropriate to the patient’s condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature. PACU or equivalent care and an appropriate handoff are required by the cited standard.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with adductor pollicis monitoring preferred and a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 confirmed before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

sources.label: Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The largest ACDF-specific source is a retrospective database study of adults receiving general anesthesia. It reports associations with 30-day outcomes, not causal effects or a detailed anesthesia-management protocol; important ACDF outcomes and blood-loss volume were not captured.
The ACDF regional-anesthesia material is a narrative review summarizing a single comparative trial and reports ambivalent outcomes; it does not supply a complete ACDF perioperative protocol.

ASA monitoring, preanesthesia and postanesthesia standards and the neuromuscular-blockade guideline support general care principles, not ACDF-specific airway, positioning, fluid, bleeding or complication protocols.
The available sources do not establish a complete ACDF anesthesia protocol, and the appropriate management details remain case-dependent.
Evidence limitation: The ACDF study reports that patients received general anesthesia but does not report airway management, positioning, monitoring, anesthetic agents, or ventilation strategy.
Evidence limitation: The ACDF study does not report anesthetic agents or intraoperative physiologic targets or critical phases.
Evidence limitation: The ACDF study does not report emergence or extubation practices, or specific postoperative anesthesia-care protocols.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Endovascular AVM embolization selectively delivers liquid embolic material through feeding arteries to obliterate or reduce the nidus; it may be staged or precede resection.
Immobility and stable physiology are priorities. General anesthesia is commonly used for INR procedures; no anesthetic mode is established as superior.
Key hazards are hemorrhage from embolic passage into draining veins, stroke or injury to normal-brain supply, and rupture during flow changes.

After embolization, close neurologic observation and procedure-specific blood-pressure management are important; the available review describes slightly low postoperative pressure without a numeric target.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Selective catheterization of AVM feeding arteries permits controlled injection of radiopaque liquid embolic material; the intended result is nidus obliteration or reduction.
Embolization may be performed with diagnostic angiography or in a later session. Staging is used in some approaches to limit risks from rapid flow alteration; treatment is individualized.
The source describing combined embolization and resection is a procedural protocol, not comparative evidence establishing a universal embolization strategy or extent.

sources.label: Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review lesion evaluation and treatment plan with the neurointerventional team; the procedural source describes selection using grading scales and multidisciplinary assessment.
Assess baseline neurologic status, airway and cardiopulmonary reserve, blood pressure, coagulation, and prior contrast or medication reactions as part of INR preparation.
Determine whether treatment is staged and whether resection is planned; embolization can carry risks from altered flow, venous outflow obstruction, and compromise of normal-brain arterial supply.

sources.label: Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use the neurointerventional angiography environment with fluoroscopic imaging; the procedural protocol places patients supine for diagnostic angiography and embolization.
Plan monitoring with the procedural and anesthesia teams. The protocol describes multimodal neuromonitoring during embolization, with modalities selected for lesion location and clinical needs.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

sources.label: Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is common for INR and can provide immobility and controlled ventilation, but the review does not establish it as superior to other anesthetic modes.

When using general anesthesia, controlled ventilation may support normocapnia or mild hypocapnia. Avoid treating hyperventilation as a universal requirement; its use is described as a possible flow-redistribution maneuver.

Select anesthetic technique according to procedural complexity, duration, immobilization needs, patient status, and interventionist preference; be prepared for airway or hemodynamic complications in the remote suite.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Injection and changing flow are critical phases. The interventionist is directed to avoid reflux into non-AVM arteries and distal embolization into draining veins.
Liquid embolic passage into a drainage vein is identified as a serious hemorrhage mechanism. Mild intraoperative hypotension may be helpful according to the review, but it supplies no target.
Onyx is described as less influenced by blood pressure than glue; this material-specific statement does not establish a general blood-pressure strategy for all embolic agents.

sources.label: Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Maintain readiness to recognize and escalate suspected hemorrhage, arterial occlusion, or neurologic change; the procedural risks include rupture, stroke, venous outflow obstruction, and injury to normal-brain supply.
Contrast reaction and contrast-associated kidney injury are relevant peri-procedural concerns; assess prior reactions and attend to hydration and renal risk in context.
For a new postoperative neurologic deficit, repeat neurologic assessment and obtain imaging as clinically indicated; the review specifically notes CT or other imaging when a deficit is detected.

sources.label: Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain appropriate hydration in view of contrast exposure and individual renal and cardiovascular risk; the available review provides no universal fluid volume or regimen.

Manage blood pressure in coordination with the interventionist. The AVM review describes slightly low postoperative pressure, but gives no numeric target; avoid importing targets from other neurovascular procedures.
The available procedural protocol advises having blood consent and products available for resection, but does not specify transfusion thresholds or an embolization-specific blood-loss plan.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The supplied sources do not establish an AVM embolization-specific postoperative analgesic or PONV regimen. Individualize symptom management and avoid delaying neurologic assessment.
Short-acting opioids are discussed in the general INR review as options to help control responses to intubation or extubation, not as a procedure-specific pain protocol.

sources.label: Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Plan emergence to permit prompt neurologic assessment when appropriate, while avoiding abrupt hemodynamic stress; the review identifies smooth recovery for immediate examination as a general INR consideration.
Extubate if clinically able and transfer for close neurologic observation; the procedural protocol describes ICU transfer after the procedure.
Continue procedure-appropriate blood-pressure and neurologic monitoring after anesthesia; postanesthesia standards require continual evaluation using methods appropriate to the patient's condition.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Comprehensive Endovascular and Open Surgical Management of Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The anesthetic review covers INR procedures and AVM embolization but reports no formal evidence grading; it states there is no clear conclusion that one anesthetic mode is superior.

This AVM source is a technical/procedural protocol describing institutional standard-of-care methods, with one representative case; it is not an anesthesia guideline and provides no comparative anesthesia or treatment outcomes.
The neuroanesthesia manual is undated and does not provide references or evidence grading; general monitoring standards support baseline monitoring but do not supply AVM-specific targets.
Available sources do not establish numeric AVM-specific intraoperative or postoperative blood-pressure targets, a procedure-specific anticoagulation protocol, or a detailed rescue algorithm.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Awake craniotomy permits cortical or subcortical mapping during resection near eloquent function. Common approaches are asleep–awake–asleep (AAA) and monitored anesthesia care (MAC); technique depends on patient, procedure, and team.

The central anesthetic priorities are reliable cooperation and mapping, effective scalp and incision analgesia, and preservation of spontaneous ventilation and a rapidly accessible airway during the awake phase.

Important intraoperative hazards include stimulation-associated seizure, airway obstruction or hypoventilation, pain, anxiety, and nausea or vomiting. Preserve access to the patient and be prepared to pause mapping and escalate support.

After surgery, promptly assess neurologic function and provide monitored postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient. Do not assume ICU admission is routine; disposition depends on clinical status and local care arrangements.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Awake craniotomy is used principally for tumor resection near eloquent cortex and for selected epilepsy surgery, enabling functional mapping while the patient performs tasks such as naming, reading, or moving a limb.

AAA uses general anesthesia or deep sedation for the initial stage, an awake mapping stage, then anesthesia or MAC for closure. MAC keeps the patient spontaneously breathing with sedation adjusted around mapping; neither approach is established as universally preferable.
The surgical and anesthesia teams should coordinate the transition into mapping and restoration of consciousness, including the planned tasks and signals that mapping can proceed.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess willingness, ability to cooperate, psychological readiness, tolerance of prolonged positioning, pain concerns, and airway risks. Explain the stages, expected sensations, scalp block, and functional tasks; preparation is part of the anesthetic strategy.
Evaluate airway difficulty and obstructive sleep apnea, as airway access may be restricted by head fixation and position. Discuss an emergency airway plan before the patient is positioned.

Review seizure history and planned electrocorticography with the team. Evidence for routine antiepileptic prophylaxis in awake craniotomy is limited; medication decisions should not be inferred from this reference.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan positioning with the surgeon and ensure the face remains visible. Supine, half-sitting, or lateral positions are described; head fixation and position can complicate airway access.

Keep airway equipment immediately available and arrange the room so the anesthesiologist can communicate with and observe the awake patient. Protect pressure points and maintain comfort during prolonged positioning.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment. Arterial access and EEG-derived depth monitoring may be considered according to the procedure and patient; sources do not establish either as mandatory in every case.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: In AAA, an endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway may be used during the asleep phase and removed for awake mapping, with airway support re-established for closure if needed. MAC is an alternative; choose the approach with airway access and transition risks in view.

During mapping, target a responsive patient with adequate spontaneous ventilation. Sedation that is too deep risks respiratory depression and hypercapnia; excessive lightness may permit anxiety or movement.

Continually assess ventilation and expired carbon dioxide during moderate or deep sedation unless precluded by the clinical circumstances. Airway obstruction may require simple airway maneuvers or escalation; access can be difficult once the head is fixed.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Scalp incision through dural opening and the transition to mapping require adequate analgesia and a smooth emergence. Restore the patient to an appropriate level of consciousness before functional testing.
Coordinate cortical stimulation and task performance with the surgeon and, where involved, speech or neurophysiology specialists. Sedative choices can affect testing or electrocorticographic signals.

A stimulation-associated seizure can interrupt mapping and threaten patient safety. Alert the surgical team; the review describes cortical irrigation with cold saline and, if needed, IV propofol as measures used in this setting.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For airway obstruction or hypoventilation, assess ventilation and oxygenation, reduce contributing sedation where appropriate, and escalate airway support if needed. Hypercarbia and obstruction can worsen brain swelling.

Pain, panic, nausea, or vomiting can impair cooperation and mapping. Reassess the block and surgical stimulus, communicate with the patient and team, and be prepared to pause or alter the anesthetic approach.

If cooperation cannot be maintained or an emergency compromises the airway, mapping may not be possible and conversion to general anesthesia may be required. The fixed head may make airway intervention challenging.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The available awake-craniotomy sources do not establish a procedure-specific fluid, blood-loss, or transfusion regimen. Manage these according to the patient, operative course, and applicable local practice rather than adopting a fixed volume.
Consider arterial pressure monitoring according to patient and procedural needs; the sources do not support making an arterial line universal for awake craniotomy.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Scalp nerve block and/or incision-line infiltration are core analgesic components. Confirm coverage for the planned incision and pin sites; sedation alone does not substitute for adequate local analgesia.

Pain may persist despite a block, particularly with dural manipulation, traction, temporalis dissection, or a prolonged procedure. Additional analgesia should be balanced against its potential to impair cooperation.
Antiemetic prevention or treatment may be considered, especially when opioids are used. Nausea and vomiting can also be associated with anxiety and surgical stimulation.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For mapping, emergence should be smooth enough for reliable neurologic testing; restore consciousness to the preoperative state. After resection, sedation may be continued until surgery is complete when clinically appropriate.

Assess speech and motor function after surgery and monitor for seizure, pain, nausea, and respiratory problems. Level of care should reflect the patient’s condition and complications rather than an assumed routine ICU destination.
Provide postanesthesia observation with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; document recovery and hand off the anesthetic and surgical course.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The two procedure-specific sources are narrative reviews, not practice guidelines. Their described techniques and regimens should be read as options, not as a single validated protocol.
The sources report evidence favoring neither AAA nor MAC as the universal approach; comparative findings are retrospective and outcomes vary across reports.
The ASA basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards support general monitoring and recovery principles, but do not prescribe an awake-craniotomy-specific protocol.

Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For chronic subdural hematoma, burr-hole craniostomy evacuates the collection by opening the dura and using suction and irrigation; general anesthesia is common, with local anesthesia a feasible alternative.
Choose the anesthetic approach in light of neurologic status and patient factors; the available evidence does not establish a selection algorithm for local versus general anesthesia.

When general anesthesia is used, preserve oxygenation, ventilation, and circulation, and attend to potential raised intracranial pressure; the sources do not establish burr-hole-specific physiologic targets.
Plan recovery around reassessment of consciousness and the patient’s clinical condition. Anesthesia standards allow an ICU or equivalent area to provide postanesthesia care when appropriate.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For chronic subdural hematoma, burr-hole craniostomy is described as the most common evacuation technique. The review describes one or two openings on the cerebral convexity, followed by dural incision and evacuation with suction and irrigation.

General anesthesia is common, while local anesthesia is a feasible alternative. The choice should not be treated as a fixed rule: the anesthesia review identifies no validated criteria for selecting one approach.
The supplied procedure reviews concern chronic subdural hematoma. They do not establish a single approach for exploratory burr holes, acute hematoma decompression, or other indications.

sources.label: Surgical techniques for evacuation of chronic subdural hematoma: a mini-review
Burr hole evacuation of chronic subdural hematoma in general versus local anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the neurologic condition and review available imaging as part of the preanesthetic assessment. In head trauma, the neuroanesthesia manual specifically calls for assessment of associated injuries and review of CT/MRI in its intracranial aneurysm preparation discussion; it does not provide a burr-hole-specific assessment protocol.

Chronic subdural hematoma populations may be older and medically complex. Reported antiplatelet or anticoagulant use varied across studies, and the review found no reported information on whether or how these agents were reversed.

Assess airway and trauma-related concerns when relevant. The manual describes full-stomach precautions and possible cervical-spine injury in severe head trauma; those observations do not establish a universal airway technique for burr-hole surgery.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Burr hole evacuation of chronic subdural hematoma in general versus local anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and clinical circumstances. ASA basic standards require continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

The cSDH anesthesia review does not specify patient positioning, vascular access, or a procedure-specific monitoring regimen. An arterial line or other additional monitoring should therefore not be represented as routine on the basis of these sources.

For an anesthetic involving neuromuscular blocking drugs, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation; this recommendation does not impose neuromuscular monitoring on local anesthesia without blockade.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Burr hole evacuation of chronic subdural hematoma in general versus local anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The review describes general anesthesia for burr-hole evacuation as involving pharmacologic agents and endotracheal intubation. It does not establish an induction sequence or a universal airway plan.

Local anesthesia, sometimes accompanied by sedation, is represented in the cSDH literature. The review does not supply a monitoring protocol for local anesthesia or criteria for conversion; do not assume every case requires intubation or general anesthesia.

For general anesthesia, ASA standards require ongoing assessment of ventilation and, with an endotracheal tube, confirmation of placement by clinical assessment and expired carbon dioxide. The sources do not specify a burr-hole-specific ventilation target.

sources.label: Burr hole evacuation of chronic subdural hematoma in general versus local anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain attention to circulation and neurologic context throughout the procedure. The supplied head-trauma manual discusses prompt correction of systemic hypotension and raised-ICP management, but those are general head-injury recommendations, not validated burr-hole-specific targets.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Reported postoperative complications in the anesthesia comparison literature varied and included cardiopulmonary events, infection, and pneumocephalus. Event definitions and reporting were not uniform, so these data do not define a case-specific complication-management protocol.

Delayed awakening, confusion, and postoperative delirium are discussed as potential concerns in older patients receiving general anesthesia; delirium was not consistently assessed with standardized tools.
If neuromuscular blockers are used, residual blockade is a recognized source of airway and respiratory complications; use quantitative assessment rather than relying on clinical signs alone.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The cSDH anesthesia review provides no fluid regimen, blood-loss estimates, or transfusion guidance. Manage these according to the actual clinical and operative circumstances rather than a universal fluid or blood plan.

The neuroanesthesia manual identifies normal saline as a traditional crystalloid in its head-trauma discussion, but this generic statement does not establish a burr-hole-specific fluid choice or volume.

bullets: Analgesic approaches in the included cSDH studies varied. Some local-anesthesia protocols included intravenous analgesics, while general-anesthesia descriptions included fentanyl; these are reported study protocols, not recommended regimens.
The review does not provide a standardized postoperative analgesia or recovery protocol. It also does not establish a burr-hole-specific antiemetic regimen.

bullets: Base extubation on neurologic and overall clinical condition, rather than a universal rule. The head-injury manual describes OR extubation as a consideration when preoperative consciousness was normal and identifies somnolence or brain swelling as reasons against it; this is general intracranial guidance, not a burr-hole-specific criterion set.
After anesthesia, provide PACU or equivalent care with observation appropriate to the patient's condition, including consciousness, oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

The supplied sources do not establish routine ICU admission, seizure prophylaxis, or a burr-hole-specific postoperative neurologic monitoring schedule. Select the recovery location and monitoring in the clinical context.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most directly relevant anesthesia source is a systematic review and meta-analysis of chronic subdural hematoma evacuation, not a stand-alone anesthesia manual or clinical guideline. Its evidence was predominantly retrospective and heterogeneous.

The surgical-technique review is a mini-review of chronic subdural hematoma and explicitly excludes acute subdural hematoma studies. Its technique descriptions should not be generalized to acute or exploratory indications without additional evidence.

The neuroanesthesia manual supplies broader intracranial and head-trauma context but has no stated publication date, references, or evidence grading. ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards inform general care, not burr-hole-specific choices.
Evidence limitation: The cSDH review does not report fluid-management guidance, blood-loss data, transfusion information, or specific intraoperative physiological targets.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Posterior cervical laminectomy and laminoplasty decompress multilevel cervical myelopathy; laminoplasty is generally considered when decompression is needed without fusion and alignment is suitable.

Prone positioning and cervical manipulation make neutral-to-slight flexion, protection from pressure injury, and avoidance of hypotension important; the available source does not establish a universal blood-pressure target.
Cervical pathology may limit neck movement and increase intubation difficulty. Avoid excessive extension; video laryngoscopy or fiberoptic-assisted intubation can help maintain neutral positioning.
SSEP/MEP monitoring may support detection of cord compromise; recovery priorities include a prompt neurological assessment and attention to new root-level weakness, particularly C5 palsy.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...
Anesthesia for Orthopedic Surgeries

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Posterior cervical laminectomy, laminectomy with fusion, and laminoplasty are approaches to cervical myelopathy. Posterior decompression is indirect: adequate cord drift away from anterior compression depends on sagittal alignment.

The review describes posterior approaches as most advantageous for multilevel myelopathy involving three or more motion segments. Significant kyphosis may limit cord drift; approach selection remains a surgical decision based on anatomy and imaging.

Laminoplasty preserves posterior elements while expanding the canal and is described for patients who do not require fusion. Laminectomy with fusion may be considered where significant neck pain or risk of progressive kyphosis informs the surgical plan.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the neurological baseline and review the degree of myelopathy, prior cervical surgery, and cervical stability. These findings affect positioning and airway planning.

Review sagittal alignment and symptoms with the surgical team: posterior decompression may be less suitable when kyphosis prevents adequate cord drift. The cited review describes laminoplasty particularly for lordotic alignment and little spondylotic neck pain.

Assess neck range of motion, airway difficulty, and neurological symptoms with extension. For severe myelopathy or poor tolerance of extension, the review advises considering awake fiberoptic intubation; it does not make this mandatory for all patients.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For the posterior approach, plan prone positioning with the neck neutral to slightly flexed and immobilized as appropriate. Keep pressure off the eyes and face, use lateral chest and abdominal bolsters to avoid abdominal compression, and consider reverse Trendelenburg while watching for hypotension.
Avoid exceeding the patient’s tolerated preoperative extension. Shoulder taping can create longitudinal tension; monitoring may help identify positioning-related brachial plexus compromise.

SSEP or MEP monitoring is recommended by the review for patients with myelopathy. In severe disease, consider a post-intubation, pre-positioning baseline; arterial pressure monitoring may be appropriate, particularly with cardiovascular lability.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Secure the airway supine before turning prone. Avoid excessive cervical extension; video laryngoscopy or fiberoptic-assisted intubation may help maintain neutral positioning when cervical pathology limits movement.

After prone positioning, reassess airway security and access to the patient. The cervical-surgery summary identifies prone positioning and the possibility of significant blood loss with multiple instrumented levels; it does not provide a procedure-specific ventilation regimen.

For cord monitoring, the cervical-surgery anesthesia summary favors TIVA and advises limiting volatile anesthetic if used; it also advises avoiding nitrous oxide. Select the technique with the monitoring team and clinical context in mind.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid hypotension and maintain adequate spinal-cord perfusion throughout the case, including before incision when prone positioning or reverse Trendelenburg may provoke hypotension. The source does not establish a universal blood-pressure target.

For patients with myelopathy, SSEP or MEP spinal cord monitoring is recommended; the review notes controversy about MEP use but says available data indicate MEPs may add useful information to SSEPs when available.

Positioning, decompression, and surgical manipulation all warrant attention to neurological monitoring and hemodynamics. The available sources support avoiding hypotension but do not provide a case-specific anesthetic depth, neuromuscular-blockade, or cord-perfusion target.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Positioning-related cord compromise and brachial plexopathy are relevant hazards. Avoid excessive neck extension and shoulder traction; use the planned monitoring and communicate concerning signal changes promptly with the surgical and monitoring teams.

Segmental root palsy, most often involving C5, is reported after laminoplasty. New postoperative weakness or sensory symptoms warrant prompt neurological assessment and communication with the surgical team.

Postoperative axial neck pain is a recognized concern, and laminoplasty is not designed to treat painful spondylosis. Counsel and plan recovery in the context of preoperative symptoms and the surgical approach.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain adequate blood pressure for spinal-cord perfusion; avoid hypotensive anesthesia. Individualize hemodynamic support to the patient and operative context rather than applying a fixed target from this evidence.

Reverse Trendelenburg may lower cervical venous pressure but can be accompanied by hypotension. Maintain vigilance before surgical stimulation, when the review says hypotension is commonly encountered.
Avoid abdominal compression and use positioning that limits venous congestion. The sources do not provide a case-specific fluid volume, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan postoperative analgesia that supports comfort and neurological assessment. A review describes cervical plexus block as an adjunct to general anesthesia for cervical surgery, but does not establish it as a routine requirement for posterior decompression.

Discuss any regional analgesic technique with the surgeon when rapid postoperative neurological examination is important. The review notes that motor block from epidural local anesthetic may impede assessment.
The procedure-specific review does not provide a complete postoperative analgesia regimen or PONV protocol; select these according to patient and institutional context.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Return the patient to a position suitable for airway management before extubation. Aim for a smooth emergence that permits neurological assessment, while individualizing extubation to airway, respiratory, and neurological status.
Assess neurological status early in recovery and communicate new deficits promptly. Continue observation for root-level palsy and other approach-related concerns.

Use postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient’s condition, with evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; transfer and handoff should communicate the perioperative course.

bullets: The procedure-specific source is a 2008 narrative review, not an anesthesia guideline, and does not provide a systematic-review method. Its recommendations and numerical outcomes draw on cited studies and author experience.
The cervical-surgery anesthesia material is an educational summary of several procedures; it supports general airway and anesthetic considerations but is not specific to laminoplasty alone.

The regional-anesthesia article is a review, and it notes that regional anesthesia for spinal surgery has not been extensively evaluated. It does not establish a single best analgesic technique for this operation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Craniotomy may be performed under general anesthesia; awake approaches are used when cortical or subcortical mapping is needed, particularly for tumors near eloquent function.

The anesthetic priorities are to preserve cerebral perfusion, avoid preventable increases in intracranial pressure, and accommodate the surgeon’s need for brain relaxation and timely neurological assessment.

Important hazards include stimulation-related hemodynamic changes, brain swelling or hemorrhage, seizures, and venous air embolism in susceptible operative settings; sudden deterioration requires prompt communication and escalation.
Recovery should permit prompt neurological assessment when appropriate, while avoiding coughing or straining and providing observation suited to the patient’s condition.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Craniotomy for tumor resection or tissue diagnosis may be undertaken with general anesthesia, sedation with local anesthesia, or local anesthesia alone. The appropriate approach depends on the surgical and mapping requirements.

For tumors near eloquent cortex, awake craniotomy permits functional mapping during resection. Described approaches include asleep–awake–asleep and monitored anesthetic care; awake techniques require patient cooperation and an experienced team.

Coordinate the anesthetic plan with the surgeon, including whether mapping, neuromonitoring, or a rapid postoperative examination is required. Available sources do not establish one anesthetic technique as appropriate for all tumor resections.

sources.label: Local anesthetics for brain tumor resection: current perspectives

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review imaging and discuss tumor size, location, and vascularity with the surgeon; these features affect the operative approach and anticipated bleeding or air-embolism risk.

Assess baseline neurological status and symptoms that may be consistent with raised intracranial pressure. For an awake approach, evaluate airway and ability to cooperate; difficult airway or obstructive sleep apnea makes candidacy less favorable.

Review steroid use and relevant metabolic or hematologic concerns. The source manual specifically notes glucose monitoring in patients receiving steroids or with diabetes, and laboratory assessment as indicated; it does not supply a comprehensive contemporary preoperative testing protocol.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Confirm the operative position and head-frame plan in advance. Position is surgeon- and tumor-dependent; the manual describes prone positioning for many posterior fossa procedures and emphasizes padding and careful airway security when the head is remote.
Pin placement is a highly stimulating phase. Plan analgesia/anesthetic depth with the team before clamp application; local infiltration is one described adjunct.

Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and case. The manual recommends invasive arterial pressure monitoring for full craniotomy; this is a source-specific educational recommendation, not a universal line-placement rule. Basic standards require continuous ECG display and regular blood pressure and heart-rate assessment.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For general anesthesia, secure the endotracheal tube and tape the eyes carefully because the head will be away from the anesthesiologist. Verify tube placement clinically and by identifying carbon dioxide in expired gas, and continually monitor end-tidal CO₂ until extubation or transfer.

During awake craniotomy, airway access can be difficult with the head turned and secured. Keep an airway rescue plan and equipment immediately available; do not assume that an airway intervention will be straightforward in the operative position.

Avoid unintended hypercapnia, which can worsen brain swelling, while coordinating ventilation goals with the surgeon. The supplied manual describes hypocapnia, whereas the case material proposes normocapnia; the available sources do not resolve a universal target.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Anticipate hemodynamic responses to pin fixation, incision, and closure. Scalp block or infiltration can reduce nociceptive and autonomic responses, but the optimal technique is not established by comparative evidence.

Maintain cerebral perfusion and avoid avoidable hypotension or hypertension, with goals agreed with the surgical team and individualized to the patient and operative phase. The supplied material does not validate a single blood-pressure target for all tumor craniotomies.

Brain swelling, hemorrhage, and seizures may arise during resection. Maintain communication with the surgeon and neuromonitoring team so changes in anesthetic or neuromuscular blockade do not compromise mapping.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: A sudden end-tidal carbon-dioxide decrease, particularly with cardiovascular change, can signal venous air embolism in a susceptible operative setting. Recognize the change promptly and alert the surgical team; the supplied sources do not establish a complete response algorithm.

New swelling, bleeding, seizure activity, or unexplained hemodynamic change warrants immediate communication and reassessment of the operative and anesthetic situation. Awake-craniotomy complications include respiratory depression and airway obstruction, with urgent intervention emphasized for airway compromise.

During awake mapping, seizures are a recognized complication, particularly with cortical stimulation. The review describes cold-saline irrigation and low-dose propofol as reported interventions; these are source-described options, not a universal protocol.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The educational manual describes glucose-free isotonic crystalloid and minimizing crystalloid to limit brain edema. This is not a comparative, procedure-specific fluid guideline; choose fluid and volume to the clinical context rather than applying a fixed regimen.

Anticipated blood loss depends on tumor and approach; the manual contrasts substantial bleeding with vascular meningiomas against lower bleeding risk in typical glioma debulking. Ensure blood availability is proportionate to the operation and team assessment, not a universal crossmatch rule.

The sources do not establish a transfusion threshold or a universal perfusion target for tumor craniotomy. The manual advises monitoring blood loss and hematocrit and transfusing if needed; decisions remain dependent on the patient and operative course.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Scalp block or incision-line infiltration can provide analgesia and blunt responses to painful phases. A complete scalp block involves six sensory nerves, but no evidence supplied establishes one block technique as superior.

Use multimodal postoperative analgesia while preserving wakefulness and ventilation needed for neurological assessment. Opioids may impair cooperation during mapping and can contribute to sedation or hypercapnia.

Nausea and vomiting are reported complications and may interfere with recovery; anticipate symptom management as part of postoperative care. The sources do not provide a craniotomy-specific antiemetic regimen.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Local anesthetics for brain tumor resection: current perspectives

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When early awakening is appropriate, aim for a smooth emergence and avoid coughing, straining, and ventilator fighting. The manual advises delayed emergence when preoperative consciousness, brain swelling, operative extent, or other clinical conditions make early extubation unsuitable.

Plan recovery location and observation according to neurological status and overall condition. Postanesthesia standards require continual evaluation with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

If a neuromuscular blocking drug was used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The case-specific evidence consists largely of narrative reviews and an educational neuroanesthesia manual, rather than a single contemporary guideline for adult tumor craniotomy. The manual provides no publication date, references, or evidence grading.

Awake-craniotomy reviews address selected patients and do not establish the routine anesthetic for all tumor resections. The local-anesthetic review also notes a lack of comparative evidence establishing superiority of scalp block over field infiltration.

Available sources conflict on ventilation emphasis: the manual describes mild-to-moderate hypocapnia as usual, while awake-craniotomy material cautions that respiratory depression and hypercapnia can contribute to brain edema. A universal case-specific carbon-dioxide target is not established.
Sources do not provide a validated universal blood-pressure target, transfusion threshold, or postoperative neurological-check interval for adult tumor craniotomy.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Surgical clipping uses a craniotomy to place a clip across the aneurysm neck. It is selected according to aneurysm anatomy and patient factors, often when endovascular treatment is unsuitable.
The central anesthetic balance is limiting aneurysm transmural pressure and re-rupture risk while preserving cerebral perfusion and obtaining adequate brain relaxation.

Avoid abrupt arterial-pressure changes, particularly hypertensive responses before the aneurysm is secured; avoid hypotension that may compromise cerebral perfusion. Individualize targets to ICP, neurologic grade, and the operative phase.
After clipping, prioritize prompt neurologic assessment and monitored neurocritical care, with attention to hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, delayed cerebral ischemia, and seizures.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Aneurysm clipping is performed through a craniotomy; the clip excludes the aneurysm neck from circulation. Choice of clipping versus endovascular treatment depends on aneurysm size, location, morphology, perforator relationships, calcification or thrombosis, and overall patient risk.

Approach and position are anatomy-dependent. Pterional approaches are commonly used for anterior-circulation aneurysms; posterior-circulation approaches may use a retrosigmoid route and park-bench positioning. Confirm the planned approach and position with the surgical team.
Clipping is often considered for complex or wide-necked aneurysms and selected middle cerebral artery aneurysms; the choice remains multidisciplinary rather than determined by a single feature.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess neurologic grade and review CT and angiography for hemorrhage burden, mass effect, hydrocephalus, aneurysm anatomy, and collateral circulation. Higher-grade SAH may involve raised ICP, brain swelling, impaired autoregulation, and increased ischemia risk.

Consider SAH-associated cardiac dysfunction, arrhythmia, pulmonary complications, and fluid, electrolyte, or glucose derangements. Correct relevant abnormalities without delaying urgent definitive treatment.
Coordinate arterial-pressure goals and rupture-response roles with the surgeon. A preoperative rupture simulation is suggested as preparation; it does not replace individualized planning.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan positioning around aneurysm location and surgical exposure, with attention to venous drainage and avoiding excessive neck flexion or rotation. For anterior approaches, the source describes supine positioning with the head turned away; posterior approaches commonly use park-bench positioning.

Use continuous arterial-pressure monitoring for clipping; establish it before induction when indicated by the clinical and procedural risk. Sources differ on whether pre-induction placement is needed for every patient.

Ensure reliable venous access, ECG, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring, temperature monitoring, and access to processed EEG where used. Neurophysiologic monitoring may include SSEPs and MEPs; consider anesthetic effects and communicate changes promptly.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For clipping under general anesthesia, plan tracheal intubation and a controlled, smooth induction. Use adequate anesthetic depth and analgesia to blunt laryngoscopy and pin-placement responses while avoiding hypotension, especially with myocardial dysfunction.

Avoid inadvertent hypo- or hypercarbia. Hypercarbia may increase ICP; aggressive hypocarbia may raise aneurysm transmural pressure and impair perfusion. Controlled, modest hyperventilation may be used for brain relaxation when appropriate, not as an automatic pre-dural-opening maneuver.

TIVA is commonly favored when evoked-potential monitoring is used, but it is not established as universally superior. Volatile agents can affect evoked potentials in a dose-dependent manner; neuromuscular blockers disrupt MEP monitoring.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Before aneurysm security, avoid rapid pressure increases and avoid relative hypotension that could threaten cerebral perfusion. The appropriate pressure range depends on ICP, neurologic grade, baseline physiology, and surgical phase; communicate targets with the surgeon.

Brain relaxation may involve head elevation, careful fluid management, controlled ventilation, osmotherapy, and CSF drainage when appropriate. Avoid excessive volatile-agent concentrations and excessive or rapid CSF drainage; choose measures in context of perfusion and rupture risk.

Temporary clipping risks focal ischemia. Coordinate clip duration and reperfusion strategy with the surgeon, use evoked-potential or EEG information when available, and respond to changes with reassessment of clip/retractor position and perfusion. A single universally safe occlusion duration is not established.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For suspected intraoperative rupture, alert the surgeon, maintain coordinated communication, and support rapid surgical control while managing pressure and perfusion deliberately. The reviewed source describes brief pressure reduction as one possible aid to visualization, not a universal response.

If evoked potentials change during clipping, promptly communicate with the surgeon and assess for clip-related ischemia or retractor effects; blood-pressure augmentation, clip adjustment, or retractor adjustment may be considered according to the situation.

Postoperative neurologic decline warrants urgent evaluation for hydrocephalus, edema, delayed cerebral ischemia, or seizure. Neurocritical care surveillance is important; DCI may occur with or without angiographic vasospasm.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain euvolemia and avoid hypovolemia; use isotonic fluid choices appropriate to the clinical context. The available reviews do not establish a routine fluid volume, transfusion threshold, or blood-product regimen for clipping.

Have blood availability appropriate to the anticipated operation and patient. Complex aneurysm trapping or reconstruction can involve prolonged occlusion and major blood loss, but this should not be generalized to every clipping procedure.

Osmotherapy may be used for raised ICP or brain relaxation, with mannitol and hypertonic saline both discussed in the sources. Select and monitor therapy in context; no universal agent or dose is established here.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use analgesia judiciously to blunt responses to laryngoscopy and cranial-pin placement while preserving hemodynamic stability and the ability to assess neurologic function. Local anesthetic pin-site infiltration or scalp block may be useful adjuncts.

Scalp block is described as reducing pain stimuli and anesthetic/opioid requirements and supporting postoperative analgesia. Technique and local-anesthetic selection should follow applicable institutional practice and patient-specific assessment.
The supplied clipping sources do not specify a postoperative analgesia regimen or a PONV prevention strategy; do not infer one from these materials.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Aim for smooth, timely emergence that permits neurologic assessment while avoiding coughing, straining, or marked hypertension. The supplied clipping reviews do not establish a specific emergence drug regimen or extubation rule.

Plan postoperative care in a neurointensive-care or equivalent high-dependency setting with close neurologic observation. Ongoing aSAH care and surveillance should be coordinated with the neurocritical-care team.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative recovery before extubation, using adductor-pollicis monitoring. This recommendation applies when blockade is used, not to every anesthetic technique.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-specific source is an educational review of clipping anesthesia, not a formal guideline or trial. It does not describe systematic-review methods or formal evidence grading.

A second source is a narrative review that explicitly reflects clinical interpretation and experience. Its recommendations are useful context, not a substitute for current institutional or specialty guidance.

Sources differ on whether an arterial line must precede induction in every patient and on temporary-clipping pressure and duration strategies. Individualize these decisions; a universally safe clipping duration or single pressure target is not established by the supplied evidence.

The sources do not provide a validated case-specific emergence/extubation protocol or a postoperative analgesia and PONV regimen. These are substantive limits of this draft; no absent universal fluid total or fixed drug regimen is implied.
