title: High-Risk Obstetric Anesthesia — Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy
aliases: High-Risk Obstetric Anesthesia — Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For most pregnant patients with cardiovascular disease, plan vaginal delivery with effective neuraxial analgesia; cesarean delivery is generally for obstetric indications or selected cardiac conditions.
Individualize monitoring and hemodynamic goals to the cardiac lesion and its severity.

Neuraxial anesthesia is often preferred when feasible, but technique and titration should reflect lesion severity, anticoagulation, and the risk of sympathectomy; general anesthesia is an option when neuraxial care is unsuitable or urgency requires it.
Recovery planning must account for postpartum hemodynamic and volume shifts, with monitoring intensity and location determined by the cardiac lesion and delivery course.

sources.label: Obstetric Anesthesia and Heart Disease: Practical Clinical Considerations
Anesthesia for Labor, Delivery, and Cesarean Section in High-Risk Heart Disease

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Favor planned vaginal delivery with effective neuraxial labor analgesia for most patients with cardiovascular disease; compared with cesarean delivery, it is associated with less blood loss, infection, and venous thromboembolism.

Cesarean delivery is generally for obstetric indications. The cardiac review identifies selected exceptions, including large expanding or dissecting aortic aneurysms, maternal warfarin anticoagulation, critical valvular stenosis, and severe decompensated pulmonary hypertension.

Choose neuraxial technique and onset deliberately. For selected severe lesions, gradual sympathectomy may be preferable to the faster hemodynamic changes associated with spinal anesthesia; technique remains dependent on lesion and clinical circumstances.

sources.label: Obstetric Anesthesia and Heart Disease: Practical Clinical Considerations

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Arrange predelivery anesthetic assessment and multidisciplinary coordination with obstetrics and cardiology. Review the lesion, severity, cardiac history and testing, obstetric factors, anticipated anticoagulation, and resources needed for urgent intervention.

Use a recognized risk framework as an aid, not a substitute for clinical assessment. The mWHO classification spans a wide range of reported cardiovascular-event risk; pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe symptomatic aortic stenosis are examples of class IV lesions.

Plan delivery location according to anticipated expertise and rescue needs. Subspecialty cardiac care warrants a higher-level center; possible cardiac surgery or ECMO support favors a hospital with cardiac-surgery capability.
Assess anticoagulation before selecting neuraxial anesthesia. Coordinate timing and eligibility decisions with the multidisciplinary team, particularly for patients with mechanical valves.

sources.label: Obstetric Anesthesia and Heart Disease: Practical Clinical Considerations
Anesthesia for Labor, Delivery, and Cesarean Section in High-Risk Heart Disease

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Match staffing, location, vasoactive capability, and monitoring to lesion severity and anticipated intervention. Coordinate roles in advance where ECG monitoring or vasoactive/inotropic drug administration exceeds routine labor-unit capability.
Use left lateral positioning in labor when appropriate to relieve gravid-uterus compression; maintain uterine displacement for cesarean delivery.

Individualize monitoring. Intra-arterial pressure monitoring may help in selected high-risk lesions, especially when precise pressure management or emergency intervention is anticipated; it is not established here as mandatory for every cardiac condition.

During labor, consider continuous pulse oximetry and heart-rate monitoring; use ECG/telemetry when arrhythmia or ischemia risk warrants it. Invasive pulmonary monitoring is reserved for selected complex circumstances, not routine use.

sources.label: Obstetric Anesthesia and Heart Disease: Practical Clinical Considerations
Anesthesia for Labor, Delivery, and Cesarean Section in High-Risk Heart Disease

Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for cesarean delivery whenever feasible, including in many patients with high-risk lesions. Consider general anesthesia when cardiopulmonary decompensation, anticoagulation, severe thrombocytopenia, refusal, or clinical urgency makes neuraxial anesthesia unsuitable.

If general anesthesia is chosen, account for the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation in the relevant lesion; the available cardiac review does not provide a general airway or induction protocol.

For pulmonary hypertension, avoid physiologic conditions that increase pulmonary vascular resistance, including hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, and high ventilation pressures when intubated; maintain attention to right-ventricular function.

sources.label: Obstetric Anesthesia and Heart Disease: Practical Clinical Considerations

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Prevent abrupt reductions in systemic vascular resistance or pressure where fixed outflow obstruction or right-to-left shunting makes them poorly tolerated. For aortic stenosis, maintain afterload and avoid tachycardia; for right-to-left shunt, reduced systemic resistance can worsen shunting and hypoxia.
For pulmonary hypertension, avoid factors that increase pulmonary vascular resistance and optimize right-ventricular function.
Anticipate cardiovascular changes during labor and the postpartum period; patients with cardiovascular disease are at greatest risk of pulmonary edema during second-stage labor and postpartum.
Treat neuraxial-associated hypotension promptly, choosing vasopressor and fluid strategy in light of lesion physiology rather than applying a universal approach.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: New hypotension, hypoxia, tachycardia, or altered cardiac status warrants immediate assessment for lesion-related decompensation and obstetric causes. The cardiac review advises a low threshold for echocardiography, chest imaging, and ECG when heart disease is suspected.

For suspected pulmonary-hypertension or right-heart deterioration, avoid worsening hypoxia, hypercarbia, or acidosis and escalate promptly to the multidisciplinary team with relevant cardiopulmonary support available.
Prepare for arrhythmia and cardiac arrest through advance emergency planning and appropriate personnel/resources. This reference does not establish a cardiac-disease-specific resuscitation algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain euvolemia, avoiding fluid overload in pulmonary hypertension or mitral stenosis. In aortic stenosis, augment preload judiciously because excess fluid can cause pulmonary edema; avoid routine fluid loading when pulmonary-edema risk is a concern.

The cardiac review notes that postpartum hemorrhage is more common in women with heart disease. Anticipate bleeding and coordinate uterotonic selection and administration with the cardiac lesion and obstetric team.

For cardiac disease, titrate oxytocin by infusion pump rather than giving a rapid bolus, because bolus administration can rapidly decrease systemic vascular resistance. Generic scheduled-cesarean ERAC regimens are not lesion-specific and should not be treated as cardiac guidance.
Avoid assuming a single hemorrhage or transfusion plan. Have blood products available when clinical risk warrants, including therapeutic anticoagulation or anticipated significant bleeding.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Provide effective labor analgesia early enough to limit pain-related catecholamine and cardiac-output fluctuations; titrate neuraxial dosing while observing hemodynamic response.

For cesarean delivery, neuraxial anesthesia is generally preferred when feasible; gradual epidural or combined techniques may be considered when a slower sympathectomy is desirable for a selected high-risk lesion.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Set the postpartum monitoring plan before delivery. Level and duration of care depend on the cardiovascular condition and events during delivery; monitor for heart failure, arrhythmia, postpartum preeclampsia, and hemorrhage as relevant.

Maintain particular vigilance for postpartum pulmonary edema or right-sided failure in patients with pulmonary hypertension or reduced ventricular function; arrange an appropriate high-acuity setting when the clinical risk warrants it.
Include breastfeeding support and newborn-care education in postpartum planning.

bullets: The principal cardiac-anesthesia source is a clinical review based on a nonsystematic literature review; its authors report limited data and note that many recommendations rely on physiologic extrapolation and expert advice.
The high-risk heart-disease reference is a continuing-education review, not a guideline or trial. Its condition-specific recommendations inform priorities but do not establish a universal regimen.

The general obstetric anesthesia guideline explicitly excludes parturients with chronic medical disease, including severe cardiac disease; its recommendations should not be used to resolve cardiac-specific questions beyond their stated scope.
Evidence for anesthetic management of cardiac disease in pregnancy is limited; many recommendations rely on physiologic extrapolation and expert advice.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Labor epidural analgesia uses a lumbar epidural catheter for adjustable neuraxial pain relief that can be maintained through labor; dilute local anesthetic with an opioid is a commonly described approach.

The key immediate hazards are unintended intrathecal or intravascular placement, high neuraxial block, and hypotension. Incremental administration with close maternal observation and fetal heart-rate monitoring supports early recognition.

Assess analgesic quality and motor function during labor, and reassess after significant additional neuraxial dosing. Poor, asymmetric, or changing analgesia may require catheter assessment rather than simply accepting an inadequate block.

Recovery priorities include monitoring maternal status, confirming regression of motor block, and recognizing post-dural puncture headache or persistent neurologic symptoms; postpartum monitoring should follow obstetric and local recovery policies.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The epidural space is commonly identified in the lumbar region using loss of resistance; a catheter is threaded into the epidural space for intermittent or continuous administration. The technique is adjustable and may be maintained throughout labor.
Dilute local anesthetic combined with an opioid is used to provide analgesia while limiting motor block; the selected maintenance method should suit available equipment and the clinical context.
Neuraxial analgesia may be offered in early labor and individually regardless of cervical dilation; the guideline advises reassurance that it does not increase cesarean delivery incidence.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Perform focused assessment relevant to neuraxial care, including maternal and anesthetic history, baseline blood pressure, airway, heart and lung examination, and back examination when neuraxial anesthesia is planned. Individualize testing rather than ordering routine platelet counts for every healthy parturient.
Consider prior spinal surgery, scoliosis, obesity, and difficult landmarks as potential technical modifiers; ultrasound may help with landmark identification in selected patients.

For thrombocytopenia, weigh the cause, bleeding history, signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation, competing risks, airway factors, and patient preference. SOAP consensus describes risk as likely low at platelet counts of at least 70,000 × 10⁶/L for specified common etiologies when there is no bleeding-history or DIC concern; lower counts require individualized assessment, not an automatic rule.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Establish and maintain IV access before neuraxial analgesia. Appropriate resuscitation equipment and drugs should be immediately available wherever obstetric neuraxial analgesia is initiated and maintained.

A qualified individual should monitor and document maternal vital signs and fetal heart rate. Before and during placement, obtain heart rate, pulse oximetry, and blood pressure; maintain direct observation after initial dosing.

During the initial post-dose observation period, monitor heart rate and pulse oximetry continuously and blood pressure at least every five minutes; the guideline recommends more frequent blood-pressure measurement when feasible during the first ten minutes.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Labor epidural placement is neuraxial analgesia, not a general anesthetic; the provided sources do not establish routine intubation, neuromuscular blockade, or a specific ventilation technique for an awake patient receiving labor epidural analgesia.

Have equipment available to maintain an airway, provide positive-pressure ventilation, and perform endotracheal intubation, because unintended high neuraxial block or systemic toxicity can require urgent escalation.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Administer neuraxial medication incrementally and observe for an unexpectedly dense or high block or symptoms suggesting intravascular local-anesthetic exposure. Aspiration and slow small aliquots are described as safeguards, but do not eliminate risk.

Hypotension can follow neuraxial sympathectomy. The obstetric guideline supports IV fluid preloading or coloading as options and permits ephedrine or phenylephrine; it advises considering phenylephrine in the absence of maternal bradycardia. It does not establish a fixed fluid volume or universal vasopressor regimen.

Continue fetal heart-rate observation as clinically appropriate; transient changes are described, particularly with rapid-onset techniques, but the review does not provide a complete monitoring protocol.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Inadequate, unilateral, or patchy analgesia may reflect catheter position, migration, or anatomy. Reassess block distribution and catheter function; described options include catheter manipulation, additional medication, or replacement when appropriate.

Unexpected rapid dense block, respiratory distress, or cardiovascular compromise after neuraxial dosing raises concern for unintended intrathecal dosing or high block and warrants immediate clinical reassessment and escalation.

Unintended dural puncture can lead to post-dural puncture headache. Persistent or severe headache despite conservative care may require specialist assessment for an epidural blood patch; monitor for neurologic symptoms as well.

Fever is not resolved as a neuraxial eligibility question by the supplied review: it describes epidural-related fever and advises surveillance for infectious causes, including chorioamnionitis. Apply clinical assessment rather than treating fever alone as an established absolute rule.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain IV access throughout neuraxial analgesia. Fluid preloading or coloading may be considered in relation to hypotension risk; the obstetric guideline explicitly does not require a fixed volume before neuraxial analgesia is initiated.

Treat clinically significant neuraxial-associated hypotension with individualized perfusion support; available guideline options include IV fluids and vasopressors, with agent choice conditioned by maternal heart rate and context.
The labor-epidural sources do not provide a procedure-specific blood-loss, transfusion, or hemorrhage-management regimen; obstetric bleeding risk should be assessed in its clinical context.

bullets: Use an individualized dilute local-anesthetic–opioid epidural strategy to provide labor analgesia while limiting motor block; the sources describe continuous infusion, patient-controlled epidural analgesia, and intermittent bolus approaches.
Assess analgesia across labor stages; first-stage visceral pain and second-stage perineal pain have different spinal distributions, and sacral sparing can produce incomplete second-stage relief.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: This is not an emergence or extubation pathway when neuraxial labor analgesia is provided without general anesthesia. Continue appropriate maternal observation and assess motor recovery before mobilization.

After vaginal delivery, the obstetric neuraxial guideline calls for postpartum blood-pressure and pulse monitoring at least every fifteen minutes for two hours, with more frequent and longer monitoring if complications occur.

Persistent motor block beyond the guideline’s stated interval after the last neuraxial medication warrants anesthesia-provider evaluation. After unintended dural puncture, continue assessment for headache and neurologic symptoms.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The contemporary labor-analgesia source is a clinical review, not a guideline or trial; it reports no systematic search method or formal evidence-quality assessment. Treat its regimens as descriptive examples, not patient-specific prescriptions.

The ASA obstetric anesthesia guideline is based on searches ending in 2015 and presents recommendations rather than absolute requirements; the 2021 ASA neuraxial guideline and 2021 SOAP thrombocytopenia consensus provide more directly relevant procedural and platelet-assessment guidance.

Available sources do not establish a comprehensive labor-epidural protocol for anticoagulant timing, allergy-specific alternatives, or detailed local-anesthetic systemic toxicity rescue. Apply the relevant specialty guidance and institutional pathways; these gaps do not justify inventing universal intervals or regimens.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For planned PAS delivery, use an experienced multidisciplinary team and a preoperative surgical plan; cesarean hysterectomy is a definitive option when required to control life-threatening bleeding.
Deliver the fetus through an incision outside the invaded uterine area and leave the placenta in situ; do not attempt placental removal, which can precipitate massive hemorrhage.
Prioritize readiness for severe hemorrhage and its consequences, including coagulopathy, acidosis, hypothermia, and injury to adjacent urinary or intestinal structures.

Plan postoperative intensive monitoring; continued blood-component therapy, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, ventilatory support, or vasopressors may be needed. The sources do not establish routine intubation or extubation criteria.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: PAS surgery should be planned in a tertiary service with an experienced multidisciplinary team; consent should address transfusion, urinary or intestinal injury, fistula, and possible hysterectomy.

For stable patients, the cited recommendation is planned delivery at 34 + 0 to 35 + 6 weeks; earlier delivery is for obstetric indications. This is a source-based planning range, not an individual timing directive.
Perform hysterotomy outside the invaded area, extract the fetus, and keep the placenta in situ. If hysterectomy is undertaken, remove the uterus with the placenta in situ rather than separating it.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review prior cesarean and abdominal surgery, obstetric history, comorbidities, medications, allergies, prior anesthetic problems, airway, cardiopulmonary status, and suitability for neuraxial anesthesia.
Coordinate the surgical team, blood bank, neonatal service, interventional radiology, and intensive care resources in advance; counsel about the possibility of extensive surgery and transfusion.
Consider ureteral stents selectively in percreta with lower invasion involving the bladder trigone or parametrium; cystoscopy is not routinely recommended by the cited PAS document.
For stable patients, the cited PAS recommendation includes antenatal corticosteroids according to standard guidelines; it does not provide an anesthesia-specific medication or laboratory protocol.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use an operating environment with rapid-transfusion capability, neonatal resuscitation resources, and access to interventional radiology where available; cell salvage is described as an option.

The PAS recommendation describes two large-caliber venous accesses, central venous access, invasive blood-pressure monitoring, reserved blood products, and intensive care beds as surgical preparation.
Position in lithotomy with left uterine displacement and legs apart to permit vaginal access. Maintain displacement as clinically appropriate.
Apply basic anesthetic monitoring and adapt additional monitoring to the anticipated hemorrhage and patient condition; the sources do not establish a PAS-specific monitor schedule.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General, neuraxial, or combined anesthesia are described options. Individualize selection to hemorrhage risk, airway and hemodynamic considerations, urgency, and patient preference.

One described strategy is neuraxial anesthesia until fetal extraction followed sequentially by general anesthesia, with prolonged surgical time cited as rationale. This is an option, not a universal conversion rule.

General anesthesia may be selected when massive hemorrhage is predicted or time is insufficient for neuraxial anesthesia. The PAS sources do not specify an airway device, intubation sequence, or ventilation protocol.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The major surgical hazard is bleeding from invasive chorionic villi and vascular neoformations. Avoid placental separation; fetal extraction and placental management should follow the planned surgical approach.
Use the planned incision and perioperative imaging as needed to locate the placental border; extraction should be outside the invaded uterine area.
Expect possible prolonged dissection and injury to adjacent organs; advanced pelvic surgical experience is recommended, including capability for bladder reconstruction and ureteral procedures.
Recognize the potential progression from hemorrhage to coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, and hypothermia; coordinate rapid reassessment and escalation with the surgical and blood-bank teams.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For unexpected PAS at delivery, do not attempt placental removal. The cited recommendation is to pause, provide blood components, reorganize the anesthetic and surgical plan, and obtain adequate exposure.
Urinary tract injury may involve bladder invasion, partial cystectomy, or ureteral reconstruction; intestinal injury and fistula are also recognized risks.

Provide postoperative intensive care; continued hemotherapy, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, ventilatory support, and vasopressors are often necessary. When the placenta is left in situ, monitor clinically for weeks to months because reported risks include hemorrhagic recurrence, infection, last-resort hysterectomy, and death.
Endovascular adjuncts are available in some centers, but the benefit for an individual patient is uncertain; prolonged aortic occlusion risks tissue injury.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Ensure reserved blood products and massive-transfusion capability are available. There is no standard PAS transfusion protocol in the cited review, so do not treat a fixed ratio or product count as universal.
Assess and treat hemorrhage and evolving coagulopathy in coordination with the clinical team; the sources do not provide PAS-specific transfusion triggers or thresholds.
Cell salvage may reduce allogeneic transfusion when suitable equipment and expertise are available; the source describes leukocyte filtration, washing, and centrifugation.
Balloon occlusion or embolization may be considered with interventional radiology, but evidence is controversial and does not establish which patients benefit.

The available PAS materials do not provide a specific PONV prevention regimen or drug dosing for this operation.

Neuraxial analgesia and conversion to general anesthesia require individualized assessment; the thrombocytopenia consensus emphasizes clinical context, bleeding history, airway risk, and patient preference.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined in the supplied summary as blood loss greater than 1000 mL after either vaginal or cesarean delivery. Causes are commonly organized as tone, trauma, tissue, and thrombin.

Priorities are rapid assessment and resuscitation alongside identifying and controlling the bleeding source. Anesthetic technique depends on hemodynamic status and whether coagulopathy makes neuraxial anesthesia inappropriate.

Prepare for rapid hemodynamic deterioration and evolving coagulopathy: clinical signs may be delayed, and fibrinogen can decrease rapidly during hemorrhage. Use repeated laboratory assessment and viscoelastic testing when available to guide hemostatic therapy.
After operative treatment, postoperative care should continue in intensive care until hemodynamically stable. The available sources do not establish a PPH-specific extubation or analgesia protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: PPH care is cause-directed rather than a single operation. Consider uterine atony, retained placenta, genital-tract trauma, and coagulation disorders; bleeding may also be concealed.

Management combines resuscitation with treatment of the cause. Depending on the clinical situation and available expertise, interventions described include placental removal, uterine tamponade or compression sutures, vessel ligation, interventional radiology, and hysterectomy.

sources.label: Management of major obstetric haemorrhage

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the trajectory of blood loss and hemodynamic status, while recognizing that pregnancy-related physiology can mask hypovolemia and that visual estimation is often inaccurate. Establish the suspected cause and the urgency and extent of anticipated intervention.

Obtain and repeat blood count and coagulation assessment, including fibrinogen; use viscoelastic testing if available. Results and clinical context inform hemostatic therapy, but the source does not establish a universal testing interval.
Consider placenta accreta spectrum and plan multidisciplinary resources when suspected; prior cesarean delivery, placenta previa, and previous uterine surgery are identified risk factors.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Secure large-bore intravenous access promptly; the PPH summary specifies at least two large-bore IVs. Activate the institution’s major-hemorrhage resources when clinically indicated and prepare the operating room if operative treatment is anticipated.

Use hemodynamic monitoring appropriate to severity; consider early invasive monitoring in major hemorrhage. Track urine output and repeat laboratory or viscoelastic assessment as the situation evolves.
The supplied PPH sources do not specify a preferred patient position or a universal central-access requirement; tailor room and monitoring decisions to the procedure and clinical condition.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose the anesthetic technique according to hemodynamic stability, coagulation status, urgency, and the existing neuraxial block. General anesthesia is preferred in hemodynamic instability; coagulopathy may contraindicate regional anesthesia.

For operative management, assess whether a functioning epidural can be extended or whether conversion to general anesthesia is needed. The source describes conversion as a consideration, not a fixed pathway.

The available PPH material does not specify airway devices, ventilation targets, induction drugs, or a universal rapid-sequence approach. Apply the selected anesthetic technique to the immediate clinical circumstances.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Resuscitation and source control proceed concurrently. Coordinate obstetric, anesthesia, transfusion, and procedural teams as hemorrhage severity and the underlying cause become clearer.
Uterotonics listed for PPH include oxytocin, carboprost, methylergonovine, and misoprostol. The supplied sources do not support a universal escalation sequence or drug regimen.

Tranexamic acid is supported for early intravenous use in PPH within three hours after birth; delayed administration reduces benefit. Refer to applicable local and specialty guidance for regimen details.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize that visible bleeding and conventional vital signs may lag behind clinically important volume loss. Reassess frequently for shock and concealed bleeding while investigating the source.

Major hemorrhage can produce consumption and dilutional coagulopathy. Large-volume crystalloid or colloid administration is associated with dilutional coagulopathy, acidosis, tissue edema, tissue hypoxia, and hypothermia.

Monitor for transfusion-related metabolic complications, including citrate toxicity, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, hypomagnesemia, and acidosis; the source advises monitoring and treatment but does not provide a PPH-specific troubleshooting algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: For major obstetric hemorrhage, follow a locally appropriate massive-transfusion protocol. The review describes packed red cells and FFP in a 1:1 ratio, with early platelet use, and cautions that large volumes of crystalloids or colloids can cause dilutional coagulopathy.

Use cross-matched blood when available; O-negative blood is an option if specific blood is unavailable and the patient is collapsing. Correct calcium during massive transfusion and monitor for related metabolic complications.

Fibrinogen can fall rapidly in hemorrhage. Assess it early and consider replacement with fibrinogen concentrate, FFP, or cryoprecipitate in the context of laboratory or viscoelastic findings and local protocol.

bullets: Analgesia should be individualized to the intervention, hemostatic status, and anesthetic technique. The supplied PPH review lists pain management but provides no regimen or technique-specific recommendations.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The obstetric-emergencies summary is an educational clinical summary, not a formal guideline or trial, and provides limited PPH-specific anesthesia detail. The major obstetric hemorrhage article is a broad review rather than a procedure-specific anesthesia study.

The sources present PPH thresholds at different levels of detail: one defines PPH as blood loss greater than 1000 mL after either delivery, while the review classifies 500–1000 mL as minor and more than 1000 mL as major. Interpret these definitions in the applicable clinical context.

Positioning, detailed airway and anesthetic drug regimens, and specific emergence protocols are not established in the PPH-specific material. These are evidence-scope limitations, not universal requirements for any one technique.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For labor analgesia and cesarean delivery, neuraxial anesthesia is generally favored when clinically appropriate; consider early anesthesiology involvement and neuraxial placement when laboring, with platelet status and the evolving clinical picture guiding selection.
Priorities are control of severe hypertension and seizure risk, careful assessment for thrombocytopenia or HELLP, and vigilance for airway difficulty, hypoxemia, and pulmonary edema.

If general anesthesia is required, prepare for a potentially difficult, edematous airway and blunt the hypertensive response to airway instrumentation; avoid treating any one airway device or drug regimen as universal.

Recovery requires continued attention to blood pressure, neurologic status, respiratory status, urine output, magnesium effects, and evolving postpartum disease; individualize monitoring to clinical condition and local obstetric pathways.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For labor analgesia, consider early neuraxial placement when there is no contraindication and platelet status has been assessed. An existing labor epidural may also provide an option if cesarean delivery becomes necessary.

For cesarean delivery, consider neuraxial anesthesia rather than general anesthesia when the maternal and procedural context permits. Technique selection remains individualized; severe disease alone does not establish a single anesthetic or delivery route.

Balance neuraxial hematoma risk against general-anesthesia airway and hemodynamic risks, considering bleeding history, coagulation concerns, airway assessment, maternal condition, and patient preference.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess current blood pressure and end-organ or neurologic features; review platelet trend, bleeding history, and possible HELLP or other coagulopathy. In HELLP, platelet counts may fall rapidly, so the timing of a count relative to neuraxial placement or catheter removal matters.

Use the SOAP thrombocytopenia consensus as a qualified decision framework, not a standalone cutoff: for a known hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, a count at or above 70,000 × 10⁶/L is described as likely low risk when there is no bleeding-history or DIC concern and neuraxial care is clinically indicated. Lower counts require individualized weighing of competing risks.

Promptly address persistent severe-range hypertension through the applicable obstetric pathway. Review magnesium use, renal function, respiratory status, and clinical signs of toxicity; the available sources support monitoring but not a universal anesthetic magnesium regimen.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use an obstetric operating environment with resuscitation equipment, difficult-airway resources, and appropriate support personnel readily available. For cesarean delivery, maintain uterine displacement, usually to the left, until delivery.

Apply monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and the patient’s condition. Basic anesthesia standards include continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

Arrange qualified fetal-heart-rate monitoring as appropriate to the delivery context, and monitor maternal magnesium effects, including respiratory status and reflexes, when magnesium is being administered.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia can avoid airway manipulation when appropriate. If general anesthesia is needed, anticipate airway edema and increased hypoxemia risk, particularly with obesity or pulmonary edema; plan skilled assistance and difficult-airway equipment.

Use a prepared airway strategy and prioritize safe, timely airway management. Video laryngoscopy is identified as an option in difficult-airway preparation; the evidence does not establish a mandatory device or endotracheal-tube size.

When general anesthesia is used, attenuate the hypertensive response to intubation while maintaining oxygenation. Select agents and technique for the individual clinical context rather than applying a fixed drug recipe.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Treat persistent severe hypertension promptly using the obstetric team’s pathway; stroke prevention is a central priority. The cited review names IV hydralazine, IV labetalol, and immediate-release oral nifedipine as commonly used agents.

Spinal sympathetic blockade and modest afterload reduction are described as generally suitable in preeclampsia, although hypotension can occur. Prevent and treat hemodynamic changes according to maternal status and the anesthetic technique.

Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis and treatment in severe-feature preeclampsia and eclampsia. Monitor clinical status and renal function for toxicity; use the relevant obstetric protocol rather than extrapolating a single anesthetic regimen.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For seizure, rapidly involve the obstetric team and prioritize maternal airway and oxygenation while following the established eclampsia protocol. The supplied review identifies magnesium sulfate as the cornerstone treatment but does not provide a universal anesthesia rescue sequence.

Consider pulmonary edema when respiratory status worsens; preeclampsia-related capillary leak and cardiac dysfunction are relevant concerns. Escalate assessment and care according to the clinical presentation rather than assuming hypovolemia from oliguria alone.

HELLP may progress rapidly, including postpartum; reassess maternal condition and laboratory findings when clinically indicated. New neurologic symptoms or concern for neuraxial hematoma warrant urgent evaluation.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Pulmonary edema is a material concern, but the supplied preeclampsia review does not establish a specific perioperative fluid regimen. Individualize fluid administration to the clinical and hemodynamic context; do not apply a universal volume target.

For neuraxial hypotension, use clinical assessment to guide treatment. Obstetric guidance allows fluid preload or coload but does not require delaying spinal anesthesia to administer a fixed volume; the enhanced-recovery fluid pathway is not a preeclampsia-specific regimen.

Assess bleeding and transfusion needs from the obstetric indication and clinical course. The available sources do not define a preeclampsia-specific transfusion protocol; platelet transfusion should not be presented as a routine prerequisite for neuraxial procedures.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia, neuraxial opioid analgesia is supported by obstetric guidance; select the technique and adjuncts for the patient and procedure rather than importing a routine regimen from an enhanced-recovery pathway.

The evidence does not support a blanket prohibition on postpartum NSAIDs for preeclampsia: the review reports proposed blood-pressure effects but inconclusive clinical-trial results. Coordinate analgesia with the obstetric team and current patient status.

Use an individualized multimodal approach and address nausea or vomiting as clinically relevant. General cesarean enhanced-recovery recommendations include antiemetic prophylaxis, but they are not a preeclampsia-specific medication prescription.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After general anesthesia, avoid an excessive hypertensive response during emergence and maintain attention to aspiration and pulmonary-edema risk. The supplied sources do not establish detailed extubation criteria specific to preeclampsia.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, apply quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery before extubation; this requirement does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Continue postanesthesia observation appropriate to maternal condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. For patients with preeclampsia, postpartum management focuses particularly on elevated blood pressure.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The preeclampsia-specific source is a clinical review, not a formal guideline or comparative trial. It supports broad priorities but does not establish a complete anesthesia protocol or specific fluid, positioning, monitoring, or emergence plan.

The neuraxial thrombocytopenia consensus is the most specific supplied society guidance for platelet-related decisions, but its authors describe limited high-quality evidence and imprecise, largely observational threshold evidence. Apply its qualifiers and clinical-context framework.

General obstetric anesthesia and monitoring standards supply relevant baseline principles, but they do not resolve all severe-preeclampsia-specific choices. Enhanced-recovery recommendations primarily concern scheduled cesarean delivery and should not be treated as a disease-specific protocol.
Timing of repeat platelet testing in preeclampsia generally remains uncertain outside the specified HELLP context; local pathways and clinical evolution remain important.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Cesarean delivery may be performed with neuraxial anesthesia or general anesthesia. Neuraxial techniques are preferred for most cesarean deliveries; for urgent delivery, an existing epidural may be used instead of initiating spinal or general anesthesia, depending on the circumstances.

The dominant priorities are timely assessment of maternal and fetal status, individualized choice of anesthetic, uterine displacement until delivery, and readiness to manage hypotension, hemorrhage, inadequate anesthesia, or airway difficulty.

General anesthesia may be appropriate for some urgent maternal or fetal circumstances. The available guidance gives examples but does not establish category-specific decision-to-delivery targets or a universal threshold for choosing general anesthesia.

Recovery priorities include ongoing assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and clinical condition, and effective multimodal analgesia. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Select the anesthetic according to maternal, obstetric, and fetal risks, patient preference, and anesthesiologist judgment. Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for most cesarean deliveries; for urgent cases, an established epidural is one option alongside spinal or general anesthesia.

General anesthesia may be appropriate in selected emergencies, including profound fetal bradycardia, uterine rupture, severe hemorrhage or abruption, and cord prolapse. These examples do not define a mandatory technique for every case with those diagnoses.
Maintain uterine displacement, usually to the left, until delivery regardless of anesthetic technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: When circumstances permit, perform a focused history and examination that includes maternal and anesthetic history, relevant obstetric history, baseline blood pressure, airway, heart and lung examination, and the back when neuraxial anesthesia is planned. Significant risks warrant obstetric-anesthesia communication.

Consider aspiration risk and prophylaxis in the context of urgency and patient-specific factors. The guideline describes aspiration prophylaxis before cesarean delivery but does not establish that an elective fasting interval can be achieved before nonelective surgery.

Base platelet testing and blood-bank preparation on clinical history, examination, anticipated hemorrhagic risk, and institutional policy; routine testing or cross-match is not specified for every healthy, uncomplicated parturient.

For thrombocytopenia, weigh the risks of neuraxial procedures against general anesthesia and other clinical risks, considering etiology, bleeding history, possible disseminated intravascular coagulation, airway assessment, and patient preference; the consensus does not support a single decision rule for all patients.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The labor-and-delivery operating suite should have resources comparable to a main operating suite, including equipment and personnel for failed intubation, inadequate anesthesia, hypotension, respiratory depression, and recovery after neuraxial or general anesthesia.
Establish and maintain IV access before neuraxial anesthesia or general anesthesia. The obstetric guideline does not require a fixed fluid volume before neuraxial anesthesia.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring for cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia and maintain uterine displacement until delivery. The available sources do not establish a procedure-specific comprehensive monitoring schedule for every emergency scenario.
Arrange qualified personnel other than the anesthesiologist attending the mother to be immediately available for newborn resuscitation.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Assess the airway and have a preformulated difficult-airway strategy and immediately available equipment for airway emergencies in the operative area. The supplied obstetric guideline does not prescribe one universal induction or intubation technique.

If tracheal intubation fails, the obstetric guideline identifies mask ventilation with cricoid pressure or a supraglottic airway as options; if ventilation or awakening is not possible, it identifies surgical airway as an escalation option. This is not a basis for a blanket prohibition on supraglottic airways.

When general anesthesia is selected, adapt airway and ventilation management to the clinical circumstances and available expertise. The provided sources do not specify a universal rapid-sequence protocol, device, or ventilation sequence for these cases.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Prevent and treat neuraxial-associated hypotension. IV fluids may be used, but initiation of spinal anesthesia should not be delayed to administer a fixed fluid volume. The guideline describes phenylephrine or ephedrine as possible treatments and qualifies phenylephrine consideration by maternal heart rate and clinical context.

For neuraxial anesthesia, assess and document the block before skin incision. If the patient reports pain, take the report seriously; when feasible, pause surgery while addressing discomfort and do not resume until the patient is comfortable.

Use prophylaxis for intraoperative nausea and vomiting as part of cesarean enhanced-recovery care. The cited review describes at least two prophylactic antiemetics with different mechanisms; medication selection should follow applicable local guidance and patient factors.

Choose uterotonic management according to the clinical situation and institutional practice. The supplied cesarean guidance supports using the lowest effective dose for adequate uterine tone but does not establish a single regimen for all urgent cases.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anticipate and respond to inadequate neuraxial anesthesia. Available options include neuraxial or systemic adjuvants and, when clinically necessary, conversion to general anesthesia; patient-reported pain should guide reassessment and support.

Maintain readiness for hemorrhagic emergencies. The obstetric guideline identifies type-specific or O-negative blood as acceptable in an emergency and says to consider cell salvage in intractable hemorrhage when banked blood is unavailable or refused, if available.

Treat airway failure as an immediate escalation problem: summon skilled help and use the institution’s difficult-airway strategy and available rescue resources. The guideline provides rescue options but does not establish a complete case-specific algorithm in the supplied text.

After neuraxial procedures, recognize suspected spinal-epidural hematoma as requiring urgent evaluation. The thrombocytopenia consensus emphasizes rapid identification, urgent MRI, and follow-up pathways rather than providing a routine treatment protocol.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Do not impose a fixed pre-spinal fluid volume or delay urgent neuraxial anesthesia to administer one. Fluid preloading or coloading may be used to reduce hypotension, with management individualized to the patient.

Maintain perfusion by promptly recognizing and addressing neuraxial hypotension; the obstetric guideline identifies vasopressors as treatment options and notes the importance of maternal heart rate when considering agent selection.
Prepare blood-product access according to hemorrhage risk and institutional practice. The sources do not provide a universal fluid total, transfusion threshold, or emergency-case blood-loss target.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia, consider neuraxial opioid analgesia rather than relying on intermittent parenteral opioids. Select the regimen according to the patient, technique, and applicable institutional guidance.

Use multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia according to ERAC protocols. Scheduled acetaminophen and NSAIDs with systemic opioids reserved for as-needed use are described in the low-risk example regimen; account for contraindications and disease-related organ dysfunction.
Use prophylactic measures to reduce intraoperative nausea and vomiting, including prevention and treatment of spinal-associated hypotension. Avoid treating pain with anxiolytics or hypnotics alone.

Discuss intraoperative pain and patient experience, and arrange appropriate follow-up for significant pain or distress. The supplied ASA statement does not give a follow-up schedule or a complete medication algorithm.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Use a PACU or equivalent recovery area after anesthesia unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Continue evaluation and monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Transport the patient with an anesthesia-care-team member who can communicate the anesthetic and surgical course to the receiving nurse; the team member remains until nursing responsibility is accepted.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are recommended. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The obstetric anesthesia guideline is a professional practice guideline, not an absolute requirement or outcome guarantee; its literature searches covered an earlier evidence period. Apply its recommendations with current institutional policy and clinical judgment.

The SOAP enhanced-recovery consensus concerns scheduled cesarean delivery, although it notes that many pathway elements may also apply to nonscheduled cases. Its example medication regimens should not be treated as emergency-specific prescriptions.
The supplied ASA pain statements describe relevant issues but their provided best-practice sections are blank; they do not establish a complete intervention, dosing, or follow-up pathway.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Blepharoplasty removes upper-lid skin, sometimes with muscle or fat; lower-lid surgery may remove skin or fat, reposition fat, or tighten the lid. Simple procedures may be done with local anesthesia; more extensive plans may need sedation or general anesthesia.

The dominant vision-threatening concern is postseptal bleeding causing retrobulbar hematoma. Meticulous hemostasis and prompt recognition of severe eye pain, proptosis, or visual symptoms are priorities.

Assess ocular surface and lid function before surgery; postoperative dry eye, lagophthalmos, and corneal exposure are relevant risks. Recovery assessment should include attention to vision and symptoms suggesting orbital compression.

Choose the anesthetic and recovery setting to the procedure and patient. If anesthesia or sedation is provided, follow applicable basic monitoring and postanesthesia-care standards; the available sources do not establish a single blepharoplasty-specific regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Upper-lid surgery commonly excises excess skin; orbicularis muscle or postseptal fat may also be addressed. Avoid assuming every operation includes these additional steps.
Lower-lid procedures vary: they may include skin or fat resection, fat repositioning, lid-cheek treatment, or lid tightening. The intended components affect surgical extent and anesthetic selection.

Simple skin-or-fat excision can be performed under local anesthesia. More extensive or combined surgery may require intravenous sedation or general anesthesia; selection is individualized rather than dictated by a single technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review ophthalmic and medical history, including baseline vision, dry-eye symptoms, visual obstruction, thyroid disease, diabetes, hypertension, steroid-treated inflammatory disease, and bleeding or clotting disorders. The procedure review recommends a full eye examination, including retinal examination.

Assess tear production and eyelid position/function when clinically relevant. Pre-existing dry-eye symptoms are important because they correlate with postoperative complications; visual-field testing can document obstruction from ptosis or dermatochalasis.

Reconcile antithrombotic therapy with the surgeon and relevant prescriber; do not infer a routine stop plan from these sources. One block review advises physician consultation before stopping anticoagulants, but that is not a blepharoplasty-specific medication-management protocol.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The reviewed blepharoplasty sources do not establish an intraoperative patient position or a procedure-specific room layout. Preoperative markings are described with the patient sitting upright in neutral gaze; this does not establish operative positioning.

For monitored anesthesia care, general anesthesia, or regional anesthesia, apply the applicable basic monitoring standards: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; determine blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.
With moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Local anesthesia, often with sedation, is an option for many oculoplastic procedures; the available evidence does not establish a natural-airway plan or a specific sedative regimen for blepharoplasty. If IV sedation is used, the procedure source calls for an anesthesia provider familiar with airway management.

General anesthesia is an option for complex or prolonged procedures and for patients unable to follow instructions or remain still. Airway-device selection remains individualized; the broad ophthalmic review describes supraglottic devices as widely used but does not make that a blepharoplasty-specific requirement.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify its position by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation or removal, or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location, perform continual end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis using a quantitative method.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Injection may be an uncomfortable phase; local anesthetic is used to permit surgery under local anesthesia, and the procedure review notes sedation during injection may be helpful. No drug or dose regimen is established by the blepharoplasty sources.

During postseptal fat resection, meticulous hemostasis is emphasized because bleeding in that compartment can cause retrobulbar hemorrhage and severe visual injury. Maintain clear communication with the surgeon about concerning bleeding or ocular symptoms.

Oculocardiac reflex is a possible response to ocular surgery or manipulation. The ophthalmic regional-anesthesia review advises that atropine or glycopyrrolate be available; it does not establish a blepharoplasty-specific prophylaxis or treatment sequence.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider retrobulbar hematoma after blepharoplasty when severe ocular pain, proptosis, or visual complaints arise; all features need not be present. This is a time-critical surgical emergency.

The described emergency treatment is orbital decompression with lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis. Escalate immediately to the ophthalmic surgeon/emergency team; the source emphasizes urgency but does not specify an anesthesia-led algorithm.

Other relevant complications include dry eye, lagophthalmos with corneal exposure, and lower-lid ectropion. Corneal lubrication is described for lagophthalmos and dry-eye management; persistent symptoms may require ophthalmology follow-up.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The procedure review provides no fluid-management guidance. Fluid choice and amount should therefore be individualized to the patient and anesthetic course; no fixed volume is supported here.
Meticulous hemostasis is emphasized, particularly during postseptal fat resection; bleeding in the postseptal compartment may cause retrobulbar hemorrhage and, in severe cases, blindness.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Surgeon-administered local anesthetic is part of the described approach. The procedure sources do not establish a postoperative analgesic regimen; avoid assuming routine opioids or a particular adjunct.

Ice packs are described as postoperative care to reduce swelling. The cited overview specifies application to the surgical site for three days; this is a surgical-care detail, not an anesthesia analgesia protocol.

No blepharoplasty-specific PONV regimen is provided. The adult ophthalmic review describes less postoperative nausea and vomiting with total intravenous anesthesia in general, but does not establish a case-specific anesthetic or prophylaxis prescription.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For general anesthesia in ophthalmic surgery, avoid coughing, straining, and retching at emergence where feasible because these can increase intraocular pressure. This is broad ophthalmic guidance, not a blepharoplasty-specific emergence protocol.

After anesthesia, use an appropriate PACU or equivalent setting, continue evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, and document the recovery period. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard, subject to its stated exceptions.

Include assessment for visual complaints and orbital hematoma symptoms in postoperative surveillance. Severe pain, proptosis, or visual complaints warrant urgent ophthalmic evaluation because decompression is emergent when orbital compartment syndrome is suspected.

bullets: The blepharoplasty chapter is a surgical-procedure overview, not an anesthesia reference; it explicitly omits anesthesia protocols, monitoring, positioning, and fluid or analgesic regimens. The 2009 overview gives brief anesthesia options and surgical details but lacks airway-management guidance, monitoring recommendations, and an anesthetic regimen. Its local/general choices should be interpreted as options, not a decision rule.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult cataract extraction is usually a short, day-case procedure using topical or other locoregional anesthesia; topical anesthesia is the most commonly used technique. The approach should reflect patient cooperation, comfort, and the procedure.

The dominant anesthetic concern is maintaining a still, communicative patient when awake techniques are used. Coughing, straining, or movement may complicate delicate eye surgery; general anesthesia is an option when the patient cannot cooperate or remain still.

Oculocardiac reflex and complications of ophthalmic blocks are relevant hazards. Have appropriate monitoring and expertise available for the selected technique, and recognize that no block is risk-free.

Recovery priorities are assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and procedure, eye-drop instructions, and vigilance for concerning visual symptoms, pain, or redness. Avoid assuming a specific recovery protocol from the available evidence.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The standard operation for a functionally significant cataract is removal of the crystalline lens and replacement with an artificial intraocular lens. The provided sources describe modern phacoemulsification, but do not establish detailed surgical steps.

Topical anesthesia, sometimes supplemented by intracameral local anesthetic, is a common approach. Selection should be collaborative and account for patient-specific comfort and the surgeon’s experience; other locoregional approaches are available.
Use an awake technique only when the patient can safely cooperate with the procedure. GA may be considered when cooperation or stillness is not achievable, or for complex or prolonged surgery.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess medical history, anxiety, comfort, and ability to communicate and cooperate with the proposed technique. Dementia, deafness, anxiety, or language barriers may affect whether an awake approach is feasible; age alone is not a reason to exclude GA.

Consider relevant systemic and ocular comorbidity and optimize when clinically indicated. Ocular conditions and anatomy may affect surgical or postoperative risk; these sources do not provide an anesthesia-specific risk score.

Routine preoperative tests are not supported for low-risk ophthalmic surgery absent a clinical indication. Testing should be directed by the history, examination, and whether the result could change management.

Fasting practice depends on the planned anesthetic and local policy: the review describes fasting for GA or deep sedation, while noting that many centers have removed fasting for routine locoregional procedures with minimal sedation. Do not apply a single fasting approach to every case.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Choose a regional anaesthetic technique according to the operation’s requirements for anaesthesia, ocular akinesia and, occasionally, paralysis of orbicularis oculi; regional anaesthesia is suitable only if the patient can lie flat and still.

For monitored anesthesia care or regional anesthesia, qualified anesthesia personnel must remain present and continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes are specified by the basic monitoring standard.

For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the method is precluded or invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. The cited standard does not prescribe a cataract-specific sampling setup.

When administering an ophthalmic block, the regional-anesthesia review calls for baseline monitoring, IV access, trained assistance, and availability of an anesthetist and airway/resuscitation equipment. This block-specific preparation should not be generalized into mandatory access for every topical-only case.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Topical and locoregional techniques are established approaches; the cited sources do not require an airway device for these techniques. Choose anesthetic depth to preserve cooperation when the procedure relies on an awake patient.

If GA is chosen, airway-device selection should reflect the patient and operation. The review describes supraglottic devices as widely used and reports fewer emergence problems, including coughing and straining, compared with tracheal intubation; it does not establish one device as universally preferred for cataract surgery.

During general anaesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. From endotracheal-tube or laryngeal-mask placement until removal or initiation of transfer, perform continual quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis. During moderate or deep sedation, continually observe qualitative clinical signs and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated by the patient, procedure or equipment.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Awake surgery depends on safe communication and cooperation. Discuss the patient’s ability to follow instructions and remain still before selecting the technique; the sources do not define a universal sedation target or a cataract-specific movement threshold.

Coughing, straining, and retching can increase intraocular pressure, including at emergence. Aim to avoid these responses through an individualized anesthetic approach; no single airway or anesthetic technique is established for all patients.

Oculocardiac reflex can occur during eye surgery and may cause marked bradycardia or hypotension. Keep the possibility in mind during ocular manipulation; the regional-anesthesia review says atropine or glycopyrrolate should be available, but provides no universal prophylaxis strategy.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize surgical complications described in the guideline, including anterior or posterior capsule rupture, dropped nucleus, zonular dialysis, iris or IOL damage, and suprachoroidal hemorrhage. The executive summary does not provide an anesthesia-specific management algorithm.

Ophthalmic blocks carry technique-specific risks. Sharp-needle blocks can cause rare serious injury, while sub-Tenon’s block avoids a sharp instrument but still has reported complications; select and perform a block only with appropriate expertise.

With suspected local-anesthetic toxicity or central spread after a block, recognize that severe neurologic and cardiovascular manifestations are possible and escalate for airway and cardiovascular support. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open-globe repair closes a full-thickness ocular wound. General anesthesia is preferred for repair when possible, but the supplied procedure sources do not establish a specific anesthetic or airway regimen.

The immediate ocular hazard is expulsion of intraocular contents. Minimize pressure on the eye and avoid manipulating prolapsed contents; surgical choices such as anterior-chamber reformation also have pressure and wound-leak trade-offs.

Stillness and avoidance of coughing, straining, or retching are important considerations: a general ophthalmic anesthesia review links these events at emergence with increased intraocular pressure, but does not define an open-globe-specific airway strategy.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia observation and attention to nausea or vomiting that could provoke pressure increases. The provided sources do not specify an open-globe-specific emergence, analgesia, or PONV regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open-globe injury (OGI) repair addresses a full-thickness corneal or scleral wound. The surgical review covers corneal-wound closure, anterior-chamber reformation, and scleral exploration and visualization.

For corneal wounds, the surgeon may reform the anterior chamber with filtered air or ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD). Air may deflate through a wound; OVD can maintain the chamber but may elevate IOP and obscure wound edges.
Scleral exploration may require conjunctival peritomy; posterior exploration and extraocular-muscle handling are surgical considerations rather than a basis for a universal anesthetic technique.

Consider pre- and intraoperative antibiotics as part of the surgical infection-prevention plan. The supplied sources do not establish a single regimen for every OGI.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Retinal-detachment repair may use vitrectomy, scleral buckling, or other vitreoretinal approaches. Adult vitrectomy is often performed with monitored anesthesia and a regional block; general anesthesia is selected when cooperation or procedural factors require it.
If intraocular gas is present, nitrous oxide must not be administered: diffusion into the gas can rapidly raise intraocular pressure and cause ocular morbidity.
Globe manipulation can provoke the oculocardiac reflex, including bradycardia and hypotension. Recognize a change promptly and communicate with the surgeon.

Recovery priorities include avoiding coughing, straining, and retching that can increase intraocular pressure, assessing for pressure elevation, and following the surgeon-prescribed postoperative position.

bullets: Retinal-detachment surgery encompasses different surgical approaches, including pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and scleral buckling. The operation and tamponade choice are surgical decisions; the supplied sources do not establish a single approach for this combined-procedure label.

For adult vitrectomy, monitored anesthesia with a retrobulbar block is a common approach in the procedure-specific review; general anesthesia is used selectively, including when the patient cannot cooperate. Discuss anticipated air travel and high-altitude exposure when the surgical team is choosing tamponade. Patients with intraocular gas should avoid air travel and other activities involving atmospheric-pressure shifts while gas remains.

Assess medical comorbidity and ability to cooperate, and select preoperative testing based on clinical indication rather than routine testing for all patients. Diabetes is relevant to perioperative assessment, but the sources do not establish a retinal-surgery-specific glucose target.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult strabismus surgery aims to realign the eyes by weakening, strengthening, or repositioning extraocular muscles. General anaesthesia is commonly used; selected cooperative adults may have topical or other limited techniques for suitable procedures.

Key intraoperative concerns are the oculocardiac reflex (OCR) during muscle traction and airway/ventilation factors that can increase its likelihood. Coordinate with the surgeon; stop traction if the reflex occurs and escalate treatment if it persists or is severe.

PONV is a relevant adult recovery issue, but the available evidence does not support describing it as uniformly the highest-risk procedure or prescribing one regimen for every adult. Use individualized prophylaxis and opioid-sparing analgesia.

Plan recovery around assessment of pain, nausea/vomiting, and alignment-related symptoms such as diplopia; diplopia is common early and often improves. Apply standard postanaesthesia monitoring and handoff requirements.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Surgery changes extraocular muscle force or position: recession weakens, resection strengthens, and transposition changes muscle position. Procedure complexity, laterality, prior surgery, and whether adjustable sutures are planned inform anaesthetic selection.

General anaesthesia is suitable across ages and commonly used, particularly for complex, repeated, or bilateral surgery. Topical anaesthesia is an option only for selected cooperative adults and suitable procedures; muscle traction and detachment can be uncomfortable.

Adjustable-suture cases may involve a later awake alignment assessment and adjustment under topical anaesthesia after anaesthetic effects resolve. Avoid assuming that a long-acting block is neutral for this pathway, as it may delay the second stage.

bullets: Clarify adult-onset symptoms and assess for underlying causes. The anaesthesia review specifically identifies thyroid function, bleeding disorders, and anticoagulant use as areas for assessment; thyroid eye disease should be stable and the patient euthyroid before surgery.

Review prior strabismus or other ocular surgery, relevant comorbidity, patient cooperation, and the planned technique. These factors may affect suitability for topical/regional techniques and the potential for difficult access or block spread.

Do not treat strabismus itself as an established malignant-hyperthermia risk factor or infer that volatile anaesthesia must be avoided. The review reports no association and describes volatile agents as commonly used in children; adult-specific comparative MH evidence is not established here.

bullets: Use standard anaesthesia monitoring appropriate to the technique. During anaesthesia, ECG is continuously displayed and blood pressure and heart rate are determined and evaluated at least every five minutes; use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Either a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) or endotracheal tube may be used for general anaesthesia. If LMA patency is in doubt, address the airway before surgery begins; mid-case exchange may contaminate the surgical field.

The review favours assisted or controlled ventilation over spontaneous breathing because hypercarbia can increase OCR risk. Maintain attention to oxygenation and ventilation and avoid factors that promote hypercarbia or hypoxaemia.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: OCR is triggered by pressure on the globe or traction on extraocular muscles and may present as bradycardia or arrhythmia. Adult reported incidence in the review is lower than in children, but the reflex remains clinically relevant.

Coordinate muscle traction with the surgeon. If OCR occurs, ask for immediate release of traction; this often restores rhythm. If it persists or recurs, anticholinergic treatment may be considered, with escalation guided by the clinical state.

OCR generally diminishes with repeated stimulation, but do not rely on this to prevent an event. The review reports that acute traction is more reflexogenic than gradual traction and that opioid and dexmedetomidine use can potentiate OCR.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For marked bradycardia, arrhythmia, or failure to recover promptly after traction stops, communicate with the surgeon and escalate anaesthetic management. The available sources describe possible severe rhythm disturbances but do not establish a single treatment sequence for every event.

Recognize that globe perforation, slipped or lost muscle, retinal detachment, and infection are reported surgical complications. Suspected globe injury or muscle loss requires prompt communication with the ophthalmic surgeon and reassessment of the anaesthetic approach if further exploration or repair is needed.
After surgery, diplopia is common in the first week and often resolves. Persistent or concerning visual symptoms warrant ophthalmic assessment rather than an assumption that symptoms are expected.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adults with an unstable ankle mortise and suitable soft tissues, ankle ORIF restores alignment and stability; fixation is fracture-specific and may involve plates, screws, or syndesmotic stabilization.

Neuraxial techniques may provide surgical anesthesia for foot/ankle surgery. Peripheral nerve blocks may be used for postoperative analgesia or as adjuncts to general or neuraxial anesthesia; a popliteal sciatic block is commonly combined with a saphenous block for foot/ankle surgery. Choose an approach based on patient and procedural factors; the supplied review does not establish a preferred approach for ankle ORIF.

The dominant case-specific concerns are soft-tissue condition and wound healing, neurovascular integrity, and comorbidities such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy. Timing should reflect the soft-tissue envelope rather than a fixed interval.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and reassessment of the operated foot’s neurovascular status, swelling, and splint. Regional analgesia may support postoperative pain control, but motor block and safe mobility require attention.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ORIF is generally selected for an unstable mortise in a patient fit for surgery when the soft tissues are favorable. The operative aim is anatomical restoration with stable fixation; fracture pattern determines the construct.

Fixation options described include plates and screws for fibular fractures, fracture-specific medial or posterior malleolar fixation, and screws or tightropes for syndesmotic diastasis. These are surgical options, not a universal construct.

Intraoperative imaging is used to assess alignment and syndesmotic stability; the described options include the Hook (Cotton) test and external-rotation stress views. Posterior malleolar anatomy may require preoperative CT for operative planning.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess fracture pattern, mortise stability, syndesmotic involvement, skin and swelling, and relevant comorbidities. Diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy can adversely affect healing; assess vascular status and baseline neurologic function.

Fracture blisters and substantial swelling signal soft-tissue risk. Definitive fixation may be delayed while swelling subsides; the evidence supports judging timing by tissue condition, not applying a fixed wait.

Complete individualized VTE risk assessment, including prior DVT, immobilization or nonweight bearing, and other relevant patient risk factors; sources do not support a universal prophylaxis regimen for all ankle-fracture patients.

For pelvic injury, anterior external fixation can reduce pelvic volume and bleeding, but conventional anterior fixation does not control posterior pelvic instability. Coordinate fixation with the broader hemorrhage-control strategy.

bullets: Perform repeated clinical assessment for compartment syndrome and neurovascular change. The ED article specifically identifies compartment syndrome and neurapraxia as monitoring concerns; it does not set a universal check frequency.

Prevent pin-related soft-tissue injury by avoiding skin tension and contact between bars, clamps or pins and the skin. Avoid pin paths that cross joints or damage structures; the review also identifies infection and neurovascular injury among important complications.

Monitor skin for blistering and pressure points and reassess readiness for definitive fixation. Pin care and conversion timing depend on clinical circumstances; the review reports no consensus for a standardized pin-infection prevention protocol.

Regional anesthesia may provide surgical anesthesia or postoperative analgesia. Choice requires weighing block coverage and duration, patient factors, and possible motor effects against recovery needs.

Priorities during anesthesia are appropriate monitoring and technique-specific vigilance. The supplied sources do not establish hardware-removal-specific physiologic targets or a dominant procedural hazard for adult orthopedic cases.
