sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum, ventilation & perfusion
bullets: For minimally invasive exposure, anticipate reduced respiratory compliance and altered venous return. Secure the airway and access, adjust lung-protective ventilation and coordinate insufflation when instability occurs.
Use individualized fluid and blood replacement for perfusion; an older recommendation for liberal fluid therapy is not a universal modern insulinoma requirement.

sections.title: After removal: glucose can rise, but cure is not immediate proof
bullets: Reduce/titrate dextrose according to measured glucose and ongoing need. Transient hyperglycemia may follow removal and can require carefully titrated insulin; avoid overshoot and subsequent hypoglycemia.

Rebound hyperglycemia is an unreliable stand-alone marker of complete tumor removal. Follow the surgical/endocrine plan for assessment of residual disease, especially with multifocal or MEN1-associated tumors.

Match anesthesia to enucleation, distal/other pancreatic resection or Whipple; a neuroendocrine label does not define surgical magnitude.

sections.title: Functioning versus nonfunctioning PanNET
bullets: Review hormone assays, symptoms, treatment response, metastatic burden and hereditary context. Hormone syndrome and anatomic operation are separate axes of risk.
Nonfunctioning tumors can still require major pancreatic surgery; conversely a small functional tumor can create major metabolic instability before any incision.

sources.label: ENETS: functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor guidance (2023)
ENETS: perioperative neuroendocrine tumor consensus (2017)

sections.title: VIPoma: diarrhea, depletion and acidosis
bullets: Secretory diarrhea may produce severe dehydration, hypokalemia and bicarbonate-loss metabolic acidosis. Stabilize volume/electrolytes and the hormonal syndrome before elective surgery when feasible.

ENETS supports somatostatin-analogue therapy for preoperative stabilization and IV fluid/electrolyte treatment when diarrhea is severe. Quantify ongoing losses rather than replacing only the presenting deficit.

sources.label: ENETS: perioperative neuroendocrine tumor consensus (2017)

sections.title: Gastrinoma: acid suppression and aspiration context
bullets: Maintain effective PPI therapy through the perioperative period, using an appropriate route when oral therapy is interrupted. Abrupt withdrawal can provoke serious rebound acid-related complications.

Assess ulcer disease, bleeding, vomiting or obstruction and the resulting aspiration/volume risk. Continue postoperative acid suppression through the specialist plan; curative-intent surgery is not an automatic reason to stop immediately.

sources.label: ENETS: functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor guidance (2023)
ENETS: perioperative neuroendocrine tumor consensus (2017)

sections.title: Glucagonoma: metabolic, nutritional and VTE risk
bullets: Assess hyperglycemia, weight loss, skin disease and nutritional deficits. Specialist therapy may include somatostatin analogues and targeted nutritional support rather than treating the tumor as only a glucose problem.
Plan thromboprophylaxis for increased DVT/PE risk while respecting bleeding and neuraxial timing. Do not copy historical “high-dose heparin” wording into a universal prophylactic dose.

sources.label: ENETS: functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor guidance (2023)
ENETS: perioperative neuroendocrine tumor consensus (2017)

sections.title: Insulinoma and less common hormone syndromes
bullets: For insulinoma, use frequent glucose testing, planned dextrose support and the dedicated insulinoma reference. Somatostatin analogues can worsen hypoglycemia in some patients.

Ectopic ACTH secretion may cause severe hypercortisolism; GHRH secretion can cause acromegaly; PTHrP secretion can cause hypercalcemia. Stabilize the actual syndrome with endocrinology rather than giving a generic “NET premedication.”

sources.label: ENETS: functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor guidance (2023)

sections.title: Carcinoid syndrome is not synonymous with every PanNET
bullets: If a mediator syndrome such as flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm or carcinoid heart disease is suspected, evaluate it explicitly. Do not automatically apply a carcinoid-crisis regimen to every pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.

Perioperative octreotide practices and evidence vary; coordinate a syndrome-specific crisis/rescue plan. The older ENETS consensus acknowledges limited evidence and no universal prophylactic regimen, so prophylaxis must not be presented as a guarantee against crisis.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

sections.title: Exposure, airway and blood preparation
bullets: Clarify enucleation, distal/central pancreatectomy, pancreaticoduodenectomy or a more extensive resection and any vascular involvement. Obtain an approach-specific airway, access, blood and postoperative plan.
Account for prolonged abdominal exposure or pneumoperitoneum/robot docking. Reassess perfusion and ventilation as position and insufflation change.

sections.title: Fluids, glucose and electrolyte trending
bullets: Replace measured volume/electrolyte losses while protecting organ perfusion and avoiding overload. Repeated potassium, acid-base and glucose assessment should follow the dominant syndrome and operative course.

Communicate tumor manipulation/removal because hormone output and treatment requirements can change. Update infusions according to measurements rather than continuing pre-resection rates automatically.

sections.title: Analgesia and anticoagulation coordination
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia adapted to incision and surgical magnitude. Thoracic epidural, wound-catheter or other regional options require assessment of coagulation, hemodynamic reserve and thromboprophylaxis timing.
Treat pain and nausea while avoiding excessive sedation that masks metabolic or respiratory deterioration.

sections.title: After resection: hormone and pancreatic consequences
bullets: Continue syndrome-directed glucose, electrolyte and volume surveillance. A biochemical change does not establish complete oncologic clearance.
After major pancreatic resection, monitor for fistula, hemorrhage, infection, delayed gastric emptying and glucose/pancreatic-function problems according to the surgical pathway.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: This is a cross-cutting surgical-planning reference: more than one active hormone disorder may matter even when only one organ is being operated on.
MEN1 classically involves parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic/duodenal neuroendocrine tumors.
MEN2A includes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid disease; MEN2B has a different phenotype without the same increased parathyroid risk.
Exclude functioning pheochromocytoma before relevant surgery in MEN2; when present, coordinate treatment before thyroidectomy to avoid catecholamine crisis.

sections.title: Start with a hormone and procedure inventory
bullets: List the planned operation, known tumors, biochemical activity, prior resections and current replacement. The organ on the booking form may not be the dominant anesthetic hazard.
Coordinate endocrinology, anesthesia and the operating team; genetics/surveillance findings can change sequencing and the need for bilateral or tissue-preserving surgery.

sources.label: NCI PDQ: genetics of endocrine and neuroendocrine neoplasias (2024)

sections.title: MEN1: parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic physiology
bullets: Assess calcium/volume/renal effects of hyperparathyroidism, pituitary hormone excess or deficiency and functional pancreatic/duodenal tumor syndromes. Multiple abnormalities can coexist.
Do not assume a previous parathyroid or pancreatic operation eliminates recurrence/multifocal risk. Review the current surveillance and biochemical status.

sections.title: MEN2A: medullary thyroid, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid
bullets: Review medullary thyroid cancer status, catecholamine screening and calcium/parathyroid disease. A thyroid operation should not proceed on the assumption that its airway risks are the only anesthesia concern.
Pheochromocytoma may be bilateral or discovered before thyroid disease. Confirm the actual biochemical results and preparation rather than relying only on absence of hypertension.

sources.label: GeneReviews: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (2023)

sections.title: MEN2B is not the MEN2A triad
bullets: MEN2B includes medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma with features such as mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus and gastrointestinal ganglioneuromatosis. Clinically significant parathyroid disease is not increased as it is in MEN2A.
For this adult library, assess current airway, gastrointestinal and endocrine consequences. Pediatric prophylactic-thyroidectomy age recommendations are outside this anesthesia reference’s scope.

sources.label: GeneReviews: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (2023)

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma screening and surgical sequence
bullets: GeneReviews recommends plasma-free or urine-fractionated metanephrine assessment before surgery in MEN2 phenotypes. If functioning pheochromocytoma is identified, adrenal treatment should precede thyroidectomy when feasible within the coordinated plan.

Life-threatening urgent surgery needs individualized expert management, not a simplified elective sequence. A known catecholamine tumor requires an explicit preparation and rescue strategy even when another organ is the surgical target.

sections.title: Catecholamine preparation and induction
bullets: When functional PPGL is present, establish specialist-directed alpha blockade and appropriate volume preparation; beta blockade, if needed, follows adequate alpha blockade. Review cardiomyopathy and relevant provoking medications.
Prepare for induction/manipulation hypertension and post-resection hypotension, with appropriate arterial/access monitoring and titratable drugs. The dedicated PPGL case gives the operational detail.

sections.title: Prior adrenal or pituitary surgery and replacement
bullets: Review remaining adrenal tissue, cortisol reserve, thyroid replacement and desmopressin needs. Previous operations can create deficiencies in addition to the syndrome’s tumor-related hormone excess.
If adrenal and thyroid axes are deficient, ensure glucocorticoid coverage before new thyroid replacement. Document postoperative dose adjustment and monitoring responsibilities.

sections.title: Calcium and renal reserve
bullets: Assess symptomatic hypercalcemia, hydration and renal function when parathyroid disease is present. After parathyroid removal, plan for hypocalcemia/hungry bone surveillance rather than assuming the preoperative calcium problem simply disappears.
Protect fragile bone/skin and consider renal function when selecting medications, fluids and analgesia. Match the plan to actual manifestations, not the syndrome name alone.

sections.title: Pancreatic tumors, fasting and glucose
bullets: Insulinoma requires fasting protection and frequent glucose checks; gastrinoma requires uninterrupted effective acid suppression; VIPoma requires volume/electrolyte stabilization. These are not interchangeable NET pathways.
Coordinate the expected post-resection change with the team and adjust support to measured response. Multifocal MEN1 disease requires follow-up beyond an immediate glucose or symptom change.

sections.title: Airway and monitoring follow the actual procedure
bullets: Use the thyroid/parathyroid, adrenal, pituitary or pancreatic reference for procedure-specific airway, position, exposure and recovery details. MEN is an additional risk map, not one standard anesthetic technique.
Keep rescue priorities visible: compressive airway/hematoma risk, catecholamine instability, cortisol deficiency and water/glucose/electrolyte disturbances may overlap.

bullets: State which hormone disorders were active, what was removed, replacement given and what must be monitored overnight. A technically successful operation does not resolve all MEN-associated disease.

Ensure coordinated endocrine/genetic surveillance continues and the patient has a clear medication and emergency plan. Avoid interpreting a negative test from an earlier operation as permanent clearance for future surgery.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: CRT patients often have advanced HF; maintain perfusion and avoid excessive myocardial depression during a potentially longer implant.
Local anesthesia with MAC is common; GA may be appropriate for patient tolerance, complexity, airway or testing needs.
Identify the exact system and dependence; external pacing/defibrillation must remain available throughout.
Assess capture, rhythm, pocket/access complications and the final device program before leaving monitored care.

sections.title: Patient physiology and implant plan
bullets: Review indication, rhythm, LV/RV function, HF status, medications, infection risk and ability to lie flat. Clarify first implant, upgrade, revision or replacement.
Confirm the planned device and lead route. Transvenous, leadless and subcutaneous systems have different access and analgesic requirements.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)
AHA scientific statement: periprocedural CIED care (2024)

sections.title: Pacing dependence, magnet response & EMI
bullets: Review underlying rhythm, interrogation, battery status, pacing dependence and the exact pacemaker/ICD/CRT or leadless model. Dependence and adequacy of the underlying rhythm may change with anesthetic depth.

An ICD magnet generally suspends tachyarrhythmia therapy without creating asynchronous pacing. Pacemaker magnet responses are model-specific; Micra has no magnet response. Coordinate reprogramming when dependence, EMI or inaccessible/sterile generator position makes a magnet unsuitable.

Use bipolar cautery or short monopolar bursts where possible and direct the return-current path away from the device. While therapies are disabled, external pacing/defibrillation must remain immediately available.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement: periprocedural CIED care (2024)

sections.title: Sedation, GA and restricted head access
bullets: Titrate sedation to local anesthesia, stimulation and cardiac reserve. Avoid hypoventilation/hypercarbia and unplanned deep sedation beneath drapes.
GA may be chosen for prolonged/complex work or painful tunneling/testing, but is not mandatory for every implant. Arrange prompt conversion if ventilation, cooperation or hemodynamics fail.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Pocket, local anesthesia & bleeding
bullets: Coordinate effective local infiltration and titrated systemic analgesia rather than using deep sedation to compensate for inadequate local anesthesia. Track the total local-anesthetic exposure when additional blocks/infiltration are used.

Review the anticoagulant/antiplatelet plan and pocket-hematoma/infection risk with EP. Do not independently bridge or interrupt therapy; reconcile postoperative instructions with actual bleeding and thrombotic risk.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)
Oxford University Hospitals: pacemaker generator replacement (patient information)

sections.title: CRT: lead placement and biventricular function
bullets: Clarify CRT-P versus CRT-D and the intended resynchronization strategy. Additional lead placement can prolong the procedure in patients with poor reserve; anticipate hypotension and difficult supine tolerance.
After implantation, confirm lead function and the prescribed pacing configuration; a QRS appearance alone does not establish adequate resynchronization or perfusion.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)
AHA scientific statement: periprocedural CIED care (2024)

sections.title: Hemodynamic and mechanical complications
bullets: Unexpected hypotension, chest symptoms or dyspnea warrants assessment for arrhythmia, perforation/tamponade, bleeding and procedure-related thoracic complications rather than sedation alone.
Treat severe bradycardia/loss of capture promptly using the agreed pacing contingency. Confirm mechanical perfusion with plethysmography or arterial pressure when ECG is obscured by EMI.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)
AHA scientific statement: periprocedural CIED care (2024)

sections.title: Comfort and respiratory recovery
bullets: Reassess pocket/tunneling pain and use the least sedating effective regimen for patient reserve. Significant HF, OSA and frailty increase the consequences of excessive systemic sedation.
Check wound/pocket swelling and access sites; unexpected severe pain or breathlessness requires evaluation, not simply more opioid.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Device restoration & monitored handoff
bullets: Document final device interrogation and programming, including sensing, capture and any changed therapies. Restore an appropriate pacing program and re-enable ICD tachytherapies before leaving a monitored setting.

Keep external rescue capability and monitoring until restoration is confirmed. Major events, external defibrillation, suspected reset or device malfunction warrant interrogation and communication with the device team.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement: periprocedural CIED care (2024)

sections.title: Room, airway access & team briefing
bullets: Apply operating-room standards to anesthesia in the EP/hybrid lab. Before draping, confirm oxygen, suction, airway equipment, emergency assistance, radiation protection and the route for urgent transfer or conversion.

Position the airway, breathing circuit, IV extensions and defibrillator connections so they remain accessible around the imaging equipment. Agree how the table and drapes will move if ventilation or resuscitation is required.

bullets: For anesthesia care, continuously assess oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Use ECG, pulse oximetry and blood pressure/heart rate at least every five minutes; moderate/deep sedation requires exhaled CO₂ monitoring unless precluded or invalidated.

Choose invasive pressure monitoring and additional access for ventricular dysfunction, expected instability, repeated induced arrhythmia or major procedural risk, not simply because the case is in a cath lab. Confirm a perfusing pulse rather than relying on an ECG pacing spike.

bullets: Perimembranous defects lie near conduction tissue. Monitor for new AV or bundle-branch block during placement and in recovery; external/temporary pacing must be available.

Consider tamponade, major access/retroperitoneal bleeding, coronary compromise, acute valve dysfunction, device malposition, arrhythmia and ventricular failure. Low ETCO₂ or rising venous pressure is a clue, not a diagnostic requirement; activate drainage, pacing/defibrillation, blood, surgical or circulatory-support rescue as indicated.

sections.title: Conduit rupture and vascular injury

sections.title: RV protection and pulmonary circulation
bullets: Assess RV function, pulmonary hypertension, venous congestion and the capacity to tolerate induction and positive-pressure ventilation. Maintain systemic perfusion without indiscriminate preload loading.

bullets: Confirm the landing zone, access and device. Native-valve/MAC, valve-in-ring and valve-in-valve anatomy have different anchoring, leak and obstruction risks.

sections.title: LVOTO: prevention is planned before induction
bullets: Anterior leaflet displacement and the implanted valve can narrow the neo-LVOT. Risk assessment is multidimensional; do not use one historic area threshold as a universal clearance rule.

sections.title: GA, TEE and access route
bullets: GA with TEE/fluoroscopy is typical. Clarify transseptal versus transapical access and how the latter changes surgical exposure, ventilation, analgesia and rescue needs.

bullets: Confirm the procedure/device-specific heparin and ACT protocol, sampling responsibility and any contraindication or alternative anticoagulant. AF-ablation or CPB targets should not be copied indiscriminately into structural cases.

sections.title: Pacing, deployment and valve position
bullets: Coordinate any rapid-pacing or ventilation requirements before deployment. Valve depth affects LVOT risk, paravalvular leak and anchoring.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Failed-bioprosthesis valve-in-valve treatment needs the exact prior valve model and anatomy, not simply the standard native-AS pathway.
Displaced old leaflets can obstruct coronaries directly or by sinus sequestration; CT planning and a coronary-protection strategy are central.
Anticipate rapid pacing, conduction disturbance, residual gradient and hemodynamic collapse.
The anesthetic may be sedation or GA, but emergency airway, coronary and surgical rescue must be planned before deployment.

sections.title: Prior prosthesis and failure mode
bullets: Confirm the old valve’s model, true internal diameter, leaflet design and stenosis/regurgitation mechanism, along with LV/RV function and coronary anatomy.
Surgical-bioprosthesis ViV and redo TAVI-in-TAVI have distinct frame/commissural and coronary-access issues. Do not assume one planning template fits both.

sections.title: Coronary obstruction and sinus sequestration
bullets: Assess coronary height, sinus/STJ dimensions, virtual valve-to-coronary and valve-to-STJ distances with the imaging team. Externally mounted leaflets and stentless designs may increase risk.
A displaced leaflet can seal the sinus at the STJ even without direct ostial coverage. Risk is not fully captured by a single CT measurement.

sections.title: Coronary protection and leaflet modification
bullets: Confirm whether protected coronary access/stenting or BASILICA is planned. These are expert preventive strategies with limitations, not guaranteed protection.
Occlusion can occur after removal of a protection wire. Communicate timing, hemodynamics and the plan for immediate coronary intervention if ischemia appears.

sources.label: Coronary obstruction after TAVR: prevention and ViV risk (2024 review)

sections.title: Anesthetic technique and monitoring
bullets: Select sedation versus GA based on access, imaging, patient tolerance and complexity. Keep airway access and rapid conversion feasible under drapes.
Maintain coronary/systemic perfusion according to the actual failed-valve physiology; a regurgitant prosthesis is not identical to isolated severe AS.

sections.title: Rapid pacing and residual gradients
bullets: Confirm reliable pacing before deployment or postdilatation and backup pacing for postimplant block.
Small prior valves may leave high gradients. Ring fracture/postdilatation may change coronary risk and requires renewed team awareness rather than being viewed as a trivial extra step.

sections.title: Sudden hypotension: procedural emergency differential
bullets: Announce deterioration and ask the operator to stop the provoking step when feasible. Check rhythm, ventilation, perfusion and access; use immediate echo/angiography according to the suspected cause rather than labeling every event “anesthetic hypotension.”

Consider tamponade, major access/retroperitoneal bleeding, coronary compromise, acute valve dysfunction, device malposition, arrhythmia and ventricular failure. Low ETCO₂ or rising venous pressure is a clue, not a diagnostic requirement; activate drainage, pacing/defibrillation, blood, surgical or circulatory-support rescue as indicated.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ICE is an imaging strategy, not a separate intervention; it can support selected structural procedures without an esophageal probe.
It may facilitate sedation and avoid GA/TEE, but does not guarantee that sedation is appropriate for the patient or procedure.
Additional venous access and intracardiac manipulation carry bleeding/perforation risks; operator expertise and image quality matter.
Maintain a defined escalation pathway for inadequate images, intolerance, hemodynamic collapse or conversion to TEE/GA.

sections.title: Which procedures and which imaging task?
bullets: Define whether ICE will guide septal puncture, PFO/ASD closure, LAAO, valve assessment or complex mitral/tricuspid work. Required resolution and catheter position differ.
TEE remains a major reference technique, especially for complex valvular work; ICE may supplement rather than replace it.

sources.label: SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: Patient and center selection
bullets: Consider anatomy, thrombus concern, renal/contrast constraints, tolerance of lying still and sedation, and availability of trained operators/imaging staff.
A TEE contraindication may favor ICE, but difficult anatomy or inability to tolerate sedation can still favor GA with an alternate imaging plan.

sources.label: SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: Sedation is a plan, not a benefit assumed
bullets: If using moderate/deep sedation, maintain continuous ventilation assessment/capnography and an accessible airway-rescue route.

sources.label: SCAI ICE position statement (2025)

sections.title: ICE access and catheter hazards
bullets: Additional venous puncture, catheter manipulation and imaging positions can cause vascular injury or cardiac perforation. Monitor access and effusion throughout.

sections.title: Image quality and expertise
bullets: 2D and 3D ICE have different capabilities. Complex valve work may need a dedicated imaging physician and a two-operator workflow.

bullets: For septal closure assess residual shunt/device position; for LAAO assess seating/seal; for valves assess gradients, regurgitation and adjacent structures.
